The US and UK governments' no-ransom policy — which meant their nationals (James Foley, Steven Sotloff, David Haines, Alan Henning, and others) were executed when no ransom was paid — was explicitly presented by ISIS as evidence of Western callousness toward its own people. The executions, filmed and released through ISIS's media infrastructure, generated precisely the global media attention that ISIS intended.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 26: The Caliphate — State-Building in Real Time (2014–2015)
subheading: The Administrative Structure
text: ISIS's media operation was the most sophisticated information warfare capability deployed by any non-state actor in history to that point. Its primary media production wing — the Al Hayat Media Center — produced content in English, French, German, Russian, Turkish, and Indonesian, among other languages. Its flagship English-language magazine Dabiq was produced to a professional editorial and design standard comparable to commercial publications. Its video production, including the execution videos that dominated Western media coverage, was technically sophisticated: multiple camera angles, professional editing, musical scores, and subtitled translations. The execution videos require analytical treatment rather than pure condemnation. Their production and release were strategic communications decisions, not merely expressions of sadism. The burning alive of Jordanian pilot Moaz al-Kasasbeh (February 2015) — filmed in a cage, produced with cinematic deliberateness — was designed to achieve specific effects: shock Western audiences into overestimating ISIS's military invincibility, provoke Jordan into escalatory military action that ISIS could then present as crusader aggression against Muslims, and demonstrate to potential recruits that the caliphate was willing to commit to total war. Whether these calculations were accurate or counterproductive is a separate question. They were calculations.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 26: The Caliphate — State-Building in Real Time (2014–2015)
subheading: The Administrative Structure
text: The social media recruitment operation functioned through a combination of official ISIS accounts (repeatedly suspended, repeatedly reconstituted on new platforms) and a distributed network of pro-ISIS sympathisers who amplified content, provided personal recruitment contacts, and operated as entry points into the encrypted communications environment where actual recruitment proceeded. The specific platform migration — from Twitter to Ask. fm to Telegram to Signal — tracked the successive attempts by major platforms to limit ISIS content; each expulsion moved the network to a less monitored environment while maintaining its recruitment reach.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 26: The Caliphate — State-Building in Real Time (2014–2015)
subheading: The Administrative Structure
text: The specific theological position — that Yazidi women could be enslaved because Yazidis were polytheists not entitled to the protected status of People of the Book — was published in ISIS's Dabiq magazine in an article titled "The Return of the Slave Girls" and elaborated in a Research and Fatwa Department pamphlet on the rules of slavery. The pamphlet — distributed to ISIS fighters and subsequently captured by Iraqi forces — addressed questions including the permissibility of intercourse with pre-pubescent slaves, the conditions for resale, and the theological status of a slave's offspring. The scale of implementation: approximately 6,417 Yazidi women and girls were captured in the August 2014 Sinjar assault and subsequent operations. They were taken to holding centres in Mosul, Raqqa, and other cities, assessed and priced according to age (a girl aged 1–9 was priced at 200,000 dinars; a woman aged 20–30 at 130,000 dinars; a woman aged 30–40 at 75,000 dinars — prices documented in an ISIS internal distribution document captured in 2014). They were distributed to ISIS fighters as rewards, sold in markets in Mosul and Raqqa, and traded as the ISIS economy evolved. The survivor testimony collected by Yazda and by journalist Nadia Murad (herself a survivor, who became a UN Goodwill Ambassador and Nobel Peace Prize laureate) provides the detailed human record of what this institutional programme meant in practice. This testimony is the most comprehensive human rights documentation produced from ISIS's territory and stands as evidence of a crime against humanity conducted with organisational deliberateness.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 26: The Caliphate — State-Building in Real Time (2014–2015)
subheading: The Administrative Structure
text: The November 13, 2015 Paris attacks — coordinated attacks on the Bataclan concert hall, bars, restaurants, and the Stade de France that killed 130 people and wounded more than 400 — were the most lethal terrorist attacks in France's history and the clearest demonstration that ISIS's external operations had reached the capacity for strategic impact. They were followed by the March 2016 Brussels bombings (32 dead), the July 2016 Nice truck attack (86 dead), the 2016 Berlin market truck attack (12 dead), the 2017 Manchester arena bombing (22 dead, primarily children and teenagers), and multiple smaller attacks across Europe, North America, and Australia.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 26: The Caliphate — State-Building in Real Time (2014–2015)
subheading: The Administrative Structure
text: ISIS's external attack strategy was explicitly articulated in its communications: it was designed to provoke Western states into military escalation in Muslim-majority countries, to pressure European governments into abandoning their multicultural frameworks, and to polarise Muslim minorities in Western countries between loyalty to their societies and loyalty to the Caliphate. The call in ISIS's magazine Rumiyah for attacks on "soft targets" using vehicles and knives — weapons that required no arms acquisition or technical expertise — was a deliberate lowering of the operational barrier to participation that multiplied the attack capacity without requiring ISIS to supply weapons or training.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 26: The Caliphate — State-Building in Real Time (2014–2015)
subheading: The Administrative Structure
text: The military escalation ISIS sought — it explicitly wanted Western ground troops in the caliphate's territory, which it assessed would generate Muslim mobilisation — did not occur at the scale it anticipated; the US-led coalition chose Kurdish and Iraqi proxy ground forces over direct Western combat deployment. The European political polarisation ISIS anticipated did occur, contributing to the electoral rise of right-wing nationalist parties — Le Pen in France, Wilders in the Netherlands, the AfD in Germany — whose platforms of anti-Muslim restrictions aligned with ISIS's narrative that Western governments were at war with Islam. Whether this was a successful strategy for ISIS's stated objectives is a different question from whether it was a successful strategy for disrupting Western liberal democracy — it may have been both simultaneously, in different registers.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 26: The Caliphate — State-Building in Real Time (2014–2015)
subheading: The Administrative Structure
text: The theological extremism that ISIS applied internally — to its own members — produced its own contradictions. ISIS members were killed for offences including smoking, listening to music, wearing certain clothes, and insufficient mosque attendance. The organisation was simultaneously attempting to govern a civilian population in which these activities were universal and to maintain an ideologically pure military organisation in which they were forbidden. The enforcement of ideological purity on the civilian population — through the religious police (hisba) who patrolled markets, enforced dress codes, and destroyed musical instruments — generated the resentment that ISIS governance consistently produced beneath the surface of apparent compliance.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 26: The Caliphate — State-Building in Real Time (2014–2015)
subheading: The Administrative Structure
text: Defection from the Caliphate became increasingly common from 2015 onward as the military situation deteriorated. The specific accounts of ISIS defectors — collected by researchers including Audrey Alexander at George Washington University and by journalists Rukmini Callimachi and Hassan Hassan — provide detailed pictures of an organisation whose ideological coherence was maintained partly by coercion (attempting to leave was punishable by death) rather than purely by conviction. The gap between the Caliphate as experienced by recruits who arrived and the Caliphate as they had imagined it from ISIS media was frequently large: the bureaucratic mundanity, the internal power struggles, the economic difficulties as revenue declined, and the psychological effects of constant military pressure all differed from the heroic narrative of media productions.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 26: The Caliphate — State-Building in Real Time (2014–2015)
subheading: The Administrative Structure
text: The US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) and the Financial Intelligence Unit specifically targeting ISIS developed increasingly sophisticated methods for identifying and sanctioning the oil traders, money transfer operators, and financial intermediaries that processed ISIS revenues. Simultaneously, coalition airstrikes specifically targeted ISIS's financial infrastructure: the Mosul central bank money stores, the cash transport convoys that moved revenue between provinces, the oil infrastructure including wells and trucks. Between September 2015 and December 2016, specific strikes destroyed what the US military estimated as $800 million in cash stockpiles. The combination of revenue decline and territorial loss created a fiscal crisis that manifested in specific ways: salary cuts for ISIS fighters (documented through captured payroll records and defector accounts), reduced subsidies for civilian populations under ISIS control, and the deterioration of services that had provided the governance legitimacy the caliphate claimed. An organisation that had justified its brutal governance with the promise of functioning Islamic administration found that administration deteriorating as the fiscal base collapsed — accelerating the defection cycle and the loss of civilian acquiescence that military pressure then finalised.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 27: The Counter-ISIS Campaign — Coalition, Kurds, and Contradictions
text: The military campaign that destroyed ISIS's territorial caliphate between 2014 and 2019 succeeded in its immediate objective and left unresolved almost every structural condition that had produced ISIS in the first place. It was fought through a coalition of inherently contradictory interests — a US that wanted ISIS destroyed but not a major troop commitment; Kurdish forces that wanted territorial autonomy that their US patron's NATO ally Turkey considered an existential threat; an Iraqi government that wanted its territory back but whose political dysfunction had produced ISIS's recruitment conditions; and a Syrian opposition that ISIS was fighting but that was simultaneously fighting Assad, whom Russia and Iran were protecting. The campaign navigated these contradictions by never resolving them — accepting the structural incoherence as the cost of achieving the specific military objective.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 27: The Counter-ISIS Campaign — Coalition, Kurds, and Contradictions
subheading: Obama's Strategy: What It Was Designed to Achieve
text: The human cost of the Kurdish military partnership was significant and underreported in Western media: the SDF lost approximately 11,000 fighters killed in the campaign against ISIS between 2014 and 2019. The US suffered 7 combat deaths in Syria over the same period. This asymmetry — an ally bearing the combat burden — was the political logic of the "light footprint" strategy made concrete in human terms.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 27: The Counter-ISIS Campaign — Coalition, Kurds, and Contradictions
subheading: Obama's Strategy: What It Was Designed to Achieve
text: The campaign to retake Mosul — Iraq's second city, with a pre-war population of approximately 1.5 million — lasted nine months (October 2016 to July 2017) and was one of the most intense urban military operations since the Battle of Stalingrad in terms of civilian population density, building density, and the duration of combat within a continuous urban environment. The operational concept was a concentric approach: Iraqi Security Forces and Kurdish peshmerga advancing from the east, north, and south, supported by coalition air power and US and other special operations forces in advisory and enabling roles. The Iraqi Counter Terrorism Service — the special operations forces trained by US advisors from the 2010–2014 period, the best-trained component of the Iraqi military — carried the main combat burden in the city's densely built interior. The Federal Police and Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF — the Iran-backed Shia militias that had been formally incorporated into the Iraqi security structure in 2016) operated on the city's southern and western approaches.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 27: The Counter-ISIS Campaign — Coalition, Kurds, and Contradictions
subheading: Obama's Strategy: What It Was Designed to Achieve
text: ISIS's defensive strategy was specifically designed to maximise civilian casualties and generate images of coalition-caused civilian deaths: fighters embedded in civilian structures, the use of civilians as human shields, booby-trapping of houses, and — when positions became untenable — the destruction of bridges and infrastructure that trapped civilians. The organisation of the defence was the most sophisticated ISIS had mounted, reflecting the organisational evolution from the open-desert manoeuvre tactics that coalition air power had destroyed to an urban defence strategy that minimised air power's advantages.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 27: The Counter-ISIS Campaign — Coalition, Kurds, and Contradictions
subheading: Obama's Strategy: What It Was Designed to Achieve
text: Coalition air strikes in Mosul killed civilians in numbers that remain contested but were substantial. The monitoring organisation Airwaves recorded approximately 9,000 coalition airstrikes in the Mosul campaign; the Iraqi Body Count identified approximately 2,521 civilian deaths from airstrikes in the Mosul area between October 2016 and July 2017, while the UN and other organisations estimated total civilian deaths in the campaign at 3,000–11,000, with the wide range reflecting the impossibility of comprehensive casualty counting in an active urban war zone. A single airstrike on a house in the Mosul al-Jadida neighbourhood on March 17, 2017 killed between 100 and 278 civilians sheltering in a structure that ISIS fighters had used — the exact number remains uncertain. It was the deadliest single US military airstrike in terms of civilian casualties since the 1991 Gulf War.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 27: The Counter-ISIS Campaign — Coalition, Kurds, and Contradictions
subheading: Obama's Strategy: What It Was Designed to Achieve
text: The old city of Mosul — including the 12th-century al-Nuri mosque from whose minaret ISIS had declared the Caliphate — was destroyed in the campaign's final weeks. ISIS destroyed the mosque itself in June 2017 rather than allow it to be retaken. The Mosul Museum, already looted by ISIS, was further damaged. The old city's buildings — the physical repository of centuries of Ottoman and medieval Islamic architectural heritage — were so thoroughly destroyed that UNESCO assessed them as beyond restoration.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 27: The Counter-ISIS Campaign — Coalition, Kurds, and Contradictions
subheading: Obama's Strategy: What It Was Designed to Achieve
text: The physical Mosul that was liberated in July 2017 was a ruin. The western half of the city — where the old city and densely populated residential areas had been the final battleground — was estimated to require $1 billion in reconstruction simply to remove rubble. The population of 250,000–300,000 civilians who had remained through the battle emerged into a city without functioning water, electricity, or sewage systems, most of whose buildings were either destroyed or structurally compromised.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 27: The Counter-ISIS Campaign — Coalition, Kurds, and Contradictions
subheading: Obama's Strategy: What It Was Designed to Achieve
text: The Raqqa that the SDF liberated was, like Mosul, largely destroyed. The city of 300,000 pre-war had been reduced to rubble over four years of ISIS governance followed by four months of intensive airstrikes. The SDF established a civilian council to administer the city, but with no reconstruction funding, no government authority (Assad's government claimed sovereign jurisdiction; the SDF operated in territory outside Syrian government control), and no international body prepared to fund reconstruction in a governance vacuum, Raqqa's recovery was minimal. As of 2022, significant portions of the city remained uninhabitable.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 27: The Counter-ISIS Campaign — Coalition, Kurds, and Contradictions
subheading: Obama's Strategy: What It Was Designed to Achieve
text: The question of what happened to ISIS fighters as the caliphate collapsed — approximately 40,000 foreign fighters plus an uncertain number of indigenous Iraqi and Syrian members — is among the most significant unresolved consequences of the campaign. Approximately 8,000–10,000 ISIS fighters were estimated to have been killed in military operations between 2014 and 2019. The remainder — the majority — dispersed: some were captured, some integrated into surrounding populations, and a significant number crossed into Turkey and subsequently returned to their countries of origin. The specific problem of returning foreign fighters — the 5,000+ Europeans, the thousands of Central Asians, the North Africans — was managed differently by different governments. France initially indicated it would prosecute returning fighters under existing terrorism laws. Belgium passed specific legislation. The UK stripped some dual nationals of British citizenship, preventing their return. Germany established a specialised prosecution and de-radicalisation programme.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 27: The Counter-ISIS Campaign — Coalition, Kurds, and Contradictions
subheading: Obama's Strategy: What It Was Designed to Achieve
text: The most consequential unresolved category was the SDF-held detention camps — particularly al-Hol camp in northeastern Syria — in which approximately 65,000 people (as of 2019–2020), mostly women and children but including a significant number of ISIS fighters, were held in conditions of inadequate food, water, and medical care. The camp became a documented environment for ISIS ideological continuation: ISIS-aligned women enforced strict codes on other camp residents, killed those who did not comply, and maintained organisational structures that continued to socialise children in ISIS ideology. The US, European governments, and the SDF held a collective responsibility for a situation that none of them had the political will to resolve through repatriation and prosecution — the obvious legal instrument — because the domestic political cost of repatriating ISIS fighters was assessed as prohibitive.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 28: Iraq After ISIS — Reconstruction, Iranian Hegemony, and Structural Persistence
subheading: The Popular Mobilisation Forces: A State Within the State
text: No account of post-2003 Iraq is complete without a precise analysis of Qasem Soleimani — the Quds Force commander who was killed in a US drone strike at Baghdad International Airport on January 3, 2020. His significance to the regional power structure was not primarily military — though his operational role in Syria and Iraq was real — but architectural: he built and maintained the network of relationships, armed groups, political parties, and financial flows through which Iranian strategic influence operated across Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, and Yemen.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 28: Iraq After ISIS — Reconstruction, Iranian Hegemony, and Structural Persistence
subheading: The Popular Mobilisation Forces: A State Within the State
text: Soleimani joined the IRGC in 1979 and commanded the Quds Force from 1998 until his death — a 22-year tenure that gave him extraordinary continuity and the relationship depth that institutional longevity produces. He was operationally involved in Iraq from 2003 onward, personally managing relationships with the Badr Corps, with Muqtada al-Sadr (with whom his relationship was complex — Sadr was never fully controllable), with Nouri al-Maliki during the prime ministerial selection processes of 2006 and 2010, and with the PMF leadership from 2014 onward. His specific contribution to Iranian influence in Iraq was the management of the recursive relationship between Iranian support and Iraqi political reality: Iran's armed groups provided the coercive capacity that Iraqi political actors needed to maintain domestic power; those political actors then used their governmental positions to facilitate Iranian interests — through procurement contracts, border management, financial transfers, and political alignment. Soleimani managed the human relationships that made this recursive loop function. When political deadlock in Baghdad required resolution, he was frequently the mediator — not because the US had no candidate but because the armed groups whose co-operation was necessary for any candidate to govern were within his network rather than Washington's.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 28: Iraq After ISIS — Reconstruction, Iranian Hegemony, and Structural Persistence
subheading: The Popular Mobilisation Forces: A State Within the State
text: His killing — ordered by Trump without congressional notification, justified on the grounds of his alleged planning of imminent attacks on US forces in Iraq — was a significant tactical decapitation. Its strategic consequences were more complex. Iran's immediate response — ballistic missile strikes on US bases in Iraq (Ain al-Asad and Erbil), which caused no fatalities but produced traumatic brain injuries in over 100 US personnel — was calibrated to be visible enough to satisfy domestic Iranian demands for retaliation without triggering a US military response that Iran was not prepared to absorb. The Iraqi parliament, in the political atmosphere following Soleimani's killing on Iraqi soil, voted to demand the withdrawal of US forces from Iraq — a vote whose legal binding force was contested and which the US ultimately ignored, but which reflected the genuine Iraqi public anger at the unilateral US killing of a foreign official on Iraqi territory.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 28: Iraq After ISIS — Reconstruction, Iranian Hegemony, and Structural Persistence
subheading: The Popular Mobilisation Forces: A State Within the State
text: The destruction of ISIS's territorial caliphate did not eliminate the organisation — it transformed it from a proto-state to an insurgency operating in the territories it had previously governed. Between 2018 and the present, ISIS conducted an estimated 1,500–3,000 attacks annually across Iraq — targeting Iraqi security forces, government officials, tribal leaders who co-operated with the government, and occasionally civilian markets. The attacks demonstrated organisational continuity, local knowledge, and operational capacity that confirmed the assessment of analysts who had argued the military destruction of the caliphate would not eliminate the underlying movement.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: Oil depletion was the primary fiscal crisis. Yemeni oil production peaked at approximately 440,000 barrels per day in 2001 and had declined to approximately 120,000 by 2010. Oil revenues, which had constituted approximately 70% of government revenue, were falling annually. Projections at the time of the 2011 uprising indicated that Yemen would cease to be an oil exporter within five to ten years — a projection that the war then accelerated dramatically. A government whose fiscal base was vanishing was structurally incapable of the spending on services, employment, and security that a governable Yemen required.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: Water depletion was potentially more catastrophic in its long-term implications. The Sana'a basin's groundwater table was falling at 6–8 metres annually. Agricultural communities in the highlands — the social base of Yemeni traditional society — were progressively losing the water table access that had sustained agriculture for millennia. The alternative crop — qat, the stimulant leaf that Yemen's population chews daily and that constitutes roughly 30% of Yemen's cultivated area — consumed approximately 40% of Yemen's water, because qat farmers were willing to drill deeper and pay more for water than food farmers. The economic logic of qat (30 times the market value of wheat per kilogram of water consumed) drove farmers toward it; the ecological consequence was accelerated water table decline and long-term agricultural collapse.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: Political fragmentation was the structural condition that translated economic crisis into political instability. Ali Abdullah Saleh — who governed Yemen from 1978 — described his management of the country as "dancing on the heads of snakes": a constant negotiation among tribal confederations, military factions, regional powers, and political movements that rewarded his brokerage capacity while systematically preventing the development of institutions strong enough to reduce his indispensability. The consequence was a state whose governmental capacity was almost entirely channelled into the management of competing claims on central patronage rather than the delivery of services or the development of productive economic capacity.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: The Houthi insurgency had been active since 2004, when Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi led the first armed rebellion in the Saada governorate of northwestern Yemen against the Saleh government's marginalisation of the Zaidi Shia community — the religious tradition of the Houthi movement — and its accommodation of Saudi Wahhabi influence in Yemen's northern highland areas. Six rounds of fighting between the Houthi movement and the Yemeni government (2004–2010) had not resolved the underlying conflict and had given the Houthi movement both battle experience and territorial roots in Saada. The Iranian support narrative — that the Houthis were an Iranian proxy from the movement's inception — is an exaggeration: Iranian involvement increased substantially only after 2011, and the Houthi movement's primary drivers were domestic Yemeni political and religious grievances that Iranian support later exploited and amplified rather than created.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) had established a significant presence in Yemen's south and east — in Marib, Shabwah, Abyan, and Hadhramaut provinces — that exploited the central government's absence from large portions of the country. AQAP conducted significant external attack operations, including the 2009 attempt to assassinate Saudi Deputy Interior Minister Mohammed bin Nayef, the 2009 underwear bomb plot targeting a US flight, the 2010 cargo plane bomb plot, and the Charlie Hebdo attack in Paris in January 2015 (carried out by brothers trained by AQAP in Yemen). US drone strikes targeting AQAP in Yemen increased through the Obama administration, generating civilian casualties that became a consistent grievance for Yemeni communities and a AQAP recruitment tool.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: The federalism proposal was the most consequential failure. The six-region proposal placed the Houthi-dominated north in a region (Azal) with no Red Sea coast and no significant oil resources — a configuration that the Houthi leadership publicly declared would create a landlocked entity unable to sustain itself economically. Whether this was a legitimate concern or a pretext for the territorial expansion they were already planning is debated; the Houthi leadership had been building military capacity and expanding their territorial control throughout the dialogue process, suggesting that the federalism objection was at minimum not their primary concern.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: The Houthi military advance — which took Sana'a in September 2014, placed Hadi under house arrest in February 2015, and prompted Hadi's flight to Aden and then to Riyadh — provided the formal pretext for Saudi intervention. Saudi Arabia assembled a coalition of Arab states (UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan, Egypt, Sudan, Senegal, and others in varying contributions) and launched Operation Decisive Storm on March 26, 2015.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: Saudi Arabia's strategic rationale had three components of varying credibility. The security argument — that a Houthi-controlled Yemen on Saudi Arabia's southern border would constitute an Iranian-aligned threat that Saudi Arabia could not tolerate — had real substance. The Houthis had been receiving increasing Iranian material support (weapons, training, and eventually ballistic missile expertise). Iranian advisors were documented in Yemen from 2015 onward. A permanently Houthi-controlled Aden — with its Indian Ocean port and Red Sea access — would significantly expand Iranian maritime reach.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: The deterrence argument — that failing to respond to the Houthi advance would signal weakness that Iran would exploit elsewhere — reflected Mohammed bin Salman's (MBS) specific strategic calculus as he asserted Saudi regional leadership in the months following his father's accession to the throne in January 2015. The Yemen intervention was, in significant part, a demonstration that the new Saudi leadership would act assertively against Iranian regional expansion rather than relying on diplomacy and American protection.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: The military overconfidence argument — the assessment that the coalition's military superiority would produce rapid Houthi capitulation and a quick restoration of Hadi's government — proved catastrophically wrong. The official expectation of a weeks-long campaign has extended to a decade. The Houthis proved militarily adaptive, strategically sophisticated, and politically resilient in ways that the Saudi military and intelligence assessment had not anticipated.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: The US and UK governments maintained arms sales to Saudi Arabia throughout — the US sold approximately $36 billion in weapons to Saudi Arabia between 2015 and 2020 — while periodically expressing "concern" about civilian casualties and conducting reviews that consistently concluded that the relationship should continue. The specific review mechanisms — the US Joint Incidents Assessment Team that the US supported Saudi Arabia in establishing to investigate its own strikes — were assessed by independent observers as systematically inadequate. The UK's arms sales were challenged in British courts; the Court of Appeal ruled in 2019 that the government had failed to properly assess civilian harm risk in approving sales; sales were temporarily suspended and then resumed after a revised assessment.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: The US role in the Yemen war extended beyond arms sales to direct military support: intelligence sharing, mid-air refuelling of coalition aircraft (terminated in 2018 after the Khashoggi murder and congressional pressure), targeting assistance in the campaign's early years, and special operations forces conducting counterterrorism operations against AQAP that were distinct from but operationally entangled with the broader coalition campaign.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: The cholera epidemic that began in October 2016 produced the largest cholera outbreak in recorded medical history: approximately 2.5 million cases by 2019, with the outbreak sustained by the destruction of water and sanitation infrastructure through a combination of deliberate targeting (documented in coalition strikes on water treatment facilities) and the collapse of the public health system's capacity for maintenance. The direct destruction of water infrastructure by coalition strikes was documented in UN reports; the public health consequences included diarrhoeal diseases beyond cholera that killed children at rates that exceeded direct conflict violence.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: Food insecurity: the UN World Food Programme assessed 21 million Yemenis — approximately 70% of the population — as food insecure in 2018–2019, of whom approximately 8.4 million were in emergency food insecurity (one step below famine). The specific mechanism was both the war's physical destruction of agricultural infrastructure and Yemen's blockade: Saudi Arabia and the UAE imposed a naval and air blockade of Houthi-controlled ports (primarily Hodeidah, through which approximately 70% of Yemen's food imports arrived) that was intermittently tightened in ways that restricted the humanitarian supply chain. The UN and humanitarian organisations repeatedly warned that the blockade was the primary driver of the famine risk; the Saudi government maintained that the blockade was necessary to prevent Iranian weapons supply.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: Child casualties: Yemen had the highest rate of child death from disease and malnutrition among conflict-affected countries through the 2016–2020 period. The specific figures — the UN estimated 85,000 children under five had died from severe acute malnutrition between 2015 and 2018 alone — were challenged by the Saudi-led coalition but are consistent with multiple independent epidemiological assessments. Total mortality: The UN Development Programme's 2021 estimate of 377,000 total deaths by end of 2021 — including both direct conflict deaths (about 150,000) and indirect deaths from disease, hunger, and health system collapse (about 227,000) — represents the most comprehensive mortality assessment available. It is almost certainly an underestimate, since Yemen's vital registration system had collapsed and independent verification was impossible across much of the territory.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: The Houthis — who now call themselves Ansar Allah and have consolidated governance of a territory containing approximately 70–80% of Yemen's pre-war population — have demonstrated a military and administrative capacity that makes their exclusion from any political settlement impossible. They have also demonstrated a willingness to absorb sanctions, blockade, and military attack without accepting terms that would reduce their territorial control or their Iranian supply relationship. The specific Houthi leadership — which combines Zaidi religious authority, tribal networks in the northern highlands, and Iranian weapons — has no incentive to accept terms that would require them to relinquish the territorial and political position they have achieved through war.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: The UAE's 2019 decision to substantially withdraw its ground forces from Yemen — while maintaining support for the Southern Transitional Council — reflected a strategic reassessment that the war as being prosecuted was not achievable and that the UAE's interests were better served by securing Aden and the southern coastline (the maritime chokepoint that matters for UAE commercial interests) than by the indefinite prosecution of a war to restore a government whose viability was questionable.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 29: Yemen — The War the World Forgot
subheading: Yemen's Pre-War Structural Vulnerabilities
text: The Houthi naval attacks on Red Sea shipping — which intensified from November 2023 in solidarity with Gaza — demonstrated that the movement had acquired weapons capabilities that made it a genuine threat to international maritime commerce. The US-led coalition's Operation Prosperity Guardian, conducting airstrikes on Houthi missile and drone launch sites from January 2024 onward, achieved limited degradation of Houthi capability while introducing a direct US military confrontation with a movement that eight years of Saudi airstrikes had failed to defeat. The structural lesson was identical to every other lesson of the period: armed groups with genuine political bases, protected sanctuaries, and external weapons supply are extraordinarily difficult to destroy through airstrikes alone.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 30: The Saudi-Iranian Cold War — Structural Drivers of Proxy Conflict
subheading: The Structural Basis: Two Incompatible State Projects
text: Saudi Arabia's state project — the Wahhabi-Al Saud compact — requires that the kingdom be the pre-eminent political and religious authority in the Islamic world. This claim rests on custodianship of Mecca and Medina, on the Wahhabi theological tradition's status as the self-appointed guardian of correct Sunni practice, and on the financial capacity to project this claim globally through mosque construction, scholarship funding, and religious education. An Iran whose revolutionary Shia Islamic model was winning political legitimacy across the Muslim world — particularly among Shia communities in Iraq, Lebanon, Bahrain, and the Gulf — directly challenged the Saudi claim to Islamic leadership and threatened the internal stability of a Saudi state whose own Shia minority (concentrated in the oil-producing Eastern Province) the Saudi government had reason to fear.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 30: The Saudi-Iranian Cold War — Structural Drivers of Proxy Conflict
subheading: The Structural Basis: Two Incompatible State Projects
text: Iran's state project — the Velayat-e Faqih model of clerical governance — requires external validation of the revolutionary model to justify its domestic political costs: economic sacrifice, international isolation, and the political suppression of the Iranian population's persistent desire for more open governance. Projecting influence through Shia communities and armed groups across the Arab world serves both the strategic interest (strategic depth, buffer zones, deterrence through proxy) and the ideological interest (demonstrating the revolutionary model's transnational appeal). A Saudi-dominated regional order in which pro-Iranian political movements were contained and the revolutionary model isolated would undermine the foundational claim that the Islamic Revolution was a world-historical event rather than a costly Iranian peculiarity.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 30: The Saudi-Iranian Cold War — Structural Drivers of Proxy Conflict
subheading: The Structural Basis: Two Incompatible State Projects
text: This does not mean sectarian identity is purely manufactured — people genuinely identify as Sunni or Shia, genuinely feel the religious affiliation as meaningful, and genuinely experience perceived threats to their community as personal threats. It means that the translation of identity difference into organised violence requires specific political actors with specific interests to make specific decisions — to fund militias, to deploy weapons, to frame political competition as existential communal threat. Those actors are states and political movements with material interests, not primordial historical forces expressing themselves through individual violence.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 30: The Saudi-Iranian Cold War — Structural Drivers of Proxy Conflict
subheading: The Structural Basis: Two Incompatible State Projects
text: The June 2017 Saudi-led blockade of Qatar — in which Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain, and Egypt severed diplomatic and economic relations with Qatar and imposed a land, air, and sea blockade — was the most dramatic demonstration of the Gulf Cooperation Council's structural fragility and revealed the specific interests competing within what had been presented as a bloc of aligned Gulf monarchies. The 13 demands presented to Qatar — including closing Al Jazeera, severing relations with Iran, expelling Turkish troops from Qatari territory, and ending support for the Muslim Brotherhood — were demands that Qatar reduce its independent foreign policy to a sub-set of Saudi foreign policy. Qatar's independent foreign policy — funding the Muslim Brotherhood internationally, maintaining relations with Iran, hosting Al Jazeera's critical journalism, supporting Hamas — had been tolerated by Saudi Arabia through the 2000s when Qatar was more modest in its ambitions. The Arab Spring, which Qatar had used Al Jazeera and financial support to shape in directions that did not align with Saudi preferences (particularly in Egypt, where Qatar supported the Brotherhood government that Saudi Arabia opposed), changed the Saudi calculation.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 30: The Saudi-Iranian Cold War — Structural Drivers of Proxy Conflict
subheading: The Structural Basis: Two Incompatible State Projects
text: Qatar's response was to refuse all thirteen demands while simultaneously executing a diplomatic pivot that demonstrated the hollowness of Saudi economic leverage: Turkey deployed additional troops to Qatar within days of the blockade's announcement; Iran opened its airspace to Qatari aircraft; and Qatar accelerated negotiations with the United States on the expansion of Al Udeid Air Base — the largest US military installation in the Middle East — as a signal of its US alliance value. The blockade lasted three and a half years; it ended in January 2021 through Kuwaiti and US mediation, with Qatar making no significant concessions to the 13 demands. Saudi Arabia's most public exercise of economic coercive power in the Gulf had failed.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 30: The Saudi-Iranian Cold War — Structural Drivers of Proxy Conflict
subheading: The Structural Basis: Two Incompatible State Projects
text: The Qatar crisis revealed three structural realities about Gulf politics. First, the GCC was not a security or political community in any meaningful sense — it was a Saudi-dominated organisation that smaller members tolerated when it served their interests and circumvented when it did not. Second, the Saudi-UAE axis that had been the primary driver of regional hardline politics toward Iran, Qatar, and the Brotherhood was not the unified front it presented publicly — UAE and Saudi interests diverged in Yemen (where UAE priorities focused on the southern coast rather than Hadi restoration), in Libya (where UAE and Saudi supported different factions), and eventually in their respective relationships with the Biden administration. Third, the US's management of the crisis — which involved Trump initially congratulating Saudi Arabia for the blockade before the State Department and Pentagon reversed course — demonstrated the incoherence of US Gulf policy when personal presidential relationships conflicted with institutional strategic interests.

subheading: The Structural Basis: Two Incompatible State Projects
text: Vision 2030 — launched in April 2016 — is a programme of economic diversification designed to reduce Saudi Arabia's oil revenue dependence by developing non-oil industries, tourism, entertainment, and financial services. Its ambitions include reducing the public employment share of Saudi citizens' working population from approximately 70% to 40%, creating 1.5 million private sector jobs, and developing giga-projects (NEOM, the Red Sea Project, Qiddiya) as anchors for non-oil economic activity. The programme is genuinely ambitious and reflects a real understanding that the current economic model is unsustainable as energy transition progresses and demographics compound the fiscal pressure.

subheading: The Structural Basis: Two Incompatible State Projects
text: The repression that has accompanied reform is not incidental but structural: MBS's political method has been to centralise power by eliminating potential rivals before implementing reforms that will inevitably create losers among the existing elite. The November 2017 Ritz-Carlton detentions — in which approximately 200 princes, businessmen, and officials were held at the Ritz-Carlton Riyadh and released after agreeing to financial settlements that transferred an estimated $100 billion to the Saudi state — was presented as anti-corruption; it was also the elimination of every significant Saudi business and political figure who was not personally aligned with MBS or who represented an independent power base.

The CIA concluded with high confidence that MBS had ordered the killing. MBS denied ordering it; he acknowledged it had occurred and that it was wrong. The specific operational evidence — WhatsApp messages between the Saudi consul-general and members of the hit team referencing "bringing the body back," the presence of a forensic expert in the consulate on the day of Khashoggi's visit — established beyond any reasonable doubt that the killing was a planned operation rather than an improvisation gone wrong.

section: Chapter 31: Turkey's Neo-Ottoman Reorientation
subheading: The AKP's Rise: Material Foundations of a Political Movement
text: The AKP's 2002 electoral victory — in which it won 34% of the vote but two-thirds of parliamentary seats under Turkey's electoral threshold system — was not primarily an expression of Islamist political aspiration in the doctrinaire sense. It was the expression of three converging political economies. The Anatolian small business class — the devout, socially conservative entrepreneurs of Turkey's interior cities (Kayseri, Konya, Gaziantep) who had been frozen out of the Istanbul-Ankara secular elite's economic networks — found in AKP a political vehicle that combined Islamist cultural identity with pro-business economic policies (fiscal discipline, central bank independence, EU-accession-era regulatory reform) that served their specific interests. This class — sometimes called the "Anatolian tigers" — was the AKP's original social base and the economic foundation of a decade of growth (Turkish GDP grew from $230 billion in 2002 to $950 billion in 2013, the most sustained growth in the country's modern history).

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 31: Turkey's Neo-Ottoman Reorientation
subheading: The AKP's Rise: Material Foundations of a Political Movement
text: Urban migrants — the rural-to-urban population that had flooded Turkey's cities from the 1980s onward, living in gecekondu (informal settlements), working in the informal economy, culturally conservative and socially excluded from the secular establishment's cultural institutions — found in AKP a combination of social service delivery (the AKP municipality model of efficient, corruption-reduced local governance) and cultural validation that previous governments had not provided. They were politically invisible to the Kemalist establishment; AKP made them the majority.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 31: Turkey's Neo-Ottoman Reorientation
subheading: The AKP's Rise: Material Foundations of a Political Movement
text: The AKP's first decade in power (2002–2012) was characterised by genuine liberalisation — judicial reform, press freedoms initially expanded, civilian oversight of the military increased, Kurdish cultural rights extended, and the EU accession process pursued with seriousness. This period demonstrated that "political Islam" was not inherently incompatible with democratic governance and economic development — a demonstration that was inconvenient for both European governments that had implied Turkish Islamic culture was incompatible with EU membership and for Arab Islamist movements that had claimed Islamism was incompatible with democratic participation.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 31: Turkey's Neo-Ottoman Reorientation
subheading: The AKP's Rise: Material Foundations of a Political Movement
text: The AKP's democratic trajectory broke most visibly around 2012–2013, driven by a specific set of events that changed Erdoğan's political calculus. The 2013 Gezi Park protests — which began as an environmental demonstration against the redevelopment of Taksim Square and rapidly expanded into a broad urban middle-class protest against AKP governance style — were the first significant domestic challenge to AKP's legitimacy. Erdoğan's response — tear gas, water cannon, mass arrests, and a rhetorical escalation that characterised the protesters as terrorists and foreign agents — was disproportionate in a way that reflected a specific political psychology: a leader who had interpreted his decade of electoral success as popular mandation for his vision and who experienced criticism not as democratic feedback but as illegitimate challenge.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 31: Turkey's Neo-Ottoman Reorientation
subheading: The AKP's Rise: Material Foundations of a Political Movement
text: The July 2016 coup attempt — whether organised by the Gülenist network (as Erdoğan immediately declared) or partially facilitated by elements of the security services with mixed motivations (as some Turkish opposition figures suggested) — produced the most dramatic post-attempt repression in modern Turkish history: 150,000 arrests and detentions, 150,000 dismissals from public employment, the closure of universities, schools, and media organisations associated with the Gülen movement, and the replacement of removed officials with AKP loyalists whose primary qualification was personal alignment with Erdoğan. The coup attempt — real, in that armed officers genuinely attempted to seize control of key institutions and killed approximately 250 people in the attempt — was used to justify a purge of scope disproportionate to the coup's actual organisational reach.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 31: Turkey's Neo-Ottoman Reorientation
subheading: The AKP's Rise: Material Foundations of a Political Movement
text: The post-coup political environment — including a 2016 referendum that expanded presidential powers and a 2018 constitutional referendum that formally instituted a presidential system eliminating the prime ministership — produced the full executive consolidation that Erdoğan had been building toward. The institutional checks that had constrained presidential power — a genuinely independent judiciary, a functioning parliament with real oversight, an independent central bank — were progressively eliminated or subordinated.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 31: Turkey's Neo-Ottoman Reorientation
subheading: The AKP's Rise: Material Foundations of a Political Movement
text: Turkey's Syria policy illustrates the gap between strategic ambition and strategic achievement with particular clarity. Turkey's initial response to the Syrian uprising — Erdoğan publicly demanded Assad's resignation in 2011 and opened Turkish territory to Syrian opposition fighters and their supply networks — was driven by the calculation that Assad would fall quickly (as Mubarak had), that a post-Assad Syrian government dominated by the Muslim Brotherhood (whose Syrian branch Turkey actively supported) would be a natural Turkish ally, and that Turkey would position itself as the patron of the new order. Every element of this calculation proved wrong. Assad did not fall. The Syrian opposition fragmented rather than consolidating around a Brotherhood-led framework. Turkey's open border policy produced approximately 3.5 million Syrian refugees on Turkish territory — the largest refugee population in the world — whose political and economic management became a persistent domestic political vulnerability. The specific armed groups that Turkey funded and harboured included factions whose subsequent development — toward jihadist affiliations, toward criminal economy participation, toward internecine warfare — created security liabilities rather than strategic assets.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 31: Turkey's Neo-Ottoman Reorientation
subheading: The AKP's Rise: Material Foundations of a Political Movement
text: Turkey's 2017 decision to purchase the Russian S-400 air defence system — despite explicit US warnings that the purchase would result in removal from the F-35 programme and potential sanctions — is the most operationally significant expression of the strategic diversification that characterises the AKP's foreign policy. The specific rationale — that NATO allies, primarily the US, had refused to provide Turkey with air defence systems on terms (technology transfer, co-production) that Turkey's defence industry aspirations required, and that Russia had offered terms that were more accommodating — was genuine as a proximate cause. The deeper rationale was strategic: Erdoğan calculated that Turkey's geopolitical centrality — NATO's second largest army, a member state straddling Europe and the Middle East, the country through which any NATO land operation in the Eastern Mediterranean would transit — gave Turkey the leverage to make the S-400 purchase without absorbing the maximum punitive response that US rhetoric suggested.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 31: Turkey's Neo-Ottoman Reorientation
subheading: The AKP's Rise: Material Foundations of a Political Movement
text: As political rhetoric, neo-Ottomanism is real: the AKP's cultural programme, Erdoğan's imagery and speech patterns, the Turkish government's projection of itself as the natural leader of Sunni Muslim political movements globally (particularly through support for the Muslim Brotherhood) — all draw on an Ottoman heritage narrative that the Kemalist secular establishment had deliberately suppressed. As a strategic programme, it is more limited than the rhetoric implies. Turkey has neither the economic base (Ottoman-era Turkey dominated trade routes that are now managed by different economic actors) nor the military capacity nor the diplomatic relationships to replicate Ottoman imperial reach across the Middle East, North Africa, and the Balkans. What it has is a significant regional military presence (in Syria, Libya, Qatar), a network of soft power instruments (TIKA development agency, the Diyanet religious authority operating in Muslim communities globally, Turkish drama series with massive viewership across the Arab world), and a diplomatic activism that consistently seeks a seat at every regional table regardless of institutional membership.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: The two-state solution — an independent Palestinian state in the West Bank and Gaza alongside Israel — has been the declared goal of every US administration since 1993, the stated preference of the majority of both Israeli and Palestinian populations in polling conducted through the 2000s, and the framework of every significant diplomatic initiative including Oslo, Camp David, the Clinton Parameters, the Arab Peace Initiative (2002), the Roadmap (2003), the Annapolis Process (2007–2008), and the Kerry talks (2013–2014). It has not been achieved and, as of the mid-2020s, is not achievable by any honest assessment of current conditions — not because either population fundamentally rejected coexistence but because the material facts on the ground have made its geographic precondition — a contiguous, viable Palestinian state — physically impossible without a scale of Israeli political will that does not currently exist.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: The specific material fact is the settlement enterprise. As of 2023, approximately 700,000 Israeli settlers live in the West Bank and East Jerusalem — up from 110,000 in 1993, the year Oslo was signed, and from 200,000 in 2000, when Camp David failed. These settlers are distributed across approximately 130 settlements (formally authorised by the Israeli government) and approximately 150 outposts (unauthorised under Israeli law, but systematically tolerated and increasingly retroactively authorised). The settler population is not uniformly ideologically motivated — a significant portion moved to West Bank settlements for economic reasons (subsidised housing, lower costs, commuting distance to Israeli job centres) rather than religious-nationalist ideology. This economic dimension makes the political problem harder, not easier: ideologically motivated settlers can potentially be compensated for relocation; economically motivated settlers who built their financial lives around settlement housing values are a different political constituency.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: The settlement distribution has fragmented the West Bank's territory in ways that most international legal and geographic analysis concludes are incompatible with a viable contiguous state. The West Bank is approximately the size of Delaware. Within it, Israeli-controlled areas (Area C, under Oslo's framework — approximately 60% of West Bank territory), settlements, military zones, settler road networks, and the separation barrier create a geography in which Palestinian-controlled areas are non-contiguous, access between them requires Israeli permission, and any Palestinian state would be structurally non-viable as an independent territorial entity without Israeli goodwill that current Israeli political dynamics show no evidence of providing.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: Hamas is the Palestinian political expression of the Muslim Brotherhood tradition — a movement that combines social service provision (the charitable infrastructure that built Hamas's popular base in Gaza through the 1980s and 1990s), an Islamist political programme (Islamic governance, rejection of Israel's right to exist in its foundational documents), and an armed wing (the Qassam Brigades) that has conducted both guerrilla and terrorist operations against Israeli military and civilian targets. These three dimensions coexist and are not easily separated.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: Hamas's founding in 1987 — during the First Intifada, as an offshoot of the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood's Palestinian branch — and its early growth deserve specific analytical attention. Israeli policy in the 1980s initially tolerated and in specific instances facilitated Hamas's growth as a counterweight to the PLO — a fact documented in Israeli security establishment memoirs and in the work of Israeli academic Benny Morris. The reasoning was explicit: a divided Palestinian political landscape was more manageable than a unified one. The policy was a strategic miscalculation of first order: the Islamist movement that Israel helped to grow became the primary obstacle to any negotiated settlement and the most significant source of terrorist violence against Israeli civilians. Hamas won the January 2006 Palestinian Legislative Council elections with 44% of the vote (Fatah received 41%), giving Hamas a parliamentary majority. The elections were assessed by international observers as free and fair. The United States and Israel refused to recognise the result, imposed sanctions on the Hamas-led Palestinian Authority government, and supported Fatah's attempts to reverse the electoral outcome through security force confrontation — a policy that produced the June 2007 Hamas military takeover of Gaza, which Hamas has governed since.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: Gaza's governance under Hamas since 2007 has occurred under conditions that make assessment of its quality almost impossible to separate from the conditions it is responding to. The Israeli and Egyptian blockade — initially imposed to isolate Hamas politically and subsequently maintained as a security measure — controls all goods entering Gaza, severely restricting construction materials (dual-use), economic inputs, and limiting population movement to exceptional cases. The blockade has produced GDP contraction, 40–50% unemployment, inadequate access to electricity (which Gaza receives through Israeli power supply that has been cut in response to conflict), and a public health system running at the edge of collapse.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: Gaza's population of approximately 2.3 million (2023) inhabits 365 square kilometres — one of the most densely populated territories on earth — with one of the youngest demographic profiles in the world (approximately 42% under 14) and no viable economic future under current conditions. The specific political consequence of these conditions — the radicalisation of a population with no economic prospects, no freedom of movement, and no political horizon — is the structural engine that Hamas and Islamic Jihad's recruitment systems exploit. Whether the blockade has achieved its stated security objectives is a question the evidence weighs against: Hamas has grown more capable militarily under the blockade than before it, developing tunnel networks, rocket production capacity, and — as October 7, 2023 demonstrated — sophisticated ground assault capability. The blockade has been effective at preventing economic development; it has not been effective at preventing military development.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: Operation Cast Lead (December 2008 – January 2009) killed approximately 1,391 Palestinians (of whom 759 were civilians, according to the Israeli human rights organisation B'Tselem; Palestinian figures were higher) and 13 Israelis (10 soldiers, 3 civilians). It was triggered by Hamas rocket fire following the expiration of an Egypt-brokered ceasefire. It achieved no durable strategic objective — Hamas's governance of Gaza was unchanged, rocket production resumed, and a new ceasefire was eventually negotiated.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: Operation Pillar of Defense (November 2012) killed 167 Palestinians and 6 Israelis over 8 days. It began with the targeted killing of Hamas military commander Ahmed al-Jabari — who had been involved in recent ceasefire negotiations — in an act whose timing was widely interpreted as designed to prevent a durable agreement. An Egyptian-brokered ceasefire ended the operation with no territorial change.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: Operation Protective Edge (July–August 2014) was the most extensive: 50 days of combat killing approximately 2,251 Palestinians (of whom approximately 1,462 were civilians by the UN's count) and 73 Israelis (67 soldiers, 6 civilians). The operation included a ground incursion targeting the tunnel network that Hamas had developed for cross-border infiltration. It destroyed extensive physical infrastructure in Gaza and temporarily degraded Hamas's tunnel capacity. Within three years, the tunnel network had been rebuilt.

section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: Operation Guardian of the Walls (May 2021) killed 256 Palestinians and 13 Israelis over 11 days. It was notable for the simultaneous internal violence between Jewish and Arab citizens of Israel — in mixed cities like Lod, Haifa, and Acre — that accompanied the Gaza conflict, demonstrating the spillover effects of the Gaza escalation on Israel's own internal communal tensions.

section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: A Hamas military defeat sufficient to displace its governance would create a governance vacuum (as in Libya and Iraq) that Israel would then be responsible for filling, which Israel does not want. The operations are therefore calibrated to degrade rather than destroy — maintaining the cycle rather than ending it.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: On October 7, 2023 — the 50th anniversary of the 1973 Yom Kippur War's beginning — Hamas launched the largest assault on Israeli territory since the state's founding. Approximately 3,000 Hamas fighters breached the Gaza perimeter fence at multiple points, overran Israeli military positions, and attacked Israeli civilian communities in the surrounding area. The assault killed approximately 1,200 Israelis — the majority civilians, including at a music festival (364 killed) and in kibbutzim along the border. Approximately 251 hostages were taken to Gaza.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: October 7 was the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust. This fact requires stating plainly, without rhetorical cushioning. The operational analysis of the attack reveals the specific intelligence and security failure that made it possible. The Gaza Division — the Israeli military command responsible for the Gaza border — had been progressively repositioned over the preceding years based on an intelligence assessment that Hamas had been deterred by the 2021 operation and was focused on economic development rather than military escalation. The specific deterrence signal — that Qatari funding for Gaza (facilitated by Israeli government approval) was conditional on Hamas restraint — had been assessed as creating a rational deterrence relationship. This assessment was wrong. Hamas's military intelligence was effectively concealed from Israeli technical collection. The IDF's Unit 8200 — the signals intelligence unit that monitors Gaza — had specific warnings that were assessed as insufficiently concrete to change the deployment posture. The "concept" (hakonceptzia) — the shared assessment that Hamas was deterred — was the same type of collective intelligence failure that had produced the 1973 intelligence failure the attack's date commemorated. The Dahlia Scheindlin analysis and the subsequent Meridor Commission investigation both identified the "concept" as the primary cause of the intelligence failure.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: Hamas's strategic logic for the attack requires assessment on its own terms, resisting both the "Israeli apologetics" framing (that the attack was pure evil without strategic calculation) and the "blowback reductionism" framing (that the attack was an understandable response to the occupation). The evidence from Hamas communications, from the testimony of released hostages, and from the attack's operational design suggests a calculated strategic gamble: that a massive attack on Israeli civilians would trigger an Israeli military response of sufficient scale and civilian cost to shatter the Abraham Accords normalisation track (specifically the pending Saudi-Israel normalisation), to re-internationalise the Palestinian issue after years of diplomatic marginalisation, and to demonstrate Hamas's capacity for strategic surprise. The gamble was partially successful on its own terms: the Saudi-Israel normalisation was indeed indefinitely postponed by the attack and the Israeli response. The Palestinian question was re-internationalised with extraordinary force — demonstrations across the world, UN General Assembly resolutions, the International Court of Justice proceedings. Hamas's continued existence through the Israeli military campaign was itself a form of strategic success by the specific metric of organisational survival.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: Israel's military response — Operation Swords of Iron — was declared on October 8, 2023 and evolved into the most intense Israeli military operation since the 1948 war. The stated objectives — destroying Hamas's military and governing capacity and returning the hostages — drove an operation that by mid-2024 had killed over 34,000 Palestinians (of whom the majority were civilians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry figures that international health organisations assess as reliable in their overall scale if not in their precise breakdown), had displaced approximately 1.7 million of Gaza's 2.3 million people, had destroyed approximately 60–70% of Gaza's structures, and had produced conditions of acute famine — the UN's Integrated Food Security Phase Classification assessed famine as occurring in northern Gaza by March 2024.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: The Abraham Accords (September 2020) — normalisation agreements between Israel and the UAE, Bahrain, Sudan, and Morocco, brokered by the Trump administration — represented a genuine diplomatic shift: Arab states formally normalising relations with Israel without a Palestinian state as a precondition. The Accords were presented by the Trump administration as a breakthrough and by Palestinian advocates as a betrayal. Both characterisations are partially correct. They were a genuine diplomatic achievement in the specific sense that they formalised what had been covert for decades — Israeli-Gulf security co-operation against Iran, commercial relationships, intelligence sharing — while extracting specific, if limited, Israeli concessions (a pause in settlement annexation announcements in exchange for UAE normalisation). They were not a breakthrough in the sense of advancing the Palestinian question — they explicitly separated Israeli-Arab normalisation from Israeli-Palestinian resolution, demonstrating that Arab states had concluded their national interests were better served by open relationships with Israel than by continued conditioning of those relationships on Palestinian statehood progress.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 32: The Palestinian Question — Structural Persistence and Political Deadlock
subheading: The Two-State Solution's Material Death
text: The Israeli majority will not accept a settlement that creates meaningful security risk; the Palestinian population will not accept a settlement that does not provide meaningful political rights and dignity. The specific configurations of territory, security, Jerusalem, and refugees that would satisfy both populations simultaneously do not exist within any proposal that either leadership has been prepared to accept.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 33: The Drone War — A New Form of Imperial Violence
subheading: The Operational Evolution: From Bush to Obama
text: The drone killing programme began under the Bush administration, initially as a counterterrorism instrument targeted at specific senior Al-Qaeda figures. The first documented lethal drone strike outside a declared war zone was the November 2002 CIA strike in Yemen that killed Qaed Salim Sinan al-Harethi — an Al-Qaeda operational figure — along with five others, including an American citizen. Obama dramatically expanded the programme. The Obama administration conducted approximately ten times more drone strikes than the Bush administration across Pakistan's Tribal Areas, Yemen, and Somalia. The specific expansion was driven by two factors: the political attractiveness of a programme that killed adversaries without risking American lives or requiring congressional authorisation, and the availability of dramatically improved drone technology (the MQ-9 Reaper's payload and loiter time made it a qualitatively different instrument from the earlier MQ-1 Predator).The programme was managed through two parallel structures: the CIA's covert action programme (primarily in Pakistan, operating under presidential findings and without legal transparency) and the military's Special Operations Command programme (primarily in Yemen and Somalia, operating under the 2001 AUMF and Title 10 military authority). The distinction mattered legally — CIA strikes had fewer reporting requirements to Congress and no requirement for the military's legal review processes — but operationally the two programmes overlapped in targeting, intelligence, and, eventually, personnel.

book: Contemporary Chaos - Gulf Wars to ISIS(1991-present)
section: Chapter 33: The Drone War — A New Form of Imperial Violence
subheading: The Operational Evolution: From Bush to Obama
text: The killing of Anwar al-Awlaki — an American-born Islamic cleric in Yemen, killed in a September 2011 drone strike — was the programme's most legally significant application. Al-Awlaki was an American citizen whose Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula connections were established by intelligence and whose specific operational role in attack planning was asserted by the government. The Justice Department's legal memo authorising his killing (released in 2014) argued that the due process required by the Fifth Amendment was satisfied by the executive branch's internal review — not by judicial review. Whether this satisfied the constitutional requirement was never adjudicated; the kill took place before any judicial review could occur. Al-Awlaki's 16-year-old son, Abdulrahman al-Awlaki — also an American citizen — was killed in a separate drone strike in Yemen two weeks after his father. He had no known operational role in AQAP.
