text: What the Meccan period established was a theological core — the absolute unity of God (tawhid), the final prophethood of Muhammad, the reality of divine judgment, the membership in a community of faith as the primary social identity — that would prove extraordinarily durable because it was simple, ethically demanding, and provided a framework for personal meaning that transcended the tribal identity whose fragility the economic changes of Muhammad's lifetime were exposing.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 4: The Hijra and the Construction of the Umma (622–630 CE)
text: Muhammad arrived in Medina (then called Yathrib) in September 622 CE, welcomed by the Ansar (Helpers) — the Medinan converts who had pledged allegiance at Aqaba.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 4: The Hijra and the Construction of the Umma (622–630 CE)
text: The Ansar themselves were divided between the two main Arab tribes — the Aws and Khazraj — whose mutual hostility had been the reason Medina needed an external arbitrator in the first place. And Medina's Jewish tribes — the Banu Qaynuqa, Banu Nadir, and Banu Qurayza — were significant economic and political actors whose relationship to the new community had to be negotiated. Muhammad's first major political act in Medina was to address all three problems simultaneously through a document that the Islamic tradition preserves as the Sahifat al-Medina — the Constitution of Medina.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 4: The Hijra and the Construction of the Umma (622–630 CE)
text: The constitutional framework gave Muhammad a formal position of authority that transcended religious identity. He was not claiming to be the political leader of the Muslims alone; he was claiming the position of hakam (arbitrator) for the entire Medinan community.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 4: The Hijra and the Construction of the Umma (622–630 CE)
text: The early Medinan suras introduce a theological framework for warfare that the Meccan period had lacked: the concept of fighting in God's cause (qital fi sabil Allah), the promise of paradise for those killed in that cause, and the explicit rejection of the pre-Islamic prohibition on fighting during the sacred months.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 4: The Hijra and the Construction of the Umma (622–630 CE)
text: Uhud (March 625 CE) was the reverse. Muhammad again moved to intercept a Qurayshi force — this time approximately 3,000 men under Abu Sufyan, seeking revenge for Badr — but chose a defensive position on the slopes of Mount Uhud north of Medina. The battle began favorably; the Muslim cavalry and infantry pushed the Qurayshi center back. But a group of Muslim archers posted on a hill to protect the Muslim flank, ordered explicitly by Muhammad to hold their position regardless of what happened below, abandoned their post when they saw the Qurayshi force apparently breaking. The Qurayshi cavalry commander Khalid ibn al-Walid — later to become the most important general of the early conquests — exploited the exposed flank and drove into the Muslim rear. The Muslim formation collapsed. Muhammad himself was wounded in the face and briefly reported as killed — a rumor that caused significant panic. The Muslim dead were approximately 70, including Muhammad's uncle Hamza, whose body was reportedly mutilated by the Qurayshi leader Hind bint Utba, who had a personal vendetta. The battle ended inconclusively — the Quraysh did not follow up their tactical victory by attacking Medina itself — but the psychological damage was severe.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 4: The Hijra and the Construction of the Umma (622–630 CE)
text: The Banu Qaynuqa, the smallest of the three Jewish tribes, were expelled from Medina in late 624 CE, approximately two months after Badr. The stated justification in the sources is an incident in which a Jewish goldsmith allegedly molested a Muslim woman, a Muslim bystander killed the goldsmith, and then a Jewish mob killed the Muslim — a blood cycle that gave Muhammad grounds for military action under the terms of the Constitution of Medina. The Banu Qaynuqa, besieged in their stronghold, surrendered after two or three weeks; they were expelled from Medina with their moveable property, their land and permanent property being appropriated. The Qaynuqa settled in Syria. The underlying dynamics are consistent with the interpretation that the Qaynuqa's expulsion was driven by economic and political factors — they were the most commercially active of the three Jewish tribes and had the most significant trading competition with the Muhajirun — as much as by the proximate incident.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 4: The Hijra and the Construction of the Umma (622–630 CE)
text: The Banu Nadir were expelled in 625 CE, following Uhud. The stated justification is an alleged Nadir plot to assassinate Muhammad during a meeting — a claim that cannot be independently verified but is consistent with the obvious fact that the Nadir's political position had been severely degraded by the Muslim community's growing strength. The Nadir were expelled with their moveable property, again their land being appropriated. Some settled in Khaybar, an oasis north of Medina with a significant Jewish agricultural community; some went to Syria. The Nadir's departure removed another significant competing economic and military presence from Medina.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 4: The Hijra and the Construction of the Umma (622–630 CE)
text: The Banu Qurayza is a case in a different category, in terms of both scale and the nature of the evidence. The episode occurred in 627 CE, in the context of the Siege of Medina — the campaign the Muslim sources call the Battle of the Trench (Khandaq). A Meccan-led coalition of approximately 10,000 men — the ahzab, confederates — supported by the Banu Nadir (now based in Khaybar and actively organizing against Medina) and several Nejdi tribes, invested Medina. The Muslims, on the advice attributed in the tradition to the Persian convert Salman al-Farisi, dug a trench (khandaq) across the northern approaches to the city where cavalry could attack — a tactic unfamiliar to the Arabian military tradition. The siege lasted approximately twenty to twenty-five days. The Meccan coalition, unable to cross the trench, unable to force the city by starvation in that time, and suffering from supply problems and internal disagreements, eventually dispersed.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 4: The Hijra and the Construction of the Umma (622–630 CE)
text: Hudaybiyya is the agreement that made the conquest of Mecca possible.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 5: The Conquest of Arabia (628–632 CE)
text: The Khalid ibn al-Walid conversion is the most vivid individual example of this logic. Khalid was the Meccan cavalry commander who had turned the Battle of Uhud against the Muslims — the ablest military mind in Mecca's service and a longstanding opponent of Muhammad. He came to Medina in 628 CE and converted to Islam along with Amr ibn al-As, who would later conquer Egypt. The tradition presents these conversions as genuine religious awakenings; the political reality was that both men were sophisticated political actors who had read the balance of forces and positioned themselves accordingly. They would become two of the most effective military commanders of the early conquests — which means their conversions, whatever their subjective character, produced real military capability for the Islamic community. The question of "genuine" versus "political" conversion is, in most cases, historically unanswerable and analytically sterile; what matters is behavior.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 5: The Conquest of Arabia (628–632 CE)
text: The conquest of Mecca in January 630 CE was achieved with a minimum of violence that reflects Muhammad's deliberate strategic choices as much as any inherent Meccan unwillingness to resist. The pretext for ending the Hudaybiyya truce — a Meccan-allied tribe's attack on a Muslim-allied tribe — may have been seized upon rather than merely responded to; the sources are equivocal about whether the truce violation was serious enough to justify the termination of a ten-year agreement only two years in. But the military preparation was serious. Muhammad assembled a force estimated by the sources at 10,000 men — likely inflated but certainly the largest Muslim military force yet mobilized — and marched on Mecca with sufficient secrecy and speed that Abu Sufyan, who came to negotiate, found himself facing a fait accompli outside the city walls. Abu Sufyan's conversion on the eve of the conquest — whatever its sincerity — was accepted, and he was sent back to Mecca with the message that those who stayed inside, those who went to their houses, and those who gathered around Abu Sufyan himself would be safe.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 5: The Conquest of Arabia (628–632 CE)
text: The Tulaqaʾ included Abu Sufyan and his family (the Umayyads), a number of other Qurayshi leaders who had been Muhammad's most persistent opponents, and individuals whose commitment to Islam was, by any reasonable assessment, primarily a function of military circumstances rather than theological conviction. Muhammad incorporated them into the Islamic system immediately and conspicuously — the sira tradition records that when distributing the spoils from the subsequent Battle of Hunayn, he gave enormous gifts to Abu Sufyan and other Tulaqaʾ figures while giving smaller shares to the Ansar, producing complaints from the Medinan converts about being treated worse than their former enemies. Muhammad's explanation — that the Ansar had Islam itself as their reward, while the Tulaqaʾ needed material inducement to bind them to the community — is politically transparent but theologically creative. The integration of the Quraysh establishment into the Islamic political system through patronage rather than exclusion would prove enormously consequential for the succession crises that followed Muhammad's death, since it meant that the men who assumed the caliphate were, in several cases, drawn from precisely the Meccan elite that had opposed Islam longest.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 5: The Conquest of Arabia (628–632 CE)
text: Those who remained in Medina rather than joining the Tabuk expedition are condemned in unambiguous terms; the Quranic distinction between the sincere believers who joined and the "hypocrites" (munafiqun) who stayed behind with various excuses made non-participation in Muslim military campaigns a matter of theological rather than merely political identity. This had permanent consequences for how the Islamic tradition understood the relationship between faith and military obligation.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 5: The Conquest of Arabia (628–632 CE)
text: The zakat — the alms tax that constitutes one of the Five Pillars of Islam — requires specific examination in the context of the Year of Delegations. In its theological formulation, zakat is a voluntary act of worship: a purifying donation by the believer to the community of the poor. The rate — 2.5 percent of accumulated wealth annually, with specific rates for agricultural production, livestock, and trade goods — is specified in considerable detail in the hadith literature. What the Year of Delegations reveals is that zakat was also a state tax: the delegations that came to Medina brought zakat, and Muhammad sent tax collectors (amil) to the newly submitting tribes to collect it. When some tribes refused to continue paying zakat after Muhammad's death, on the grounds that their obligation was personal to Muhammad and did not extend to his successors, the response was military compulsion — the Ridda wars. The distinction the tradition preserves between zakat as religious duty and zakat as political tax was real in the minds of some participants and entirely fictional to others; the subsequent history of the early caliphate turned on this ambiguity.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 5: The Conquest of Arabia (628–632 CE)
text: The Farewell Pilgrimage (March 632 CE) was Muhammad's first and only completion of the full hajj pilgrimage after the Meccan conquest. Its significance was recognized at the time: the sources record that approximately 100,000 people participated, the largest single gathering of the Islamic community in Muhammad's lifetime. The tradition of a farewell sermon — the Khutbat al-Wada — is preserved in multiple versions with some variation in detail, but with consistent core themes: the sanctity of Muslim life and property, the abolition of pre-Islamic blood debts and interest, the rights of women within the Islamic framework, the equality of all Muslims regardless of ethnic origin, and the completeness of the divine message. "Today I have completed your religion for you, and I have fulfilled My blessing upon you, and I have chosen Islam as your religion" (Quran 5:3) is traditionally dated to the revelation that occurred during this pilgrimage.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 5: The Conquest of Arabia (628–632 CE)
text: He died on June 8, 632 CE, in the house of his wife Aisha, his head reportedly in her lap.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 5: The Conquest of Arabia (628–632 CE)
text: The immediate political crisis revealed by Muhammad's death was twofold: the absence of any designated successor and the denial, by Umar ibn al-Khattab, that Muhammad had died at all. The tradition preserves Umar's outburst — his declaration that Muhammad had not died but had been taken up like Moses and would return — as a momentary breakdown in an otherwise iron-willed man. Its political function, whether conscious or not, was to prevent the community from moving immediately to the succession question before the senior leadership had managed it. Abu Bakr's response — his public declaration that "whoever worshipped Muhammad, let him know Muhammad has died; whoever worships God, let him know God is alive and does not die," followed by his recitation of Quran 3:144 ("Muhammad is no more than a messenger") — is one of the rhetorically decisive moments in early Islamic political history. It ended the denial phase and opened the succession crisis proper.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 6: Abu Bakr and the Ridda Wars — Empire by Compulsion (632–634 CE)
text: The tradition that Muhammad had designated Ali as his successor at Ghadir Khumm — a pool between Mecca and Medina where Muhammad reportedly told the assembled pilgrims returning from the Farewell Pilgrimage that "whoever has me as his master, Ali is also his master" — is the theological foundation of Shia Islam. Whether this constitutes a political designation of succession or a statement of Ali's religious authority is disputed; the Sunni tradition generally reads it as an expression of personal affection and religious esteem, while the Shia tradition reads it as an unambiguous designation of political succession deliberately frustrated by Abu Bakr and Umar. The historical truth of what Muhammad said and intended cannot be established with certainty. The political reality is that the manner of Abu Bakr's selection created a legitimate grievance that would generate civil war within twenty-four years.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 6: Abu Bakr and the Ridda Wars — Empire by Compulsion (632–634 CE)
text: When Muhammad died, these communities regarded their obligations as discharged. They were not rejecting God or the Quran; they were rejecting the claim that their political obligations continued after the death of the specific person they had recognized. This distinction — between religious conversion and political submission — is exactly the distinction that the zakat question crystallized. When the emissaries from Medina arrived to collect zakat, the refusal of some tribes to pay was framed by them as: we acknowledge God, we acknowledge Muhammad as prophet, but our arrangement was with Muhammad and does not extend to his successor. From Abu Bakr's perspective, this was apostasy — you cannot accept Islam and reject its financial obligations. From the tribes' perspective, it was straightforward contractual logic.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 6: Abu Bakr and the Ridda Wars — Empire by Compulsion (632–634 CE)
text: Abu Bakr's response to the Ridda was immediately and decisively military, over the objections of some of his senior advisers — the tradition records that Umar initially argued that the zakat-refusing tribes should not be fought since they had accepted Islam. Abu Bakr's reported response — "By God, I will fight those who differentiate between prayer and zakat" — established the principle that political and religious obligations were inseparable, that a Muslim who refused the financial obligations of the community had effectively left the community, and that such defection was to be suppressed by force. This was not a theologically obvious position, and the debate recorded in the sources about it reflects a genuine dispute within the early Muslim leadership about what kind of institution the caliphate was. Abu Bakr's position prevailed because he was the caliph, because the military logic of allowing Arabia to fragment was obvious, and because Khalid ibn al-Walid was available to enforce it.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 6: Abu Bakr and the Ridda Wars — Empire by Compulsion (632–634 CE)
text: Khalid ibn al-Walid is one of the genuinely remarkable military figures of the ancient world, and his record in the Ridda wars establishes his credentials before the even more spectacular campaigns in Syria and Iraq. He operated with a speed and operational decisiveness that consistently caught his opponents before they could concentrate their forces. He defeated the Banu Asad and their prophet Tulayha at the Battle of Buzakha (late 632 CE), then turned south to engage the Banu Tamim and their various internal factions, then drove into the Yamama to confront Musaylima's Banu Hanifa — the most militarily capable of all the Ridda movements.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 6: Abu Bakr and the Ridda Wars — Empire by Compulsion (632–634 CE)
text: The deaths of so many Quran memorizers at Aqraba is the stated reason for the first systematic compilation of the Quran as a written document. The Quranic text existed during Muhammad's lifetime in the memories of the huffaz (plural of hafiz), on scattered writing materials of various kinds, and in the practice of the community's prayer — but not as a single, authoritative written codex. The deaths at Aqraba alarmed Umar, who proposed to Abu Bakr that the text be compiled in writing before more memorizers died. Abu Bakr assigned the task to Zayd ibn Thabit, Muhammad's former secretary, who undertook the collection of written fragments and the testimony of those who had memorized relevant passages. The result was a written compilation — a mushaf — stored with Abu Bakr and then with the Prophet's widow Hafsa after Abu Bakr's death. This was not yet the standardized canonical text; that would require the additional step of Uthman's caliphate. But Aqraba, by threatening the oral transmission chain, directly produced the institutional drive toward written canonization that fixed the Quranic text.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 6: Abu Bakr and the Ridda Wars — Empire by Compulsion (632–634 CE)
text: The question of whether you were a Muslim was, from 633 CE onward, decided not merely by your theological convictions but by whether you paid zakat to the caliphate's tax collectors, accepted the caliphate's military authority, and refrained from organizing politically independent communities. Religion and state were not merely associated in early Islam; they were merged in a way that made religious dissent and political rebellion structurally identical. This fusion, established in the Ridda wars, would shape every subsequent political crisis in Islamic history.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 7: The Iraq Conquests — Khalid's Campaigns (633–637 CE)
text: Controlling Iraq meant controlling an economy that dwarfed anything Arabia had ever produced. The Arab commanders who marched into it probably did not fully appreciate what they were taking, but they understood enough to keep taking it.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 7: The Iraq Conquests — Khalid's Campaigns (633–637 CE)
text: The terms imposed on Hira established the template that Khalid would apply throughout the Iraq campaign and that the subsequent conquest of Syria and Egypt would broadly follow. The population was classified into categories. Those who actively resisted and were captured were dealt with as prisoners of war. Those who submitted became dhimmis — protected subjects (ahl al-dhimma) — in exchange for the payment of jizya, a tribute tax levied on non-Muslim free adult males. The rate at Hira appears to have been 1 dirham per head per year for the wealthy, with reduced rates for the poor and exemptions for monks, the destitute, the elderly, and children. In exchange, the Muslim authorities undertook to protect the population from external attack and internal predation. The Nestorian Christian churches were left intact. The Zoroastrian fire temples were unmolested (in Hira at least; practices elsewhere varied). The existing property arrangements, with the exception of any property belonging to the Sasanian state and the Lakhmid royal family, were preserved.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 7: The Iraq Conquests — Khalid's Campaigns (633–637 CE)
text: The economic logic of the jizya arrangement deserves examination because it is fundamental to understanding how the early Islamic empire sustained itself financially. The jizya was not charity; it was tribute, specifically extracted from non-Muslim populations on the explicit theological basis that they were tolerated but subordinate. The theological framework articulated in Quran 9:29 — "Fight those who do not believe in God or the Last Day, who do not forbid what God and His messenger have forbidden, who do not follow the religion of truth among the People of the Book, until they pay the jizya while they are subdued" — could not be more explicit about the coercive and hierarchical nature of the arrangement. The payment of jizya was performed in ways designed to humiliate: the payer was required to present himself in person, the tax collector was permitted to slap him or pull his beard (according to some legal traditions), and the receipt was accompanied by verbal acknowledgment of subordinate status. Whether these humiliating protocols were universally practiced or were legal theory that often went unenforced is debated; but the theological framework established that the dhimmi's continued existence in his own homeland was conditional on regular financial submission to the Muslim state.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 7: The Iraq Conquests — Khalid's Campaigns (633–637 CE)
text: The early caliphate actively discouraged mass conversion for exactly this reason — the mawali (non-Arab converts) who sought the social and religious equality that Islamic theology promised would find themselves frustrated by a fiscal and administrative system built on the revenue from their non-conversion.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 7: The Iraq Conquests — Khalid's Campaigns (633–637 CE)
text: The Sasanian imperial treasury — accumulated over centuries of imperial taxation of one of the world's most productive agricultural regions — was found largely intact. The sources describe gold, silver, jewels, silks, royal regalia, and the famous Baharestan carpet (the "Spring of Khosrow"), an enormous woven representation of a spring garden that Persian kings reportedly used in winter to remind themselves of summer. The carpet was cut up and distributed as booty; the treasury was systematically inventoried and dispatched to Medina. The financial windfall from Ctesiphon — Tabari cites specific sums that are probably exaggerated but that represent a genuine massive transfer of accumulated wealth — funded the subsequent campaigns in Persia itself and provided the capital for the garrison city infrastructure that Umar's administrative system required.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 7: The Iraq Conquests — Khalid's Campaigns (633–637 CE)
text: The decision to concentrate Arab military power in separate cities, intended to preserve cultural purity, instead created the conditions for the first internal political crises of the mature caliphate — because concentrated, literate, politically engaged populations in Kufa and Basra could organize opposition to caliphal policy in ways that dispersed tribal populations could not.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 8: The Syria Conquests — Crushing Byzantium (634–641 CE)
text: Heraclius's reported words on abandoning Syria — "Farewell, O Syria, and what an excellent country this is for the enemy" (or variant translations thereof) — appear in multiple source traditions and may be legendary, but they accurately capture the strategic reality: Yarmouk had consumed the last Byzantine field army capable of contesting Syria. Heraclius retreated to Anatolia, the natural defensive line of the Taurus Mountains, and spent the remaining six years of his life (he died in 641 CE) organizing the defense of Anatolia rather than attempting to retake Syria. He never did.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 8: The Syria Conquests — Crushing Byzantium (634–641 CE)
text: The fall of Jerusalem in 637–638 CE deserves particular attention because of its symbolic weight and the specific terms of its surrender. Jerusalem, as the holiest city of Christianity — containing the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the site of the Crucifixion and Resurrection — had enormous political significance for Byzantium. Its garrison commander, Sophronius the Patriarch (simultaneously the city's bishop and its de facto civil administrator), held out after Yarmouk for approximately six months while negotiations proceeded. He reportedly refused to surrender to anyone but the caliph himself. Umar ibn al-Khattab traveled from Medina to receive the city in person — a journey that the sources describe in terms clearly designed to contrast his austere simplicity with the ceremonial pomp of Byzantine imperial culture. He arrived reportedly on a camel, wearing patched clothes, accompanied by a small retinue. The Patriarch Sophronius, conducting Umar through the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, allegedly remarked that what he was witnessing was the abomination of desolation predicted in the Book of Daniel. When the time of Muslim prayer came while Umar was inside the church, he declined to pray inside it — saying that if he did, Muslims would claim the right to convert it into a mosque. He prayed outside instead. Whether these details are historically accurate or later elaborations designed to show Islamic religious respect for Christian holy sites, they entered the tradition as normative and had genuine influence on subsequent Islamic policy toward Jerusalem's Christian community.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 8: The Syria Conquests — Crushing Byzantium (634–641 CE)
text: The naval raids on Cyprus (649 CE), Rhodes (654 CE), and the first Arab siege of Constantinople (674–678 CE) were the eventual consequences of a decision made in the early 640s when Muawiyah recognized that Byzantine naval supremacy was the one military domain where his land forces could not follow.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 9: The Egypt Conquest — Amr ibn al-As's Gamble (639–642 CE)
text: Amr was not primarily a battlefield commander in the mold of Khalid; he was a political entrepreneur, a former Meccan merchant aristocrat of sharp intelligence and considerable duplicity whose conversion to Islam had been a political calculation as much as a religious experience, and who had subsequently demonstrated in Palestine and the Sinai that he was also a capable operational commander. He was exactly the right man to negotiate the complex politics of an Egypt divided between its Greek-speaking Chalcedonian administration and its Coptic Miaphysite majority.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 10: The Final Fall of Persia (637–651 CE)
text: The governor of Khuzestan, Hormuzan, conducted a protracted and occasionally effective resistance before his final defeat and capture. He was sent to Medina — the tradition records a scene in which Umar was preparing to execute him when Hormuzan asked for water, then refused to drink while his execution threatened, forcing Umar to guarantee his safety before he would drink. The legal puzzle this created — Umar felt bound by his inadvertent guarantee of safety — led to Hormuzan's conversion and his residence in Medina, where he would later be killed during the chaos following Uthman's assassination, the beginning of the first civil war.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 10: The Final Fall of Persia (637–651 CE)
text: He was killed near Merv in 651 CE — not by Arab soldiers but by a local miller, according to the most detailed account in the sources, who murdered him for his possessions after his last retainers had dispersed. The last Shahanshah of the Sasanian dynasty, the heir of Cyrus and Darius, was killed by a provincial miller with no political motive more elevated than robbery. The manner of his death captures the degree to which Sasanian legitimacy had dissolved.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 10: The Final Fall of Persia (637–651 CE)
text: The Miaphysite majorities of Syria and Egypt had religious reasons to be disaffected from Byzantine rule, as analyzed above, but they were still Christians — their religion was a variant of the same tradition that the conquering power could at least treat as a scriptural People of the Book. Coptic Christianity and Syrian Orthodoxy survived under Arab rule in recognizable form. Zoroastrianism had no such protected status in the initial Islamic legal framework: Jews and Christians were explicitly acknowledged as ahl al-kitab (People of the Book) with a defined dhimmi status. Zoroastrians occupied a more ambiguous category — they had scriptures (the Avesta) and a complex theology, but they were not in the Quranic prophetic lineage, and early Islamic legal opinion was divided on whether they qualified for dhimmi protection or should be treated as simple pagans (mushrikun) who must choose between conversion and death. In practice, most Arab commanders extended dhimmi-like protection to Zoroastrian communities — the fiscal logic of tribute was as compelling in Persia as anywhere else — but the theoretical ambiguity created conditions for harsher treatment of Zoroastrian communities, particularly fire temples (some were destroyed in the conquest period, others preserved), and for stronger conversion pressure over the following century.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 10: The Final Fall of Persia (637–651 CE)
text: The phenomenon of the Persian mawla — the Iranian convert who became a Muslim client of an Arab tribal patron — was sufficiently widespread by the mid-seventh century to create a recognizable social category: educated, often literate in both Pahlavi and Arabic, competent in the administrative traditions of the Sasanian bureaucracy, and resentful of the social discrimination that mawali status imposed despite formal religious equality. This class would eventually supply the intellectual and administrative cadre of the Abbasid caliphate, conducting what one historian has aptly called a "cultural counter-conquest" — the absorption of Persian administrative, literary, and philosophical traditions into the Arabo-Islamic synthesis.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 11: Umar's Administrative Revolution — Building a Caliphate (634–644 CE)
text: Umar ibn al-Khattab was not a man of whom anyone speaks neutrally. The Islamic tradition, both Sunni and Shia, acknowledges his exceptional capabilities while disagreeing fundamentally about whether his exercise of those capabilities was legitimate: Sunni tradition reveres him as the model of just caliphal governance, the architect of the early Islamic state, and the standard against which later rulers are measured and found wanting; the Shia tradition, whose foundational grievance is his role in blocking Ali's succession at Saqifah, regards his reign with a combination of acknowledgment of his effectiveness and condemnation of his fundamental usurpation. What both traditions agree on is that Umar built something. The institutional architecture of the early Islamic empire — the diwan, the amsar, the kharaj system, the provincial appointments, the legal framework for dhimmi status — was substantially constructed during his ten-year caliphate.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 11: Umar's Administrative Revolution — Building a Caliphate (634–644 CE)
text: The diwan — the register of Muslim warriors and their dependents, which served simultaneously as a muster roll, a welfare register, and a distribution mechanism for the state's financial resources — was Umar's foundational institution. The word itself is Persian, one of many administrative terms that the early Islamic state borrowed from the Sasanian bureaucratic tradition it had just conquered. The diwan worked as follows: every Muslim warrior was registered by tribe and lineage, and received an annual stipend (ata) from the state treasury, graduated by the order of his conversion and military service. The earliest converts and closest companions of the Prophet received the highest stipends; the Tulaqaʾ (those who converted at the fall of Mecca) and the tribes that converted after the Ridda wars received lower stipends; subsequent converts received still less. Widows and dependents of warriors received smaller stipends. The scale of the system, once the conquests' revenues began flowing in, was substantial: the sources record stipend levels ranging from 5,000 dirhams annually for the most senior companions to 200 dirhams for ordinary warriors, with dozens of intermediate grades.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 11: Umar's Administrative Revolution — Building a Caliphate (634–644 CE)
text: Kufa and Basra in Iraq, Fustat in Egypt, Jabiya in Syria: these were not cities in the pre-Islamic sense of organic urban growths but purpose-built administrative and military installations, organized by tribal quarter (each tribe occupying its designated neighborhood with its mosque), governed by appointed commanders, and supplied from the kharaj revenues of the surrounding agricultural territory. The Arab warriors who lived in them were, in effect, a professional standing army on retainer, available for rapid mobilization, concentrated in accessible locations, and administratively separated from the non-Muslim population they were nominally protecting and actually taxing.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 11: Umar's Administrative Revolution — Building a Caliphate (634–644 CE)
text: In its received form, the Pact of Umar contains provisions prohibiting dhimmis from building new houses of worship, displaying religious symbols publicly, wearing the same clothing as Muslims, carrying weapons, riding horses, and various other restrictions designed to mark the subordinate status of the non-Muslim population visibly. Scholars are divided on how much of this represents genuine seventh-century practice and how much is the retrospective systematization of a later period that was dealing with the political problem of large non-Muslim populations in established Muslim governance structures. The general principle — that non-Muslims were protected but subordinate, permitted to practice their religion privately but prohibited from public religious competition with Islam — is consistent with early caliphal practice; the specific restrictions in their received form are probably later elaborations.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 11: Umar's Administrative Revolution — Building a Caliphate (634–644 CE)
text: Umar's assassination in November 644 CE was, in the sources' presentation, both shocking and somehow fitting. He was stabbed six times by the Persian slave Piruz Nahavand — called Abu Lulua in the Arabic sources — while leading the dawn prayer in Medina's mosque. Piruz was a craftsman, a slave of the governor Mughirah ibn Shuba, who reportedly had a grievance about the level of tribute he was required to pay his master. The tradition records that he had previously complained to Umar and that Umar had ruled against him. Whether the assassination was purely personal — a slave with a grievance against the caliph who had upheld his enslavement — or political, connected to Persian resistance to Arab rule, or part of a broader conspiracy, was disputed at the time and remains disputed in the scholarship. Piruz died immediately after the attack, apparently by suicide, which eliminated the most direct source of information about his motives.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 12: Uthman and the First Fitna — The Caliphate Fractures (644–661 CE)
text: Umar, on his deathbed, had appointed six of the most senior surviving companions of Muhammad — Uthman, Ali, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Talha, Zubayr, and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas — to deliberate and choose one of their number. The deliberations, as preserved in the sources, reveal the political divisions that would soon tear the caliphate apart. The final choice came down to Uthman and Ali. Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, acting as the council's informal chairman, reportedly asked each man whether he would govern according to the Quran, the example of the Prophet, and the precedents set by Abu Bakr and Umar. Ali qualified his answer — yes to the Quran and the Prophet, but he would use his own judgment where precedent was unclear. Uthman gave an unqualified assent. Abd al-Rahman then selected Uthman, and the council ratified the choice.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 12: Uthman and the First Fitna — The Caliphate Fractures (644–661 CE)
text: Uthman ibn Affan was from the Umayyad branch of the Quraysh, the clan that had produced Abu Sufyan and that had been Muhammad's primary aristocratic opposition in Mecca before the conquest. He was personally one of the earliest converts — the tradition counts him among the first ten — and had married two of Muhammad's daughters sequentially (Ruqayyah and then Umm Kulthum after Ruqayyah's death), giving him the honorific title Dhu al-Nurayn (Possessor of the Two Lights). He was personally pious, personally wealthy, and personally unexceptional as a military or administrative leader. His caliphate would demonstrate that personal piety and administrative competence are not substitutes for political acumen in the management of an empire undergoing rapid internal transformation.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 12: Uthman and the First Fitna — The Caliphate Fractures (644–661 CE)
text: The Quran was compiled into the standardized canonical text — the mushaf — under the direction of Zayd ibn Thabit, with Uthman ordering the collection of all existing written fragments, the comparison with the memories of living huffaz, and the production of multiple copies to be sent to the major garrison cities. The variant readings and partial collections that had circulated before were ordered destroyed. This act — the canonical fixation of the Quranic text — was theologically necessary to prevent the fragmentation of Islamic scripture that had occurred in Judaism and Christianity, but it was also a political assertion of caliphal authority over the religious life of the community. The burning of non-canonical Quranic manuscripts was controversial at the time and remains so in modern historical scholarship, which wonders what was lost.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 12: Uthman and the First Fitna — The Caliphate Fractures (644–661 CE)
text: The pattern was unmistakable: the Umayyad clan, which had been the Prophet's primary Qurayshi opposition and which had converted last, was now managing the empire.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 12: Uthman and the First Fitna — The Caliphate Fractures (644–661 CE)
text: The mawali — non-Arab converts to Islam — were, in Islamic theology, full members of the community with equal rights. In administrative practice, they received lower diwan stipends than Arab Muslims, were excluded from the tribal organization of the garrison cities, were often required to continue paying jizya even after conversion (a practice that was legally dubious but fiscally convenient for provincial governors), and were treated as social inferiors. The grievances of the mawali, particularly in Iraq and Persia where their numbers were growing rapidly, found expression in religious movements that challenged the Arab tribal aristocracy's monopoly on political and military power.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 12: Uthman and the First Fitna — The Caliphate Fractures (644–661 CE)
text: By 654 CE, delegations from the garrison cities — Kufa, Basra, Fustat — were arriving in Medina with lists of complaints against their governors and demands that Uthman remove them. The tradition records multiple rounds of negotiation, in which Uthman promised reforms, removed some governors, and then — apparently under pressure from Marwan and the Umayyad faction in Medina — reversed or delayed the promised changes. The most famous incident involves a letter, allegedly forged by Marwan without Uthman's knowledge, that was intercepted by the Egyptian delegation as they were returning to Egypt. The letter, ostensibly from Uthman to the governor of Egypt, ordered the execution or punishment of the delegation's leaders on their return. The delegation turned back to Medina, besieged Uthman's house, and demanded his abdication.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 12: Uthman and the First Fitna — The Caliphate Fractures (644–661 CE)
text: Uthman was killed on June 17, 656 CE. The rebels broke into his house and found him reading the Quran. He was stabbed multiple times; his wife Naila tried to shield him and reportedly had her fingers cut off. The specific identities of the killers are disputed in the sources — various tribal groups from Egypt, Kufa, and Basra are implicated — but the political responsibility was collective. The murder of the caliph, in his own house, in the sacred city of Medina, while reading the Quran, was a theological and political catastrophe. The tradition records that Uthman's blood splattered on the page he was reading — Quran 2:137, "So God will be sufficient for you against them" — and that the bloodstained Quran was preserved and displayed by the Umayyads as evidence of his martyrdom and the illegitimacy of those who allowed or caused his death.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 12: Uthman and the First Fitna — The Caliphate Fractures (644–661 CE)
text: Ali ibn Abi Talib was proclaimed caliph within days of Uthman's death, in circumstances that guaranteed his caliphate would be contested from the beginning. He was the closest surviving male relative of Muhammad, the husband of the Prophet's daughter Fatima, the father of Muhammad's only surviving grandsons (Hasan and Husayn), one of the earliest converts, a veteran of every major battle of Muhammad's career, and — in the view of his supporters — the rightful caliph who had been unjustly passed over in favor of Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman. He was also, from the perspective of the Umayyads and others who questioned the legitimacy of his selection, a man who had failed to protect the previous caliph, who had been proclaimed by the same rebels who had just committed murder, and whose authority was therefore tainted by association with that murder.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 12: Uthman and the First Fitna — The Caliphate Fractures (644–661 CE)
text: Aisha, the Prophet's widow and a figure of considerable political influence, opposed Ali openly, reportedly on the grounds that he had failed to protect Uthman and that Uthman's killers needed to be punished before any other business could proceed.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 12: Uthman and the First Fitna — The Caliphate Fractures (644–661 CE)
text: The Battle of the Camel (December 656 CE), fought near Basra in southern Iraq, was the first military engagement between Muslim forces and marked the definitive end of the political unity of the early Islamic community. Talha, Zubayr, and Aisha had moved to Basra and organized a force to demand justice for Uthman. Ali marched from Medina with a force drawn from the Medinan Ansar, the Meccan Muhajirun who supported him, and various tribal contingents. The battle was named for the camel on which Aisha sat in a covered howdah, directing her forces — a detail that the tradition records with evident discomfort, since a woman's participation in combat leadership violated emerging norms about female propriety. The engagement was vicious. Both Talha and Zubayr were killed, either in the battle or in its immediate aftermath. Thousands died — the sources give numbers that are certainly inflated but that indicate casualties in the thousands. Aisha was captured unharmed and sent back to Medina, where she would live for another twenty years but never again play a direct political role.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 12: Uthman and the First Fitna — The Caliphate Fractures (644–661 CE)
text: The Battle of Siffin was not a single engagement but a series of clashes over multiple days, characterized by high casualties on both sides and no clear tactical advantage. The sources preserve numerous individual combat narratives — the single combat challenges in the Arabian tradition, the heroic deaths, the eloquent speeches — that are more valuable as literature than as military history, but the general picture is of an attritional engagement that neither side could decisively win. Ali's forces appear to have been gaining the upper hand when Muawiyah's commander, Amr ibn al-As (who had joined Muawiyah's cause after being removed from the governorship of Egypt), reportedly ordered the Syrian forces to affix pages of the Quran to their spears and call for arbitration according to God's book. The arbitration proposal (tahkim) was, from Ali's perspective, a political trap. Accepting arbitration implied that the question of the caliphate's legitimacy was open to human judgment rather than already decided by the community's oath of allegiance. Refusing arbitration, however, would make Ali appear to reject the Quran's authority in favor of military force. A significant portion of Ali's army — particularly the pious Iraqi tribesmen who had joined him specifically on religious grounds — demanded that he accept arbitration. Ali accepted, appointed Abu Musa al-Ash'ari as his representative, and withdrew from the field. The arbitration proceedings, held at Adhruh in Jordan in early 658 CE, were a political disaster for Ali. The details are confused in the sources, which preserve multiple contradictory accounts, but the outcome was clear: Abu Musa and Amr ibn al-As (Muawiyah's representative) announced that both Ali and Muawiyah should be deposed and the community should choose a new caliph. Abu Musa, thinking this was a mutually agreed position, announced Ali's deposition. Amr then announced that while he agreed Ali should be deposed, Muawiyah remained the legitimate avenger of Uthman's blood and the rightful claimant. Ali rejected the arbitration's outcome as fraudulent, but the political damage was done.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 12: Uthman and the First Fitna — The Caliphate Fractures (644–661 CE)
text: The Kharijite position was theologically radical: any Muslim who committed a major sin was no longer a Muslim and could be killed; political leadership should go to the most pious Muslim regardless of tribal lineage; and the entire existing political order — Ali's caliphate, Muawiyah's governorship, the tribal aristocracy, the diwan system, the distinction between Arab and non-Arab Muslims — was corrupt and needed to be destroyed and replaced with a purified Islamic community.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 12: Uthman and the First Fitna — The Caliphate Fractures (644–661 CE)
text: Ali's assassination on January 28, 661 CE, was carried out by the Kharijite Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam, who struck him with a poisoned sword while he was leading morning prayer in the Kufa mosque. Ali died two days later. Ibn Muljam was executed, but the political theology the Kharijites represented could not be executed. Ali's son Hasan ibn Ali was proclaimed caliph in Kufa, but within months he had negotiated a deal with Muawiyah: in exchange for a pension and guarantees of personal safety, Hasan abdicated, and Muawiyah was proclaimed caliph.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 13: Muawiyah and the Umayyad Settlement — Pragmatism as Policy (661–680 CE)
text: Hasan, who had been proclaimed caliph in Kufa after Ali's death, held military forces loyal to his father's memory and to the claim that the caliphate belonged to the ahl al-bayt — the family of the Prophet.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 14: The Second Fitna and the Consolidation of Umayyad Power (680–705 CE)
text: The Karbala crisis began as a question of allegiance and ended as the foundational martyrology of Shia Islam. Husayn ibn Ali, the younger son of Ali and Fatima and therefore the Prophet's grandson, had refused to swear allegiance to Yazid. His position was principled: the caliphate belonged to the family of the Prophet, not to the Umayyad clan that had opposed Muhammad longest and converted latest. He withdrew from Medina to Mecca, probably intending to avoid direct confrontation while signaling his non-recognition of Yazid's authority. Letters arrived from Kufa — dozens of them, according to the tradition — inviting him to come to Iraq where the Kufan community would support his caliphate. Husayn's cousin Muslim ibn Aqil was sent to Kufa to assess the situation; he reported that support was substantial and that Husayn should come. Husayn departed Mecca for Kufa in September 680 CE with approximately seventy or eighty people — family members, supporters, a small number of armed men. This was not an army; it was a religious community moving under the assumption that Kufa's population would protect them when they arrived. The assumption was catastrophically wrong. Yazid's governor in Kufa, Ubaydallah ibn Ziyad (son of Ziyad ibn Abihi), had learned of Husayn's departure and had systematically intimidated and bribed the Kufan leadership into withdrawing their support. Muslim ibn Aqil was captured and executed. By the time Husayn's party reached the outskirts of Kufa, the city that had promised to support him had locked its gates.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 14: The Second Fitna and the Consolidation of Umayyad Power (680–705 CE)
text: The encounter at Karbala on October 10, 680 CE was not a battle but an execution. A Kufan force of approximately 4,000 men under Umar ibn Sa'd (son of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, the conqueror of Qadisiyya — the ironies of lineage are bitter in this narrative) surrounded Husayn's party near the Euphrates. Negotiations were attempted; the Umayyad command demanded unconditional surrender, which Husayn refused. The camp was besieged, cut off from water, and after several days of increasingly desperate conditions, was assaulted. Husayn's male companions and relatives were killed in fighting or executed after capture. Husayn himself was killed and beheaded. His head was sent to Damascus as proof of the suppression. The women and children — including Husayn's sister Zaynab and his infant son Ali ibn Husayn, who survived because he was too ill to fight — were taken captive and paraded through the streets of Kufa and then Damascus.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 14: The Second Fitna and the Consolidation of Umayyad Power (680–705 CE)
text: The annual mourning of Ashura — the tenth day of Muharram, anniversary of Husayn's death — became the central ritual of Shia Islam, transforming a political defeat into a perpetual indictment of Sunni political legitimacy.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 14: The Second Fitna and the Consolidation of Umayyad Power (680–705 CE)
text: For approximately nine years (683–692 CE), the Islamic world had two competing caliphates: the Marwanid Umayyad caliphate based in Damascus and the Zubayrid caliphate based in Mecca.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 14: The Second Fitna and the Consolidation of Umayyad Power (680–705 CE)
text: Iraq was consumed by a Kharijite revolt under Mukhtar al-Thaqafi, who claimed to be acting on behalf of Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya (Ali's son by a wife other than Fatima) and who built a coalition that included significant numbers of mawali — non-Arab converts who saw in Mukhtar's movement a chance to assert equality with Arab Muslims. Mukhtar captured Kufa in 685 CE, executed those he identified as responsible for Husayn's death (a systematic purge that had significant popular support), and controlled much of Iraq before being defeated and killed by Zubayrid forces in 687 CE.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 14: The Second Fitna and the Consolidation of Umayyad Power (680–705 CE)
text: Abd al-Malik's reconsolidation of Umayyad power was methodical and required the extraordinary service of al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, who would become simultaneously the most effective and the most reviled governor in Umayyad history.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 14: The Second Fitna and the Consolidation of Umayyad Power (680–705 CE)
text: The siege and sacking of Mecca in 692 CE was the military resolution of the Zubayrid challenge. Hajjaj, before his appointment to Iraq, had been given command of the forces sent to reduce Ibn Zubayr's last stronghold. He besieged Mecca, reportedly using catapults to bombard the city — including damage to the Kaaba, which was hit and partially destroyed. Ibn Zubayr was killed in fighting near the Kaaba. The sacred character of Mecca, which had been respected during the conquests and which Islamic law protected, did not protect it from military assault when the Umayyads' survival required its conquest. The tradition records this with discomfort, and later Umayyad propaganda attempted to minimize the damage and blame natural causes rather than deliberate bombardment, but the basic fact of the assault stands. The Umayyads had demonstrated that political survival trumped religious scruple.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 14: The Second Fitna and the Consolidation of Umayyad Power (680–705 CE)
text: The new Islamic coinage, introduced in 696–697 CE, bore no human or animal images (conforming to the emerging Islamic prohibition on figural representation) and inscribed instead the shahada and Quranic verses asserting God's unity.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 14: The Second Fitna and the Consolidation of Umayyad Power (680–705 CE)
text: The Dome of the Rock, constructed in Jerusalem on the Temple Mount between 688 and 692 CE, was Abd al-Malik's most enduring monument and the earliest surviving Islamic architectural masterpiece. The structure was built on the site identified in Islamic tradition as the location of Muhammad's Night Journey and Ascension, directly adjacent to the ruins of the Second Temple. Its architectural form — a central-plan domed structure — was adapted from Byzantine martyrium architecture, but its decoration was distinctively Islamic: elaborate mosaics and inscriptions in Arabic, Quranic verses emphasizing God's unity and Jesus's status as prophet rather than divine, and a deliberate aesthetic that competed with the Christian churches of Jerusalem and Constantinople. The inscriptions inside the Dome of the Rock include some of the earliest surviving Quranic text and some of the clearest statements of Islamic theology directed at Christian audiences: "O People of the Book, do not go to extremes in your religion, and do not say anything about God except the truth: the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was nothing more than a messenger of God" (Quran 4:171).

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 15: The Great Conquests Extended — North Africa, Spain, Central Asia (695–750 CE)
text: Over the following century, Iberia would develop a distinctive Islamic culture — al-Andalus — that would become one of the jewels of medieval Islamic civilization, but in 711–712 CE it was simply another conquest.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 15: The Great Conquests Extended — North Africa, Spain, Central Asia (695–750 CE)
text: The Battle of Talas (751 CE), fought on the Talas River in modern Kazakhstan between Arab forces under Ziyad ibn Salih and a Tang Chinese army, was the point of maximum eastern expansion. The battle was a Muslim victory — the Chinese forces withdrew and never again attempted to contest the region west of the Pamirs — but its military significance was limited. What made it consequential was the technological transfer: Chinese prisoners taken at Talas included paper-makers who brought the technology to Samarkand, from where paper-making spread across the Islamic world and eventually to Europe. Paper, which was cheaper to produce than papyrus or parchment and more durable than papyrus, revolutionized Islamic administrative and scholarly culture. The bureaucracies, libraries, and madrasas of the Abbasid period were sustained by paper, and the technology transfer at Talas is one of the more consequential unintended results of a military engagement in world history.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 16: What the Conquered Became — Social Transformation Under Arab Rule
text: The traditional Parsi account, preserved in the Qissa-i Sanjan, describes refugees fleeing religious persecution in Persia and being granted asylum by a Hindu king in Gujarat. The historical reality was probably more complex — economic as well as religious motivations, multiple waves of migration, and gradual rather than sudden establishment. What is certain is that the Parsi community preserved Zoroastrian religious practice, the Avestan language, and the memory of Persian cultural identity in a South Asian environment for over a millennium, making them one of the more remarkable examples of religious survival under demographic pressure in world history.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 17: The Abbasid Revolution — End of the Umayyad World (718–750 CE)
text: The Abbasid dawah (call, propaganda movement) began, according to the traditional chronology, around 718–719 CE, in the caliphate of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz. The movement's origins are obscure because the sources were written after the Abbasids had won and had reasons to systematize a narrative that was originally more improvised. What is clear is that descendants of Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib — the Prophet's uncle — began organizing a political movement that claimed to represent the restoration of legitimate authority to the "family of the Prophet" (ahl al-bayt). The deliberate vagueness of this formulation was strategically brilliant: it could appeal to Alid sympathizers who wanted rule by the Prophet's family, to those who wanted rule by the Hashimite clan generally (which included both Alids and Abbasids), and to those who simply wanted an alternative to the Umayyads without committing to a specific vision of what that alternative should be. The slogan "the chosen one from the family of Muhammad" (al-rida min al Muhammad) named no names and promised everything.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 17: The Abbasid Revolution — End of the Umayyad World (718–750 CE)
text: Abu Muslim al-Khorasani is the figure who converted the dawah from a propaganda network into a military movement. His origins are disputed in the sources: some say he was a Persian mawla, others that he was an Arab of obscure lineage, still others that he was of Central Asian origin. What is certain is that he emerged in the late 740s CE as the dawah's military organizer in Khorasan, that he commanded exceptional loyalty from his followers, and that he possessed political and military skills that rivaled the greatest commanders of the conquest period. He was appointed by the Abbasid family — specifically by Ibrahim al-Imam, the Abbasid claimant recognized by the movement before the revolution's success — to lead the armed phase of the revolution. He raised the black banners that became the symbol of Abbasid military forces, mobilized a coalition army from the Khorasani Arab tribes and the mawali population, and began military operations against the Umayyad provincial administration in 747 CE.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 17: The Abbasid Revolution — End of the Umayyad World (718–750 CE)
text: Marwan reached Egypt and attempted to organize resistance, but the Egyptian garrison had no particular loyalty to him and limited capacity for effective military action. He was killed in August 750 CE in the village of Busir in the Egyptian Fayyum, not in battle but in a farmhouse where he had taken refuge. The last Umayyad caliph died in circumstances as ignominious as Yazdegerd III's death a century earlier — a parallel that was not lost on contemporary observers.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 17: The Abbasid Revolution — End of the Umayyad World (718–750 CE)
text: The Abbasids invited the surviving Umayyad princes and notables to a reconciliation banquet; when they arrived, they were seized and executed, reportedly beaten to death with clubs while the Abbasids continued dining on the corpses. This atrocity story appears in multiple sources and may be embellished, but that a systematic purge occurred is beyond dispute. The Abbasids were determined that the Umayyad dynasty would not survive to organize a restoration. The bodies of the Umayyad caliphs — even those long dead — were reportedly exhumed and desecrated, except for Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, whose reputation for piety was so strong that even the Abbasids did not dare violate his grave.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 17: The Abbasid Revolution — End of the Umayyad World (718–750 CE)
text: One Umayyad prince escaped the massacre: Abd al-Rahman ibn Muawiyah, a grandson of the caliph Hisham, fled through North Africa and crossed to Iberia in 755 CE, where he established an independent Umayyad emirate in al-Andalus. His survival and his creation of a rival power center in the west meant that the Umayyad legacy was not entirely eliminated, but the dynasty as an imperial force was destroyed. The Umayyad state that had ruled the Islamic world from Damascus for ninety years was erased, and the Abbasid caliphate that replaced it was, from the beginning, an institutionally and ideologically different entity.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 17: The Abbasid Revolution — End of the Umayyad World (718–750 CE)
text: The city was designed as a perfect circle — the Round City, Madinat al-Salam (City of Peace) in official nomenclature — with the caliph's palace and the great mosque at the center, surrounded by concentric rings of administrative buildings, barracks, and markets. The design was consciously Persian in inspiration, drawing on Sasanian models of ceremonial cities, and the architects and builders included Persian experts.

book: Muhammad, Rashidun & Early Islamic Conquests
section: Chapter 17: The Abbasid Revolution — End of the Umayyad World (718–750 CE)
text: The office of wazir (vizier), borrowed from Sasanian administrative tradition, became the effective head of the caliphal bureaucracy, responsible for day-to-day administration while the caliph retained ultimate authority. The Persian bureaucratic families — particularly the Barmakids, originally Buddhist temple administrators from Balkh who converted to Islam and served as wazirs for three generations under the early Abbasids — brought Sasanian administrative expertise, literary culture, and political philosophy into the Islamic imperial system. The Abbasid court adopted Persian ceremonial forms, Persian artistic traditions, and Persian literary genres (particularly mirrors for princes and administrative manuals).

book: Ottoman & Safavid Empires- The Gunpowder Age
section: Chapter 1: The Ottoman Emergence (1299-1453)
text: In 1299, when Osman I supposedly declared independence from the Seljuk sultanate, his beylik controlled perhaps a few hundred square kilometers of territory in northwestern Anatolia. A century and a half later, his descendants ruled an empire stretching from the Danube to the Euphrates. This

book: Ottoman & Safavid Empires- The Gunpowder Age
section: Chapter 1: The Ottoman Emergence (1299-1453)
text: The traditional ghazi narrative portrays early Ottoman expansion as religiously motivated holy war against Christian infidels. While this ideology certainly existed and provided legitimacy for conquest, material incentives drove expansion more consistently than theological fervor. Raiding Byzantine territories offered plunder, captives for enslavement, and land grants for warrior followers. The ghazi ethos legitimized what were fundamentally predatory economic relationships, allowing the Ottomans to attract Muslim warriors from across Anatolia who sought enrichment through frontier warfare. Religious ideology made excellent warriors, but land, booty, and tax revenues made sustainable states.

book: Ottoman & Safavid Empires- The Gunpowder Age
section: Chapter 1: The Ottoman Emergence (1299-1453)
text: The timar system granted cavalry warriors revenue rights from specific territories in exchange for military service, creating a self-sustaining cavalry force without requiring salaries from the central treasury.

book: Ottoman & Safavid Empires- The Gunpowder Age
section: Chapter 1: The Ottoman Emergence (1299-1453)
text: The conquest of Constantinople in 1453 culminated 150 years of Ottoman expansion and transformed the empire's character. Mehmed II's preparations demonstrated the combination of technological capability, administrative organization, and strategic vision that distinguished the Ottomans from frontier raiders. The siege required months of logistical preparation, assembling an army of perhaps 80,000 men and a siege train including massive cannons cast specifically for destroying Constantinople's ancient walls. The Hungarian engineer Orban, who offered his services to both Byzantines and Ottomans and chose the latter because they could pay him, cast a cannon requiring 60 oxen to transport and capable of firing stone balls weighing over half a ton. This weapon and others like it represented the cutting edge of 15th-century military technology.

book: Ottoman & Safavid Empires- The Gunpowder Age
section: Chapter 1: The Ottoman Emergence (1299-1453)
text: The integration of the Greek Orthodox hierarchy as an administrative instrument exemplified Ottoman pragmatism. Rather than attempting to directly govern millions of Christians through Muslim administrators, the Ottomans recognized the Patriarch as the millet-bashi (head of the religious community) with authority over marriage, inheritance, and communal disputes. This system reduced administrative burden while maintaining control through a compliant Christian leadership. The Patriarch and his bishops, dependent on sultanic approval for their positions, had incentives to prevent Christian rebellion and ensure tax collection. This millet system would be extended to other religious communities and became a characteristic feature of Ottoman governance.

book: Ottoman & Safavid Empires- The Gunpowder Age
section: Chapter 2: Imperial Consolidation Under Mehmed II and Bayezid II (1453-1512)
text: Mehmed II, who titled himself Kayser-i Rum (Caesar of Rome), pursued this claim through systematic expansion in the Balkans, Anatolia, and the Black Sea littoral. The period from 1453 to 1512 saw the consolidation of Ottoman territorial gains, the development of imperial institutions, and the emergence of ideological frameworks justifying Ottoman supremacy. It also saw the limits of expansion tested through costly wars with Venice, the Mamluks, and ultimately the recognition of a new threat in the Safavid movement that would reshape the Middle Eastern strategic landscape.

book: Ottoman & Safavid Empires- The Gunpowder Age
section: Chapter 2: Imperial Consolidation Under Mehmed II and Bayezid II (1453-1512)
text: The appointment of Gennadios Scholarios as the first post-conquest Patriarch exemplified this arrangement. Gennadios, a learned theologian who had opposed the union with Rome promoted at the Council of Florence, represented the Orthodox faction that preferred Ottoman rule to Catholic domination. His appointment signaled to Orthodox Christians that the Ottomans would protect their religious autonomy against Catholic pressure. In return, Gennadios and subsequent Patriarchs preached submission to Ottoman authority and condemned rebellion as sinful. This alliance between Ottoman power and Orthodox hierarchy would persist for centuries, to the mutual benefit of both.

book: Ottoman & Safavid Empires- The Gunpowder Age
section: Chapter 2: Imperial Consolidation Under Mehmed II and Bayezid II (1453-1512)
text: The arrival of Jewish refugees from Iberia after the expulsions of 1492 provided the Ottoman Empire with skilled populations that enriched its economic and intellectual life. The Spanish and Portuguese monarchs' expulsion of Jews and Muslims, motivated by religious ideology and political consolidation, sent waves of refugees eastward. The Ottomans, operating under different incentives, welcomed these refugees. Bayezid II reportedly mocked Ferdinand and Isabella for impoverishing their kingdoms to enrich his. Jewish physicians, merchants, financiers, craftsmen, and scholars settled in Istanbul, Salonika, and other Ottoman cities, bringing skills and commercial networks that benefited the empire. Jewish involvement in textile production, printing, medicine, and finance became significant. The establishment of Hebrew printing presses in Ottoman cities predated the introduction of Turkish printing by decades; the Ottomans had no ideological objection to printing in non-Arabic scripts, and Jewish printers produced religious and secular texts. Jewish merchants facilitated trade connections with Europe, North Africa, and the Levant. Physicians trained in European universities served in the Ottoman court. This immigration demonstrated the Ottoman Empire's relative tolerance compared to contemporary European states; while Jews remained subject to the restrictions of dhimmi status, they suffered no equivalent to the Inquisition or forced conversions.

book: Ottoman & Safavid Empires- The Gunpowder Age
section: Chapter 2: Imperial Consolidation Under Mehmed II and Bayezid II (1453-1512)
text: The cultural synthesis developing in this period combined Byzantine, Islamic, and Turkish elements into a distinctive Ottoman civilization. Mehmed II patronized both Muslim and Christian scholars, collecting manuscripts in multiple languages and supporting translations. Italian artists worked at his court, creating portraits and architectural designs. Greek scholars served as translators and advisors. This cultural eclecticism reflected the empire's multinational, multi-religious character and the elite's sophisticated cosmopolitanism. Ottoman high culture would develop its own aesthetic traditions, but it remained open to influences from the diverse populations under Ottoman rule.

book: Ottoman & Safavid Empires- The Gunpowder Age
section: Chapter 3: The Safavid Revolution (1501-1524)
text: The Safavid order originated in the 14th century as a Sunni Sufi tariqa (mystical order) based in Ardabil in northwestern Iran. The order attracted followers through its spiritual teachings and the charisma of its leaders, who claimed descent from the seventh Shia Imam, Musa al-Kadhim. Under Sheikh Junayd (died 1460) and his son Haydar (died 1488), the order transformed from quietist Sufism to militant activism. Junayd allied with the Turkmen Aq Qoyunlu confederation, married into its ruling family, and began leading ghazi raids against Christian Circassians in the Caucasus. This shift from spiritual contemplation to military action attracted Turkmen warriors who combined religious devotion with desire for plunder and land.

book: Ottoman & Safavid Empires- The Gunpowder Age
section: Chapter 3: The Safavid Revolution (1501-1524)
text: Haydar intensified this militarization and introduced innovations that created the distinctive Qizilbash identity. He ordered his followers to wear a distinctive red cap with twelve folds representing the twelve Shia Imams, giving them their name: Qizilbash (redheads). He preached an increasingly heterodox version of Shiism that merged Sufi mystical beliefs, Shia veneration of Ali and the Imams, and elements of pre-Islamic Iranian religious traditions. His followers regarded the Safavid sheikhs as manifestations of divine power, practically worshipping them as incarnations of God. This extreme veneration, combined with promises of paradise for those who died fighting in the order's campaigns, created fanatically loyal warriors willing to sacrifice themselves for their leader.

book: Ottoman & Safavid Empires- The Gunpowder Age
section: Chapter 3: The Safavid Revolution (1501-1524)
text: The conquest of Tabriz in 1501 and Ismail's proclamation as Shah marked the Safavid revolution's beginning. His forces, estimated at perhaps 7,000 cavalry, defeated the Aq Qoyunlu at the Battle of Sharur in 1501, capturing Tabriz and executing the Aq Qoyunlu ruler. Ismail immediately ordered the public cursing of the first three caliphs—Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman—whom Sunnis revered but Shias regarded as usurpers who deprived Ali of his rightful leadership. This cursing (tabarru), performed in Friday prayers and public ceremonies, signaled the violent imposition of Shiism on a population that was predominantly Sunni. Resistance was met with execution; Ismail's forces massacred Sunni scholars who refused to convert and destroyed Sunni institutions.

book: Ottoman & Safavid Empires- The Gunpowder Age
section: Chapter 3: The Safavid Revolution (1501-1524)
text: Herat and Khorasan fell in 1510 after Ismail defeated the Uzbek khan Muhammad Shaybani, whose skull Ismail had mounted in gold and used as a drinking cup.

book: Ottoman & Safavid Empires- The Gunpowder Age
section: Chapter 3: The Safavid Revolution (1501-1524)
text: The forced conversion of Iran to Twelver Shiism was violent and systematic. Sunni mosques were confiscated and converted to Shia use. Sunni scholars were executed, exiled, or forced to convert. The tombs of Sunni saints were desecrated. The public cursing of the first three caliphs, which Sunnis regarded as blasphemy deserving death, was made mandatory in Friday prayers. Anyone refusing to curse Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman faced execution. Ismail imported Shia scholars from Jabal Amil in Lebanon, from Bahrain, and from Shia communities elsewhere to staff the new religious establishment. These scholars, granted generous patronage and official positions, provided the intellectual infrastructure for converting Iran's religious identity.

book: Ottoman & Safavid Empires- The Gunpowder Age
section: Chapter 3: The Safavid Revolution (1501-1524)
text: The distribution of provinces as suyurghal (grants) to Qizilbash tribal leaders created regional power bases that challenged central authority. The Ustajlu tribe controlled Azerbaijan, the Shamlu governed Herat, the Rumlu held Anatolia's border regions. These governors collected taxes, maintained armies, and administered justice with minimal oversight from the central government. While this system mobilized military resources without requiring a centralized bureaucracy, it also meant provincial governors could rebel or pursue independent policies. The shah's authority depended on his personal charisma and military success; any sign of weakness invited challenges from ambitious tribal leaders.

book: Ottoman & Safavid Empires- The Gunpowder Age
section: Chapter 3: The Safavid Revolution (1501-1524)
text: Safavid propaganda circulated in Anatolia, preaching that the Ottomans were illegitimate Sunni tyrants and that true Muslims should support the Safavids. Several rebellions in Anatolia combined social and economic grievances with Qizilbash ideology, threatening Ottoman control. The most serious, Shah Qulu's rebellion in 1511, required substantial Ottoman forces to suppress and demonstrated the genuine appeal of Safavid ideology among Anatolian Turkmen. Selim I's response was systematic genocide aimed at eliminating the Qizilbash fifth column. In 1512-1514, Ottoman forces massacred an estimated 40,000 Anatolian Qizilbash, including women and children. Villages suspected of Qizilbash sympathies were destroyed, their populations executed or enslaved. This was not conventional warfare against enemy armies but the deliberate extermination of Ottoman subjects whose religious loyalties were suspect. The massacres were effective; Qizilbash rebellions in Anatolia largely ceased, and the ideological threat was contained through terror. Modern debates over whether this constitutes genocide miss the point that Selim's purpose was eliminating a security threat through mass killing, and by that measure, it succeeded.

book: Ottoman & Safavid Empires- The Gunpowder Age
