section: Chapter 8: The War of Attrition and the Soviet Military Presence in Egypt (1967–1970)
subheading: 8.6 Nasser's Death and Sadat's Accession
text: Anwar Sadat's succession was initially treated — both within Egypt and by external analysts — as likely to be brief. Sadat was a Free Officers founding member but had been marginalised in Egyptian political life for years, serving as a largely ceremonial vice-president with no significant power base. The assumption was that he would be a transitional figure, quickly displaced by the more substantial political actors — Ali Sabri, the pro-Soviet faction leader, and the security services network — who considered him a placeholder. Sadat survived by outmanoeuvring the Ali Sabri faction in May 1971, arresting its leading members in what he called the "Corrective Revolution," and establishing his personal control over the security services, the party apparatus, and the military command with a decisiveness that surprised all observers. His subsequent strategic choices — the expulsion of Soviet advisors in July 1972, the decision to go to war in October 1973, the peace initiative of 1977 — were all departures from Nasser's framework so fundamental that they constituted a genuine rupture rather than continuity. But Sadat's ability to execute those departures rested on the institutional inheritance Nasser had built: a centralised Egyptian state with a powerful military and security apparatus that, once controlled, gave its leader extraordinary freedom of action.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 9: Jordan, the PLO, and Black September (1970–1971)
subheading: 9.1 The Post-1967 Palestinian Political Landscape
text: The Battle of Karameh in March 1968 — in which Israeli forces crossed into Jordan to destroy Fatah's main base in the Karameh refugee camp and encountered unexpectedly fierce Palestinian and Jordanian resistance that inflicted significant Israeli casualties (29 killed, 69 wounded, several vehicles captured) before the Israeli forces withdrew — was militarily a clear Israeli victory: Karameh was destroyed and Fatah's military infrastructure in it eliminated. Politically, it was Fatah's founding myth: the first time Palestinian fighters had stood and fought Israeli forces rather than withdrawing. Arafat's claim that Karameh represented a military success was dishonest in strict operational terms but accurate in its more important sense — the battle demonstrated that Palestinian armed resistance was possible and could impose costs.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 9: Jordan, the PLO, and Black September (1970–1971)
subheading: 9.1 The Post-1967 Palestinian Political Landscape
text: Karameh produced a wave of recruitment into Fatah and the other Palestinian organisations that transformed the PLO from an Egyptian-sponsored talking shop into a genuine political-military movement. By late 1968, Palestinian armed organisations had recruited tens of thousands of fighters, established training bases in Jordan and Lebanon, and were conducting operations against Israel at a scale that the PLO's Arab League founders had never intended. The PLO's fifth National Council in February 1969 confirmed Arafat as PLO chairman and Fatah as the dominant organisation within the PLO framework — completing the transformation of the organisation from an Arab state instrument into something claiming to represent Palestinian national will.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 9: Jordan, the PLO, and Black September (1970–1971)
subheading: 9.1 The Post-1967 Palestinian Political Landscape
text: The PFLP's specific contribution to Palestinian politics in this period was the use of international terrorism — aircraft hijacking, hostage-taking, attacks on Israeli targets in European capitals — as a political instrument. The PFLP's rationale was explicit: the Palestinian cause was invisible in international politics; spectacular acts of violence would make it visible. The calculation was partly correct in its diagnosis and entirely wrong in its prescription. Palestinian armed struggle did become internationally visible; it also ensured that the international visibility was framed primarily in terms of terrorism rather than occupation, and that the states whose support the Palestinian movement needed — Western European governments, the United States — were placed in positions where domestic political pressure made accommodation with Palestinian demands politically difficult.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 9: Jordan, the PLO, and Black September (1970–1971)
subheading: 9.2 The Palestinian State-Within-a-State in Jordan
text: Every Palestinian fedayeen operation from Jordanian territory produced an Israeli reprisal against Jordanian targets — villages, military installations, economic infrastructure — that the Jordanian army was obligated to respond to while being unable to prevent the Palestinian operations that triggered them. Israel was punishing Jordan for Palestinian actions that Jordan could not control because it had agreed to tolerate Palestinian armed presence. King Hussein's political position — between Palestinian organisations whose popular support within Jordan was substantial and whose armed capacity he could not easily suppress, and an Israeli military that was retaliating against his territory regardless of his preferences — was genuinely untenable.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 9: Jordan, the PLO, and Black September (1970–1971)
subheading: 9.3 The September 1970 Crisis: Hijackings, Syrian Intervention, and the Jordanian Army
text: The September 1970 crisis was triggered by the PFLP's simultaneous hijacking of four commercial aircraft on September 6 — TWA, Swissair, and Pan Am flights diverted to Jordan's Dawson's Field desert airstrip (the Pan Am aircraft was eventually flown to Cairo and blown up there), and an El Al flight foiled mid-air. The Dawson's Field hijackings, combined with the hostage-taking of approximately 300 passengers held as bargaining chips for the release of Palestinian prisoners in European and Israeli jails, were precisely the kind of spectacular international operation that Habash's PFLP calculated would force the conflict onto the global agenda. They also forced Hussein's hand. The Jordanian government could not tolerate the operation of an international hostage-taking in the middle of its territory without losing whatever claim to sovereignty it retained. On September 16, Hussein declared martial law and ordered the Jordanian army to move against Palestinian armed organisations throughout Jordan.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 9: Jordan, the PLO, and Black September (1970–1971)
subheading: 9.3 The September 1970 Crisis: Hijackings, Syrian Intervention, and the Jordanian Army
text: The Jordanian army's offensive — executed by Bedouin units with strong personal loyalty to the Hashemite crown and no sympathy for Palestinian political aspirations — was conducted with a ruthlessness that produced approximately 3,000 Palestinian casualties in ten days of fighting, according to Palestinian sources; Jordanian official figures were lower. The fighting in the Wehdat and Karameh camps was particularly intense, with Jordanian artillery used against urban areas. The PLO's armed capacity in Jordan was not eliminated in September — that would take until July 1971 — but it was decisively broken as a political-military alternative to Jordanian state authority.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 9: Jordan, the PLO, and Black September (1970–1971)
subheading: 9.3 The September 1970 Crisis: Hijackings, Syrian Intervention, and the Jordanian Army
text: The Syrian tank intervention of September 19–20 was the crisis point at which the conflict threatened to expand into a regional war. Syria's Ba'athist government dispatched approximately 200 tanks and armoured vehicles across the Jordanian border in support of the Palestinian organisations — framed as a pan-Arab duty to prevent the massacre of Palestinians, executed under the command of Rifaat Assad and elements of the Syrian army and Palestinian Liberation Army units under Syrian operational control. The intervention was also the product of a factional conflict within the Syrian Ba'ath between the Defence Minister Hafez al-Assad, who opposed the intervention as strategically reckless, and the party's civilian leadership under Salah Jadid, who ordered it.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 9: Jordan, the PLO, and Black September (1970–1971)
subheading: 9.3 The September 1970 Crisis: Hijackings, Syrian Intervention, and the Jordanian Army
text: Jordan's army held but was in genuine difficulty — its air force was the decisive counter to Syrian armour, but Hussein needed political cover to use it against another Arab state. The cover came from two directions simultaneously: Israel mobilised armoured forces on the Golan Heights in a demonstrative show of force that signalled willingness to intervene against Syrian forces if they advanced further into Jordan, and Washington signalled through back-channels that it would support Israeli action if needed to prevent Jordan's overthrow. The combination of Israeli mobilisation, American diplomatic signalling, and Hafez al-Assad's internal refusal to commit Syrian air cover to the tank columns (leaving them vulnerable to Jordanian air strikes) produced Syrian withdrawal on September 22. Assad's refusal to commit Syrian air power — a decision that isolated the tank columns and exposed Jadid's military adventurism — was also Assad's political coup: he used the episode to discredit Jadid and complete his own takeover of Syria in November 1970.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 9: Jordan, the PLO, and Black September (1970–1971)
subheading: 9.4 The Expulsion of the PLO from Jordan
text: For Palestinian politics, the expulsion from Jordan — called Black September by Palestinian nationalists, a name adopted by the assassination organisation that emerged from it — was the third major displacement of Palestinian political aspirations after 1948 and 1967.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 9: Jordan, the PLO, and Black September (1970–1971)
subheading: 9.5 The Munich Massacre and the Internationalisation of Palestinian Armed Struggle
text: On September 5, 1972, eight Black September operatives seized eleven Israeli athletes and coaches in the Olympic Village. After a failed West German rescue attempt at Fürstenfeldbruck airport, all eleven hostages, one West German policeman, and five of the eight attackers were killed. The operation was a tactical disaster — the PLO received no intelligence benefit and no prisoner exchanges — and a political catastrophe: it produced revulsion in Western European public opinion, gave Israeli intelligence the political mandate for a sustained targeted killing campaign (Operation Wrath of God, authorised by Golda Meir) against the operation's planners and executors, and damaged whatever goodwill the Palestinian cause had accumulated in international opinion.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 9: Jordan, the PLO, and Black September (1970–1971)
subheading: 9.5 The Munich Massacre and the Internationalisation of Palestinian Armed Struggle
text: West German security failure was specific and documentable. German authorities had intelligence warning of a possible Palestinian operation at the Olympics; they had no counter-terrorism capacity — no trained hostage-rescue force, no practised protocol for responding to a barricade situation in a residential compound. The decision to attempt the rescue at the airport, with inadequate snipers and no coordinated assault capability, was taken by officials without military special operations expertise and without seeking Israeli assistance that might have produced different results. The German government's post-Munich establishment of GSG 9 — the federal border guard counter-terrorism unit — was the direct institutional consequence.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 9: Jordan, the PLO, and Black September (1970–1971)
subheading: 9.5 The Munich Massacre and the Internationalisation of Palestinian Armed Struggle
text: Israel's Operation Wrath of God — conducted by Mossad over several years through Western Europe, Lebanon, and elsewhere — eliminated most of the operational planners of the Munich operation and a number of other Black September figures. The campaign was not without error: the killing of a Moroccan waiter in Lillehammer, Norway, in July 1973, who was mistakenly identified as Ali Hassan Salameh (the Black September operational commander), resulted in two Mossad officers being tried and convicted in Norwegian courts. Salameh himself was eventually killed in Beirut in January 1979.The Munich massacre and its aftermath established the template for the international counterterrorism framework that would develop through the 1970s: state-sponsored targeted killing as a response to non-state terrorism, the particular vulnerability of large international gatherings, and the tension between intelligence sharing requirements and the sovereignty constraints of operations in third countries. It also established the dynamic that would characterise Israeli counterterrorism for decades: maximum operational effectiveness against the specific perpetrators combined with political effects on Palestinian civilian populations that the operations were not designed to consider.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 9: Jordan, the PLO, and Black September (1970–1971)
subheading: 9.6 The PLO as Diplomatic Actor
text: Arafat's address to the UN General Assembly in November 1974 — the famous "olive branch and freedom fighter's gun" speech — marked the formal entry of the PLO into the international diplomatic arena with observer status. The speech was simultaneously a gesture toward international legitimacy (the olive branch) and a demonstration of continued commitment to armed struggle (the gun) that served Arafat's specific political requirements: he needed to be seen by Palestinian hardliners as maintaining the armed struggle option while demonstrating to the international community that the PLO was a political actor capable of negotiated settlement.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 10: The Oil Weapon — OPEC, the 1973 War, and the End of Cheap Energy
subheading: 10.1 The Pre-War Oil Geography
text: The Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries was established in Baghdad in 1960 by Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, and Venezuela in direct response to the Seven Sisters' unilateral reduction of the posted price in 1959 and 1960 — price cuts that reduced producer government revenues without any consultation with the governments whose primary revenue source was being diminished. OPEC's initial decade was more significant as a statement of producer government intent than as an operational cartel: member governments lacked the technical expertise, the unified political will, and the legal instruments to override company pricing decisions effectively. But OPEC's existence created the institutional framework within which the 1973 revolution would operate.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 10: The Oil Weapon — OPEC, the 1973 War, and the End of Cheap Energy
subheading: 10.1 The Pre-War Oil Geography
text: Libya's Muammar Gaddafi, who took power in 1969, used Libya's particular leverage — Libyan oil was high quality, geographically close to European markets, and had become critical to several companies' European supply chains — to extract successively more favourable terms from individual companies, breaking the unified front that the Seven Sisters had previously maintained against bilateral renegotiation. The Tripoli and Tehran agreements of 1971 established the principle that producer governments could collectively renegotiate the terms of concessions that companies had previously treated as inviolable. Iraq's nationalisation of the Iraq Petroleum Company in 1972 demonstrated that a producer government could seize a major oil installation and sustain production without the technical assistance of the international companies, provided it had access to Soviet technical support and alternative marketing channels.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 10: The Oil Weapon — OPEC, the 1973 War, and the End of Cheap Energy
subheading: 10.1 The Pre-War Oil Geography
text: The Organisation of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries — OAPEC, distinct from the broader OPEC — had been established in 1968 by Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Libya specifically as a vehicle for Arab producers to coordinate oil policy in connection with the Arab-Israeli conflict. OAPEC's membership was more restricted than OPEC's, excluding non-Arab producers, and its mandate included the use of oil supply as a political instrument in ways that OPEC's more commercially focused mandate did not explicitly authorise. By October 1973, the price of Saudi Arabian crude had risen from approximately $1.80 per barrel in 1970 to approximately $3.00 per barrel — a substantial increase but one that still represented cheap energy by historical standards and that still left the producer governments dependent on company pricing mechanisms they did not control. The structural conditions for a price revolution were in place; the 1973 war provided the political trigger.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 10: The Oil Weapon — OPEC, the 1973 War, and the End of Cheap Energy
subheading: 10.3 The October War: Military Operations and Strategic Balance
text: The Egyptian canal crossing on October 6, 1973 — the tenth of Ramadan in the Islamic calendar and Yom Kippur in the Jewish one, both dates chosen to maximise the element of surprise — was a remarkable military operation that reversed the humiliation of 1967 through meticulous planning and execution of the specific limited objectives for which Egyptian forces had been prepared. The crossing was preceded by an artillery bombardment of approximately 10,500 guns firing simultaneously along the canal front, followed by the crossing of the first wave in rubber dinghies, the clearing of Israeli sand ramparts using high-pressure water jets from equipment obtained from West Germany, and the deployment of bridges sufficient to carry tanks and armoured vehicles. The Bar-Lev Line — the Israeli defensive network of fortified positions along the eastern bank — was overrun in the first hours; its garrisons had been thinned by budget constraints and Israeli overconfidence, and many positions fell before reinforcement arrived.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 10: The Oil Weapon — OPEC, the 1973 War, and the End of Cheap Energy
subheading: 10.3 The October War: Military Operations and Strategic Balance
text: The Israeli armoured counter-attacks of October 7–8 were the critical test. Israeli armoured doctrine called for immediate aggressive counter-attack against any crossing to destroy bridgeheads before they could be reinforced. The armoured brigades that attacked on October 7–8 were devastated by a weapons combination that Israeli tactical doctrine had not been adapted to: Soviet-supplied RPG-7 anti-tank rockets, Sagger wire-guided anti-tank missiles, and SA-6 and SA-7 surface-to-air missiles that neutralised Israeli air support. The destruction of approximately 200 Israeli tanks in the first two days of fighting in the Sinai was a shock whose strategic significance — that Soviet anti-tank technology had shifted the tactical balance between armour and infantry in favour of the defence — was not lost on Western military establishments observing the engagement.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 10: The Oil Weapon — OPEC, the 1973 War, and the End of Cheap Energy
subheading: 10.3 The October War: Military Operations and Strategic Balance
text: The Syrian offensive on the Golan was simultaneously executed and almost succeeded in a way that the Egyptian crossing, with its deliberately limited objectives, was not designed to do. Syrian armoured forces — approximately 1,400 tanks against Israel's initial force of approximately 170 on the Golan — overran Israeli positions and, by the evening of October 7, were approaching the Jordan River. The Israeli garrison of the Golan — specifically the 7th Armoured Brigade in the northern sector — conducted defensive actions of extraordinary intensity that delayed Syrian penetration in their sector until reinforcements arrived. Had the Syrian armoured commanders pressed their advantage through the night of October 7–8 rather than stopping to consolidate, the outcome might have been different.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 10: The Oil Weapon — OPEC, the 1973 War, and the End of Cheap Energy
subheading: 10.3 The October War: Military Operations and Strategic Balance
text: The Soviet resupply airlift that began on October 10 and the American counter-airlift that began on October 14 were the decisive external inputs that determined the war's final outcome. The Soviet airlift delivered replacement equipment — tanks, aircraft, ammunition — to Syria and Egypt at rates that compensated for combat losses. The American airlift — delayed by Nixon administration uncertainty about the political costs of visible American support for Israel in the context of the oil relationship, and by European allies' refusal to allow American aircraft to use European bases for the resupply — eventually delivered approximately 22,000 tons of equipment and ammunition to Israel, providing the logistical basis for the Israeli counter-offensive.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 10: The Oil Weapon — OPEC, the 1973 War, and the End of Cheap Energy
subheading: 10.3 The October War: Military Operations and Strategic Balance
text: The Egyptian armoured push into the Sinai on October 14 — ordered over the objections of Egyptian military commanders who understood that advancing beyond the SA-6 missile umbrella would expose Egyptian armour to Israeli air attack — achieved the political objective of relieving Syrian pressure by drawing Israeli forces to respond, but at catastrophic military cost: approximately 250 Egyptian tanks destroyed in a single day. The subsequent Israeli crossing of the Suez Canal on the night of October 15–16, exploiting a gap between the two Egyptian armies, produced the encirclement of the Egyptian Third Army by October 22.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 10: The Oil Weapon — OPEC, the 1973 War, and the End of Cheap Energy
subheading: 10.4 The Superpower Airlift Competition and the Nuclear Alert
text: The specific crisis of October 24–25 — the superpower confrontation that brought the Cold War to its most acute Middle Eastern moment — was triggered by Brezhnev's message to Nixon proposing joint Soviet-American military intervention to enforce the ceasefire, and threatening unilateral Soviet action if the United States refused. Soviet airborne divisions were reported on alert; a Soviet naval force was repositioned toward the eastern Mediterranean. Nixon's response — a worldwide American military alert to DEFCON 3, the first since the Cuban Missile Crisis — was intended to signal that unilateral Soviet military intervention in Egypt would be matched by American counter-deployment. Soviet forces were not deployed; the ceasefire was reinforced through diplomatic pressure on Israel to allow humanitarian supplies to the encircled Third Army.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 10: The Oil Weapon — OPEC, the 1973 War, and the End of Cheap Energy
subheading: 10.5 The Oil Embargo and Its Economic Consequences
text: The OAPEC oil embargo, announced on October 17 in response to the American airlift to Israel, was the instrument through which the Arab oil states translated military events into economic leverage of a kind that would permanently alter the global economic order. The embargo's mechanics were straightforward: OAPEC members announced a 5% monthly reduction in oil production combined with a complete embargo on oil exports to the United States and the Netherlands (the latter for its pro-Israeli position). The price increase was separate from the embargo and was announced by OPEC — including non-Arab members Iran and Venezuela — as a unilateral revision of the posted price: from approximately $3.00 per barrel before October 6 to $5.12 on October 16, and then to $11.65 per barrel on January 1, 1974, a near-quadrupling within three months. The economic consequences for the oil-importing world were immediate and severe. Western Europe, which imported approximately 80% of its oil from the Middle East, faced both physical supply shortages — petrol rationing, Sunday driving bans, speed limits — and price shocks that fed inflation and reduced economic growth simultaneously. Japan, which imported approximately 90% of its oil from Middle Eastern sources, experienced the embargo as an existential economic threat and conducted frenetic diplomacy to secure exemption from the Arab embargo by distancing its public position from American support for Israel. The United States, a domestic oil producer but increasingly dependent on imports to meet growing consumption, faced gasoline shortages and price increases that produced long queues at petrol stations and a political crisis that shaped energy policy for a decade.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 10: The Oil Weapon — OPEC, the 1973 War, and the End of Cheap Energy
subheading: 10.5 The Oil Embargo and Its Economic Consequences
text: The specific economic mechanism through which the oil shock transmitted to Western economies was the simultaneous combination of cost-push inflation (energy costs rising, driving up prices throughout the economy) and demand compression (consumer spending declining as energy costs absorbed more income), producing what economists labelled "stagflation" — the previously theoretically impossible combination of high inflation and high unemployment. The stagflation of 1973–1975 discredited the Keynesian economic consensus that had governed Western economic policy since the Second World War and created the political conditions for the monetarist counter-revolution associated with Milton Friedman, whose prescriptions would shape Reagan and Thatcher economic policy in the 1980s. The economic policy revolution of the late 1970s and 1980s was, in part, the long-term political consequence of the 1973 oil shock.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 10: The Oil Weapon — OPEC, the 1973 War, and the End of Cheap Energy
subheading: 10.6 The Political Consequences: Petrodollar Recycling and Gulf State Transformation
text: The petrodollar recycling mechanism — the investment of surplus oil revenues in Western financial markets, primarily in American Treasury bonds and European bank deposits — became the central financial relationship of the 1970s. Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency (SAMA) deposits in American and European banks, combined with direct Saudi government purchases of American Treasury securities, created a financial relationship in which Saudi Arabia was financing American government deficits at the same time that the United States was guaranteeing Saudi security. This financial interdependence would prove more durable than any formal treaty commitment and would survive political crises — including significant Arab-American friction over the Israeli question — that might otherwise have disrupted the relationship.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 10: The Oil Weapon — OPEC, the 1973 War, and the End of Cheap Energy
subheading: 10.7 Kissinger's Shuttle Diplomacy: Keeping Moscow Out
text: Henry Kissinger's shuttle diplomacy between the October War ceasefire and the Egyptian-Israeli Disengagement Agreement of January 1974 and the Syrian-Israeli Disengagement Agreement of May 1974 was the most significant display of American diplomatic skill in the Middle East in the Cold War period, and its structure — personal mediation by the Secretary of State, bilateral American negotiations with each party rather than multilateral conferences — was designed as much to exclude Soviet involvement as to achieve any specific territorial outcome. Kissinger's strategic framework was explicit in his memoirs: the Soviet Union had been Egypt's arms supplier and political patron but had not been able to deliver the political outcome Egypt needed — recovery of the Sinai. Only the United States could deliver Israeli concessions, because only the United States had the political leverage with Israel that Soviet arms supply gave Moscow with its Arab clients but that Moscow could not translate into Israeli action. If Kissinger could demonstrate that American mediation could produce Egyptian territorial recovery without Soviet participation, Egypt would have every incentive to reorient toward Washington — which was precisely what Sadat wanted and what Kissinger wanted to enable.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 11: Lebanon's Civil War — The State That Failed
subheading: 11.1 The Confessional State: Structural Instability by Design
text: The Lebanese Republic established under the French Mandate and institutionalised at independence in 1943 was built on the National Pact — an unwritten agreement between Maronite Christian and Sunni Muslim political leaders, brokered under French guidance, that distributed governmental positions among the major religious communities in proportions derived from the 1932 census conducted under French auspices. The census — the last ever conducted in Lebanon, because subsequent demographic change would have invalidated the entire political settlement — found a slight Christian majority, which justified a 6:5 ratio favouring Christians in parliamentary representation and a specific distribution of high offices: the President of the Republic would be a Maronite, the Prime Minister a Sunni, the Speaker of Parliament a Shia, and the senior military commands distributed among the communities in fixed proportions.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 11: Lebanon's Civil War — The State That Failed
subheading: 11.1 The Confessional State: Structural Instability by Design
text: The 1932 census was politically constructed from the beginning. The French Mandatory authority had an interest in a result that justified Lebanese independence as a separate entity from Syria — and a Christian-majority result supported the argument that Lebanon was a distinctive political community rather than a province of a broader Arab Muslim majority. The census methodology counted Lebanese emigrants — disproportionately Christian in their composition — as part of the Lebanese population, inflating the Christian count. It excluded or undercounted the mobile and statistically elusive Shia population of the Bekaa Valley and the south. Contemporary Lebanese historians' estimates suggest the actual Muslim majority at the time of the census was probably larger than the official count recorded. By 1975, the demographic reality of Lebanon had shifted decisively against the 1943 settlement. The Shia Muslim population — the poorest and most marginalised of Lebanon's major communities, concentrated in the agricultural south and in the Bekaa, with significant migration to Beirut's southern suburbs — had grown faster than any other community through higher birth rates and lower emigration. Estimates of the 1975 population distribution suggest Shia Muslims constituted approximately 30–35% of the population, Sunni Muslims approximately 20–25%, Maronite Christians approximately 22–25%, with the remaining communities including Greek Orthodox, Druze, and Armenian Christians making up the balance. The political system was still distributing power according to a census that was forty-three years old and demographically obsolete.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 11: Lebanon's Civil War — The State That Failed
subheading: 11.2 The Palestinian Factor: The Erosion of Lebanese Sovereignty
text: The PLO's relocation to Lebanon after the 1971 expulsion from Jordan added an element to Lebanon's already unstable political equation that the Lebanese state was constitutionally incapable of managing. The Palestinian armed presence in Lebanon was not a marginal irritant — by 1975, the PLO had established a territorial presence in southern Lebanon and the Palestinian camps of Beirut that constituted a genuine state-within-a-state, with military forces, taxation authority, social services, and political institutions that duplicated and often displaced Lebanese state functions. The Cairo Agreement of 1969 — negotiated under Nasser's mediation between the Lebanese government and the PLO — had formally recognised Palestinian armed operations from Lebanese territory and Palestinian self-governance in the refugee camps in exchange for nominal PLO commitment to avoid destabilising Lebanese internal politics. The agreement was the product of a Lebanese government too weak to resist the PLO's demands and an Egyptian mediator whose interest was in maintaining Palestinian military capacity rather than Lebanese state integrity. Its practical effect was to legalise the extra-territoriality of the Palestinian military presence — to acknowledge that Lebanese sovereignty did not extend to the camps and to the PLO's operational areas in the south.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 11: Lebanon's Civil War — The State That Failed
subheading: 11.2 The Palestinian Factor: The Erosion of Lebanese Sovereignty
text: The Palestinian military presence had specific consequences for Lebanon's internal politics. The Maronite communities, particularly those in the northern and eastern mountains, experienced the armed Palestinian presence as a direct military threat to Christian demographic and territorial security, and the Phalange militia — the Kataeb, founded by Pierre Gemayel — responded by expanding its own armed capacity and organising the military defence of Christian areas. The Muslim and leftist communities, particularly the Sunni parties of Beirut and Tripoli and the Druze Progressive Socialist Party under Kamal Jumblatt, experienced the Palestinian armed presence as a potential military resource in a confessional political competition that they were losing under the existing institutional arrangements. The Palestinian issue thus simultaneously raised the military stakes of the internal political contest and provided all parties with a template for the use of armed force as a political instrument.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 11: Lebanon's Civil War — The State That Failed
subheading: 11.2 The Palestinian Factor: The Erosion of Lebanese Sovereignty
text: The Israeli factor was direct and cannot be omitted. Israeli military operations in southern Lebanon — retaliations for PLO attacks on northern Israeli settlements and attacks on Israeli civilian targets abroad — had been escalating since the early 1970s. The Israeli retaliations fell primarily on Lebanese Shia villages in the south, killing civilians and destroying infrastructure in a pattern that the Lebanese state could neither prevent nor compensate. The primary political consequence was the displacement of southern Shia villagers to Beirut's southern suburbs — the Dahiyeh — where they arrived without employment, housing, or social services and without political representation proportionate to their numbers. This displacement was the material precondition for Musa al-Sadr's Amal movement and eventually for Hezbollah: an impoverished, politically marginalised, geographically concentrated Shia urban population whose grievances the existing political system was structurally incapable of addressing.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 11: Lebanon's Civil War — The State That Failed
subheading: 11.3 The Outbreak: April 1975 and the Political Fracture Lines
text: The proximate trigger of the civil war — the Phalange attack on a bus carrying Palestinian passengers through the Ain al-Rummaneh neighbourhood of Beirut on April 13, 1975, killing approximately twenty-seven people — was the culmination of a week in which Phalange leader Pierre Gemayel had survived an assassination attempt attributed to Palestinian gunmen. The bus attack was retaliation in kind, but it ignited the accumulated political combustion of years of militia build-up, Palestinian-Lebanese friction, and communal competition that had made violence increasingly likely.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 11: Lebanon's Civil War — The State That Failed
subheading: 11.3 The Outbreak: April 1975 and the Political Fracture Lines
text: Syria's calculation in 1975–1976 was the most consequential external factor in the war's early phase and the one most consistently misrepresented in Western accounts that focus on Israeli and Palestinian roles. Hafez al-Assad's Syria had specific and clearly articulated interests in Lebanon that were not primarily ideological. Syria had never recognised Lebanese independence as fully legitimate — the Syrian nationalist tradition had always regarded Lebanon as a province of Greater Syria artificially detached by the French — and Syrian strategic doctrine treated Lebanon's political orientation as a matter of Syrian national security rather than Lebanese sovereignty. Assad's specific concern in 1975–1976 was that a Palestinian-leftist victory over the Lebanese Front would create an ungovernable Palestinian-dominated state on Syria's western flank that would draw Israel into direct military intervention, destabilising Syria's position and potentially triggering a war for which Syria was not prepared.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 11: Lebanon's Civil War — The State That Failed
subheading: 11.3 The Outbreak: April 1975 and the Political Fracture Lines
text: Syria's intervention in June 1976 — dispatching the Palestinian Liberation Army units under Syrian control, followed by Syrian army regular units, into Lebanon — was directed against the Lebanese National Movement and the Palestinian organisations that were on the verge of defeating the Maronite militias militarily. The spectacle of Syrian Ba'athist forces attacking Palestinian organisations and Lebanese leftists while being tactically aligned with the Maronite militias they had been rhetorically denouncing illustrated the degree to which state interests — Syrian strategic concerns about the post-war Lebanese order — overrode the ideological alignments that public rhetoric suggested. The Lebanese Arab Deterrent Force framework, created at the Riyadh and Cairo conferences of October 1976, provided the multilateral legitimacy for a Syrian military presence in Lebanon that Assad would maintain for the next three decades.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 11: Lebanon's Civil War — The State That Failed
subheading: 11.4 External Actors: The Economy of the Lebanese War
text: Lebanon's civil war was sustained at extraordinary intensity for fifteen years because of the continuous inflow of external financial and military support to virtually all parties, creating a war economy in which armed factions could sustain themselves regardless of their territorial control or their political support among the civilian population. Saudi Arabia's primary clients were the Maronite militias — the Phalange and its allies — financed through Palestinian-Lebanese channels and through direct payments to militia leaders whose loyalty the Saudis regarded as a bulwark against both Palestinian radicalism and leftist Arab nationalism. Saudi financial support for the Lebanese right was part of the broader Saudi strategy of financing conservative, Western-aligned political forces across the Arab world as a counterweight to the radical Arab nationalism that Nasser had represented.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 11: Lebanon's Civil War — The State That Failed
subheading: 11.4 External Actors: The Economy of the Lebanese War
text: Libya under Gaddafi funded the Palestinian organisations and the Lebanese Muslim left, primarily as an expression of Gaddafi's idiosyncratic anti-Western pan-Arabism rather than as a coherent strategic investment. Iraqi Ba'athist support — directed toward Palestinian factions hostile to the PLO mainstream and toward anti-Syrian Lebanese organisations — reflected the Ba'athist competition between Damascus and Baghdad that operated across all the arenas where their proxies competed.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 11: Lebanon's Civil War — The State That Failed
subheading: 11.4 External Actors: The Economy of the Lebanese War
text: Iran's role in the Lebanese war became significant after 1979 and is discussed in the context of the Islamic Revolution's regional consequences. The initial Iranian involvement — the supply of money to the Amal movement under Musa al-Sadr, which had connections to Iranian Islamic reformist circles through the Iranian-Lebanese Shia networks — pre-dated the revolution and established the relationship between the Iranian religious establishment and Lebanese Shia politics that the revolution would transform.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 11: Lebanon's Civil War — The State That Failed
subheading: 11.4 External Actors: The Economy of the Lebanese War
text: Israel's relationship with Lebanon was primarily defined by the PLO presence in the south and by the strategic opportunity that Lebanon's collapse created. The "Good Fence" policy, established in 1976, allowed Lebanese villagers from border areas to cross into Israel for work and medical treatment, creating an economic relationship that served Israeli intelligence purposes and that built the clientelist base for the South Lebanon Army (SLA) — a predominantly Shia and Christian militia that operated under Israeli command in a buffer zone along the border from 1978 onward.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 11: Lebanon's Civil War — The State That Failed
subheading: 11.5 Operation Litani and the South Lebanon Precedent
text: Israel's first major military intervention in Lebanon — Operation Litani in March 1978 — established a pattern of Israeli military engagement in Lebanon that would culminate in the far larger 1982 invasion. Litani's immediate trigger was the Coastal Road massacre of March 11, 1978, in which a Fatah seaborne operation landed on the Israeli coast and attacked vehicles on the Haifa-Tel Aviv highway, killing thirty-seven Israeli civilians. The Litani operation deployed approximately 25,000 Israeli troops into southern Lebanon up to the Litani River, clearing PLO forces from the area and establishing the conditions for the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) that was deployed under Security Council Resolution 425.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 11: Lebanon's Civil War — The State That Failed
subheading: 11.6 The Economic Destruction of Beirut
text: Beirut in 1975 was the financial and commercial capital of the Arab world in a sense that no other city matched. Its banking system — regulated by a Bank of Lebanon framework that maintained genuine regulatory independence and a freely convertible currency — serviced the surplus revenues of Gulf oil producers, facilitated trade financing across the Arab world, and provided the commercial infrastructure for regional investment that no other Arab city could offer. Lebanese banks held deposits from Palestinian exile communities, Gulf oil revenues, Saudi royal family diversification portfolios, and European institutional investors seeking regional exposure. The Beirut Stock Exchange, the advertising and media industries, the publishing houses and universities, and the liberal professional culture of a city that was simultaneously Arab and cosmopolitan, religious and secular, represented an economic and cultural infrastructure that had taken decades to build. The fifteen years of civil war destroyed most of it. The commercial district of central Beirut — the downtown core that had been the financial and trading centre — became a no-man's land between the militias, physically destroyed and then divided by the Green Line that separated the eastern (predominantly Christian) from the western (predominantly Muslim) halves of the city. Bank deposits migrated to Cyprus, London, and Geneva; the financial sector's physical and institutional infrastructure was dismantled; the advertising and publishing industry relocated to Paris and London. The universities continued to function sporadically but lost faculty, infrastructure, and the international students whose fees and economic activity had sustained them.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 11: Lebanon's Civil War — The State That Failed
subheading: 11.6 The Economic Destruction of Beirut
text: The aggregate economic cost is difficult to quantify precisely, but estimates of physical infrastructure destruction alone range from $10 billion to $25 billion. The human capital lost — through emigration of the educated professional class that Lebanon's university system had produced — was arguably more costly in the long run. Lebanon's diaspora grew from approximately 400,000 in 1975 to more than a million by 1990, representing a brain drain that removed precisely the skilled professionals whose contribution to economic reconstruction would have been most valuable.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 12: Sadat's Separate Peace — Camp David and Its Consequences
subheading: 12.1 Sadat's Strategic Reasoning: The Military Option Exhausted
text: By 1976–1977, Sadat had reached conclusions about Egypt's strategic situation that no previous Egyptian leader had been willing to articulate publicly and that most of his Arab counterparts regarded as a betrayal of collective Arab commitments. The conclusions were straightforward and, on their merits, defensible: Egypt could not defeat Israel militarily under any realistic scenario; the Soviet military relationship was a dependency that constrained Egyptian diplomatic options without delivering the political outcomes Egypt needed; and the Palestinian question, while morally compelling, was not Egypt's existential strategic problem in the way that Sinai recovery was. Egypt's national interests and pan-Arab solidarity had become genuinely divergent, and Sadat made the choice that Egyptian national interests required.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 12: Sadat's Separate Peace — Camp David and Its Consequences
subheading: 12.1 Sadat's Strategic Reasoning: The Military Option Exhausted
text: The economic dimension of this calculation was primary. Egypt in 1976 was approaching fiscal crisis: oil revenues were negligible compared to Gulf producers, the canal remained closed, population growth was outpacing agricultural and industrial development, and the military burden — approximately 20% of GDP — was consuming resources that the development of a population that had grown to 37 million required. The International Monetary Fund's conditions for stabilisation loans — reduction of food and fuel subsidies that kept the urban poor's real income barely above subsistence — had already produced the January 1977 "bread riots" in which demonstrations against subsidy cuts turned violent, killing approximately 79 people, and were suppressed by army deployments. Sadat's government had been forced by the riots to reverse the subsidy cuts, demonstrating that the fiscal adjustment the economy required was politically impossible within the existing strategic framework.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 12: Sadat's Separate Peace — Camp David and Its Consequences
subheading: 12.2 The Jerusalem Visit: Calculated Shock
text: Sadat's announcement on November 9, 1977, before the Egyptian National Assembly, that he was prepared to travel to Jerusalem and address the Israeli Knesset was, by the standards of Middle Eastern diplomatic practice, an act of extraordinary audacity. No Arab head of state had set foot in Israel since the state's establishment; no Arab government had publicly acknowledged the legitimacy of Israeli parliamentary institutions; and the gesture of addressing Israel's legislature implied a recognition of Israel's democratic legitimacy that the Arab refusal to negotiate directly had always withheld.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 12: Sadat's Separate Peace — Camp David and Its Consequences
subheading: 12.3 Camp David: Negotiations, Concessions, and Deliberate Ambiguity
text: Sadat's position was that a genuine Egyptian-Israeli peace required Israeli commitment to Palestinian self-determination in the West Bank and Gaza — a "comprehensive peace" framework in which Egypt's bilateral deal was embedded in a broader settlement that addressed the Palestinian question. The specific mechanism agreed in the Camp David frameworks — a five-year "transitional period" of Palestinian autonomy in the West Bank and Gaza, to be negotiated among Egypt, Israel, Jordan, and Palestinian representatives, leading to a determination of the territories' permanent status — was deliberately ambiguous about whether the endpoint of that process was Palestinian statehood. The ambiguity was functional — it was the price of agreement — but it was not symmetrical. Begin's interpretation was explicit in his public statements both during and after Camp David: Palestinian autonomy meant personal autonomy for the Arab inhabitants of the territories, not political sovereignty; Jordan would retain "some role" in the West Bank; and Israeli settlement construction would continue during the autonomy period. Sadat's stated interpretation — that autonomy was a transitional arrangement leading to Palestinian self-determination — was incompatible with Begin's. Both interpretations survived the Camp David agreements because the text was written to permit both.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 12: Sadat's Separate Peace — Camp David and Its Consequences
subheading: 12.4 The Egyptian-Israeli Peace Treaty: Terms and Provisions
text: Egypt undertook to normalise relations with Israel — to exchange ambassadors, open borders to Israeli tourists and commerce, end the economic boycott — and to ensure freedom of navigation for Israeli shipping through the Suez Canal and the Straits of Tiran. The normalisation provisions were implemented, with some friction over pace and scope, and the Egyptian-Israeli border has been the most peaceful in Israel's regional geography for the four decades since the treaty. The United States made specific financial and military commitments to both parties as inducements: annual military assistance of $1.8 billion to Israel and $1.3 billion to Egypt were institutionalised as the price of peace, creating a combined annual commitment of approximately $3 billion that has continued without interruption for more than four decades. The specific figures were negotiated as compensation — Israel for the Sinai oil fields it was surrendering, Egypt for the Soviet military assistance it was foregoing — and their persistence reflects the degree to which the Camp David peace became embedded in both countries' domestic political economies in ways that make revision politically difficult regardless of the strategic logic of the original payments.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 12: Sadat's Separate Peace — Camp David and Its Consequences
subheading: 12.5 The Arab Response: Expulsion, Boycott, and Strategic Isolation
text: The boycott's material consequences for Egypt were cushioned by the American assistance package that replaced the Arab financial transfers that stopped. Saudi Arabia, which had been providing Egypt with annual financial transfers as part of the post-1967 war support commitment, terminated those payments. American economic and military assistance more than compensated in financial terms, but the broader Arab economic relationship — Egyptian workers in Gulf states, Egyptian exports to Arab markets, Egyptian participation in Arab development funds — was disrupted in ways that imposed real costs.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 12: Sadat's Separate Peace — Camp David and Its Consequences
subheading: 12.7 Camp David's Palestinian Failure
text: The West Bank settler population, which was approximately 7,000 at the time of Camp David, had grown to approximately 28,000 by 1984 and would reach 110,000 by 1992. The physical infrastructure of settlement — roads, water systems, military installations — was being constructed on West Bank land at an accelerating rate through the 1980s, each increment making the territorial contiguity that a Palestinian state would require harder to achieve. The deliberate ambiguity of the Camp David autonomy framework gave Israeli governments the diplomatic cover to claim compliance with the letter of the Camp David commitments while systematically violating its spirit.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 12: Sadat's Separate Peace — Camp David and Its Consequences
subheading: 12.7 Camp David's Palestinian Failure
text: Sadat's assassination on October 6, 1981 — shot by Islamist soldiers within his own military during a parade marking the eighth anniversary of the October War crossing — was the final confirmation that the domestic political costs of the peace he had made were unsustainable through normal political management. His assassins were members of Egyptian Islamic Jihad, motivated by his peace with Israel, his suppression of Islamist political organising, and his personal authoritarianism. His successor, Hosni Mubarak, maintained the peace treaty as a strategic framework while maintaining the "cold peace" — correct diplomatic relations without warm normalisation — that Egyptian public opinion demanded and that Mubarak used to manage his own domestic Islamist pressure.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 13: The Islamic Revolution in Iran — A Material Analysis
subheading: 13.1 The White Revolution: What It Changed and What It Destroyed
text: The White Revolution — announced by the Shah in January 1963 in a referendum on six reform principles, expanded over subsequent years to nineteen points — was a genuine attempt at modernisation that was also a calculated political move to undercut the traditional social bases of opposition to the Pahlavi monarchy. Its principal elements were land reform, the sale of state-owned factories to the private sector, women's suffrage and eligibility for public office, nationalisation of forests, profit-sharing for workers in industry, and the Literacy Corps (the deployment of educated conscripts to rural villages for basic education). The political targeting was explicit: land reform struck at the landowning class that had supported the National Front, while simultaneously undermining the Shia clergy's extensive landholdings and the religious endowments (waqf) on which clerical economic independence had partly rested.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 13: The Islamic Revolution in Iran — A Material Analysis
subheading: 13.2 The Political Economy of Oil Revenues: Boom, Inflation, and Displacement
text: Iran's oil revenues increased from approximately $4.4 billion in 1973 to approximately $17.8 billion in 1974, a near-quadrupling that followed the October War price increases and was amplified by Iran's production volume — approximately 5.8 million barrels per day — that was far larger than any Arab Gulf producer. The Shah's response was to dramatically accelerate his development program: the Fifth Development Plan (1973–1977) was revised upward to incorporate the oil windfall, with massive increases in military procurement, industrial infrastructure, and urban construction. The Shah's personal ambition — to make Iran a major industrial and military power within a generation, the "Great Civilisation" of his rhetoric — found its material foundation in the oil revenues that could, if spent at sufficient scale and speed, compress decades of development into years. The specific problem was absorptive capacity: Iran's economy could not efficiently absorb the capital injection that the oil revenues represented. The construction sector was overwhelmed with simultaneous major projects — highways, factories, power plants, ports, military bases — that competed for scarce skilled labour, materials, and management capacity. Foreign contractors and technicians flooded into Iran to execute contracts that Iranian industry lacked the capacity to undertake, creating a visible foreign presence that combined with the general Westernisation of elite culture to produce the image — accurate in Tehran's northern suburbs, caricatured but recognisable in the popular perception — of American and European technical workers living in compounds of conspicuous affluence while Iranian workers who had left their villages for the construction sites lived in urban shantytowns without adequate services.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 13: The Islamic Revolution in Iran — A Material Analysis
subheading: 13.2 The Political Economy of Oil Revenues: Boom, Inflation, and Displacement
text: Inflation — driven by the demand surge that the oil boom investment created against the supply constraints of a limited productive capacity — accelerated rapidly from 1974 onward. Official Iranian inflation figures suggest approximately 15–20% annually in the mid-1970s; the actual experience of urban populations was likely higher, particularly for the food and housing costs that absorbed the majority of lower-income urban household budgets. The specific group most severely affected was the urban poor — migrants from rural areas who had come to Tehran and the other major cities for employment in the construction and service sectors, whose wages had risen in nominal terms but whose real purchasing power was being eroded by the inflation their employment was helping to generate.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 13: The Islamic Revolution in Iran — A Material Analysis
subheading: 13.2 The Political Economy of Oil Revenues: Boom, Inflation, and Displacement
text: The Shah's anti-profiteering campaign of 1975–1976 — in which the government, under political pressure from the visible price inflation, dispatched inspection teams to the bazaar to identify and prosecute merchants accused of price gouging — was politically catastrophic. Thousands of bazaari merchants were fined, jailed, and publicly humiliated. The campaign's economic logic was inverted: in an inflationary environment driven by monetary excess and supply bottlenecks, prosecuting merchants for raising prices to cover their own costs did not reduce inflation but did generate political mobilisation among the precise social group — the bazaari — whose financial networks and physical infrastructure (the bazaar complex, which connected directly to the mosque network) would prove essential to the revolutionary mobilisation.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 13: The Islamic Revolution in Iran — A Material Analysis
subheading: 13.3 Why SAVAK Failed
text: The Shah's secret police — SAVAK (Sazeman-e Ettelaat va Amniyat-e Keshvar, the National Intelligence and Security Organisation) — was established in 1957 with CIA and Israeli Mossad assistance and by the mid-1970s had an estimated strength of 5,000–15,000 full-time agents plus a much larger network of informers. Its methods — surveillance, arrest, torture, imprisonment — were well-documented by Amnesty International and other human rights organisations and were a persistent irritant in the American-Iranian relationship during the Carter administration's initial human rights emphasis.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 13: The Islamic Revolution in Iran — A Material Analysis
subheading: 13.3 Why SAVAK Failed
text: The mosque infrastructure — approximately 90,000 mosques in Iran by the late 1970s, served by approximately 90,000 clerics at various levels of the clerical hierarchy — was the physical network through which Khomeini's messages (distributed on cassette tapes, a technology that combined near-perfect reproducibility with near-impossible interception) reached every urban neighbourhood and rural village in Iran. The mosque was simultaneously a physical gathering point that could not be easily monitored without the political cost of visible suppression of religious observance, a financial network through which religious taxes (khums and zakat) collected independently of the state could fund political activities, and a social institution that provided the poor and newly urbanised population with community, identity, and practical assistance that the state's social services did not adequately supply. SAVAK could arrest known political figures, and it did — systematically, and with the torture that the documentation of the period records in detail. What it could not do was arrest the idea, distributed through an infrastructure too large, too socially embedded, and too religiously authoritative to suppress without political costs that would have exceeded the costs of the revolution itself.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 13: The Islamic Revolution in Iran — A Material Analysis
subheading: 13.4 Khomeini's Ideology: Velayat-e Faqih
text: Khomeini's political theory — the Guardianship of the Jurist (Velayat-e Faqih) — was not a straightforward deduction from classical Shia political theology. It was a specific and contested innovation that departed from the dominant tradition of Shia quietism in ways that Khomeini's clerical critics considered theologically unjustifiable. Classical Shia political theology had developed, during the period of the Greater Occultation (the physical absence of the Twelfth Imam since 874 CE), a tradition of clerical withdrawal from political authority. In the absence of the infallible Imam, legitimate political authority could not fully exist; the duty of the pious was to maintain religious community and await the Imam's return rather than to construct a fully legitimate political order. This tradition had produced significant Shia clerical opposition to both monarchical and republican governments throughout Iranian history — not because the clerics were apolitical but because their theology constrained them from endorsing any temporal authority as fully legitimate.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 13: The Islamic Revolution in Iran — A Material Analysis
subheading: 13.4 Khomeini's Ideology: Velayat-e Faqih
text: Khomeini's innovation was to argue that the Greater Occultation was not a reason for political withdrawal but for political engagement: in the absence of the Imam, a qualified jurist (faqih) who met specific religious criteria was obligated to assume political as well as religious authority. The faqih's guardianship extended to all the functions that the Imam would have exercised — governance, legislation, judicial authority — making the senior religious authority simultaneously the supreme political authority. This was not merely a claim for clerical influence over political decisions; it was a claim for direct clerical governance that made the faqih superior to any other governmental institution, including elected ones.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 13: The Islamic Revolution in Iran — A Material Analysis
subheading: 13.5 The Revolutionary Coalition and Khomeini's Consolidation
text: The revolution that overthrew the Shah was not made by Khomeini's clerical movement alone. It was made by a coalition whose breadth — Marxist guerrillas, Islamic socialists, liberal nationalists, the bazaar, the urban poor, and eventually the military rank and file — was the specific condition of its success and the immediate cause of the post-revolutionary power struggle that Khomeini's forces won.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 13: The Islamic Revolution in Iran — A Material Analysis
subheading: 13.5 The Revolutionary Coalition and Khomeini's Consolidation
text: The Mojahedin-e Khalq (MeK) — the Islamic Marxist guerrilla organisation that had conducted armed operations against the Shah's government and American targets since the early 1970s — was the most militarily organised element of the revolutionary left. Its ideology attempted a synthesis of Islamic identity with Marxist-Leninist political analysis that was intellectually incoherent but politically appealing to the generation of Iranian students who could not accept either the pure secularism of the Tudeh or the pure religiosity of Khomeini's movement. Its importance to the revolution was primarily military — the threat it and other guerrilla organisations represented had absorbed significant SAVAK capacity — rather than mass mobilisation.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 13: The Islamic Revolution in Iran — A Material Analysis
subheading: 13.5 The Revolutionary Coalition and Khomeini's Consolidation
text: The National Front liberals — the political heirs of Mosaddegh's constitutional nationalism — contributed Mehdi Bazargan as the first Prime Minister of the provisional government, providing the liberal constitutional veneer that made the revolution internationally presentable. Bazargan's government was almost immediately rendered irrelevant by the parallel power of the Revolutionary Council and the revolutionary committees that Khomeini's clerical network controlled.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 13: The Islamic Revolution in Iran — A Material Analysis
subheading: 13.5 The Revolutionary Coalition and Khomeini's Consolidation
text: Khomeini's consolidation of power between February 1979 and mid-1981 was methodical and brutal. The Kurdish autonomy movement was militarily suppressed. The MeK, which had initially supported Khomeini and provided military capacity against the old regime's holdouts, was expelled from the political coalition, driven underground, and eventually subjected to mass executions — approximately 3,000–4,000 MeK members and supporters were executed in 1981–1982 in response to the MeK's assassination campaign against Revolutionary Council leaders. The Tudeh Party was tolerated briefly, then arrested en masse in 1983, with leaders tortured into televised confessions and subsequently executed. Bazargan's government resigned after the American embassy seizure; the liberal nationalist political space was systematically closed.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 13: The Islamic Revolution in Iran — A Material Analysis
subheading: 13.5 The Revolutionary Coalition and Khomeini's Consolidation
text: The American embassy hostage crisis — the seizure of the embassy on November 4, 1979, by revolutionary students who held fifty-two American diplomats for 444 days — served specific domestic political purposes for Khomeini beyond its anti-American ideological content. The crisis prevented the moderate Bazargan government from developing the working relationship with Washington that its liberal political orientation would have sought; it destroyed the political careers of Iranian officials who sought negotiated release; and it radicalised the domestic political environment in ways that made the subsequent consolidation of clerical power easier to achieve. The hostage crisis was simultaneously a genuine expression of anti-American sentiment and a political instrument in an internal power struggle, and its use as the latter is essential for understanding why Khomeini permitted it to continue for 444 days after its initial political purposes had been served.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 13: The Islamic Revolution in Iran — A Material Analysis
subheading: 13.6 The Carter Administration's Response
text: Carter's human rights policy, which had led his administration to express public concern about SAVAK's methods and to reduce the unconditional character of American support for the Shah, had the unintended effect of encouraging the opposition while creating uncertainty about American backing that weakened the Shah's political resolve without deterring the revolution. The Shah's own psychological deterioration — he was suffering from cancer, which his close circle knew but which the Americans did not fully understand — produced an indecisiveness in his response to the revolutionary mobilisation that American signals of ambivalence reinforced rather than countered.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 13: The Islamic Revolution in Iran — A Material Analysis
subheading: 13.6 The Carter Administration's Response
text: The hostage crisis defined the final year of the Carter presidency and contributed to his 1980 electoral defeat in ways that are directly traceable to the failed rescue mission of April 1980 — Operation Eagle Claw — whose mechanical failures in the Iranian desert killed eight American servicemen and left their equipment abandoned at the Desert One staging site. The crisis's resolution — the Algiers Accords of January 1981, under which the hostages were released minutes after Ronald Reagan's inauguration in an arrangement that involved the unfreezing of Iranian assets — was achieved through Algerian mediation and left a legacy of deep mutual hostility between Washington and Tehran that would shape American-Iranian relations for decades.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 13: The Islamic Revolution in Iran — A Material Analysis
subheading: 13.7 Regional Consequences: The Revolutionary Export Threat
text: The Shia populations of Iraq, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province were the immediate targets of Iranian revolutionary messaging. In each case, the specific material grievances of marginalised Shia communities — political exclusion from governance structures dominated by Sunni ruling establishments, economic discrimination, cultural suppression — provided a genuine base for the Iranian message that Islamic revolution was the path to Shia political dignity. The Iranian government established the Wali al-Faqih's office for export of the revolution, funded Shia political organisations in Gulf states, and used the radio and the mosque network — the same infrastructure that had served the Iranian revolution — to reach Gulf Shia communities. The November 1979 Grand Mosque seizure in Mecca — executed by the Saudi millenarian movement led by Juhayman al-Otaybi, an event structurally unrelated to the Iranian Revolution but temporally proximate and ideologically resonant — terrified the Saudi government and led directly to the intensification of the internal Wahhabi religious establishment's political authority as a counter-mobilisation against Iranian Khomeinism. The Saudi response to the Iranian revolutionary challenge was to double down on its own Islamist credentials — more religious programming, stricter social enforcement, greater clerical authority over education — creating a dynamic in which Iranian Shia Islamism and Saudi Sunni Wahhabism competed to define the political Islam of the Muslim world.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 13: The Islamic Revolution in Iran — A Material Analysis
subheading: 13.7 Regional Consequences: The Revolutionary Export Threat
text: Iraq's Shia majority — approximately 60% of the Iraqi population — was the most acute concern for Saddam Hussein's Ba'athist government, which was simultaneously Sunni-dominated, secular in ideology, and governed through coercion of the Shia south that the revolution's rhetoric directly challenged. Saddam's decision to go to war against Iran in September 1980 — the Iran-Iraq War that is Chapter 15's subject — was substantially driven by the calculation that a revolutionary Iran weakened by internal purges and Western sanctions represented a military opportunity and that eliminating the revolutionary government before it could consolidate and export its model was a strategic necessity. The war he initiated in that calculation would consume eight years, approximately one million lives, and the economic surplus that his oil revenues had accumulated.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 14: The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan and the Islamist Mobilisation
subheading: 14.2 The April Revolution and the Afghan Communist Catastrophe
text: The Saur Revolution of April 27, 1978 — in which the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan (PDPA) overthrew the government of Mohammed Daoud Khan in a military coup — brought to power an Afghan communist party whose internal divisions, ideological rigidity, and catastrophic governance errors created the conditions that the Soviet invasion was attempting to salvage. The PDPA was divided from its founding into two factions — Khalq ("Masses") and Parcham ("Banner") — whose differences were partly ideological (Khalq was more militantly Marxist, Parcham more pragmatic and Soviet-oriented), partly ethnic (Khalq was predominantly Pashtun, Parcham more ethnically mixed), and substantially personal (the mutual hatred between Khalq leader Nur Mohammad Taraki and Parcham leader Babrak Karmal was institutionalised in the party's structure). The coup brought Khalq to power; Parcham leaders were immediately marginalised and eventually exiled as ambassadors, a standard communist method of removing internal enemies while maintaining the fiction of party unity.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 14: The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan and the Islamist Mobilisation
subheading: 14.2 The April Revolution and the Afghan Communist Catastrophe
text: Khalq's governance from April 1978 to December 1979 was an exercise in ideological maximalism that demonstrated with brutal precision why revolutionary programs imposed on societies without the social preconditions for their success produce catastrophic violence rather than transformation. The land reform — redistributing land from landlords to peasants — was implemented without provision for the credit, water rights, and market access that made Afghan agricultural land productive; peasants who received land could not farm it without the support structures the reform destroyed. The literacy campaign — requiring women to attend literacy classes alongside unrelated men — violated the specific gender segregation norms of Afghan rural society in ways that triggered rebellion among populations whose religious and cultural identity made the reform intolerable regardless of its educational merit. The abolition of the bride price and the reduction of the minimum marriage age were experienced by rural communities as an assault on the family economic arrangements that structured their social reproduction.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 14: The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan and the Islamist Mobilisation
subheading: 14.2 The April Revolution and the Afghan Communist Catastrophe
text: The resistance to Khalq's reforms was not irrational conservatism; it was the rational response of communities whose social and economic survival was organised around arrangements that the reforms were destroying without replacement. By early 1979, rebellion had spread from isolated incidents to a generalised insurgency across rural Afghanistan. The Herat uprising of March 1979 — in which Afghan army units mutinied, joined the population in attacking government officials and Soviet advisors, and were suppressed only by aerial bombardment that killed thousands of people — was the event that convinced the Soviet leadership that the PDPA government was losing control. Approximately fifty Soviet advisors were killed in Herat, some of them reportedly mutilated, which produced in Moscow the combination of alarm about the regime's viability and outrage about Soviet personnel that drove the subsequent escalation.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 14: The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan and the Islamist Mobilisation
subheading: 14.3 The Soviet Decision to Invade
text: The Soviet analysis rested on two fundamental miscalculations. The first was about Afghan society's capacity for sustained resistance: the PDPA's failures were attributed to specific personnel and tactical errors rather than to the structural incompatibility of the Soviet model with Afghan social conditions. Replacing Taraki (who had been murdered by his deputy Hafizullah Amin in September 1979) with Babrak Karmal, bringing Soviet organisational competence to bear on the governance problems, and providing the military stabilisation that the Afghan army could not deliver — these interventions were assessed as sufficient to establish a viable Soviet-aligned government. The second miscalculation was about the international and regional response: the Brezhnev Doctrine — the Soviet claim to the right to intervene militarily in socialist states under threat — was expected to produce the same acquiescence it had produced in Hungary (1956) and Czechoslovakia (1968). Afghanistan was different: it was a Muslim country, adjacent to Pakistan and Iran, accessible to supply from the Gulf, and in a regional political environment transformed by the Iranian Revolution.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 14: The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan and the Islamist Mobilisation
subheading: 14.3 The Soviet Decision to Invade
text: The specific operation — the airlifting of Soviet troops into Kabul airport, the movement of motorised rifle divisions across the Amu Darya river from Soviet Central Asia, and the simultaneous execution of Amin (killed by KGB Alpha Group operatives in his own palace on the night of December 27) — was militarily competent. The political consequences were immediately catastrophic: the UN General Assembly condemned the invasion 104 to 18; the Carter administration suspended SALT II ratification; the American-led boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics removed the diplomacy of international sport; and the Carter Doctrine — proclaiming American willingness to use military force to prevent any hostile power from gaining control of the Persian Gulf region — established a security framework that directly threatened Soviet interests in a way the Afghan invasion itself had not justified.

book: The Cold War Middle East - 1948-1991
section: Chapter 14: The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan and the Islamist Mobilisation
subheading: 14.4 The CIA-ISI-Saudi Triangle: Operation Cyclone
text: The American response to the Soviet invasion — Operation Cyclone, the CIA's covert support program for the Afghan mujahideen — was the largest covert operation in CIA history, eventually spending approximately $3 billion and matching that with equivalent Saudi contributions.
