book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 4: The Caucasus and Central Asian Conquests - Russian Imperial Expansion (1800-1881)
text: Russian motivations for Central Asian conquest were multiple. Strategic concerns about British expansion from India into Afghanistan and potential British influence in Central Asia drove the Great Game competition. Economic interests in cotton cultivation—particularly important after the American Civil War disrupted global cotton supplies—made Central Asian agricultural lands attractive. Imperial prestige and the momentum of expansion encouraged further conquests. Opportunity created by Central Asian khanates' military weakness, internal divisions, and political instability made conquest feasible.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 5: Iran Under the Qajars - Weakness and Concessions (1800-1906)
text: The doctrine of velayat-e faqih (guardianship of the jurist) potentially granted leading ulama authority to interpret religious law and judge political legitimacy. In practice, most ulama avoided direct political confrontation with the shah but reserved the right to declare policies un-Islamic and mobilize popular opposition when state actions threatened religious interests or offended religious sensibilities.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 5: Iran Under the Qajars - Weakness and Concessions (1800-1906)
text: Naser al-Din Shah's long reign (1848-1896) witnessed failed modernization attempts, growing debt and concessions, and increasing popular opposition to foreign exploitation. The young shah, who ascended the throne at age seventeen, initially relied on his capable chief minister Mirza Taqi Khan Amir Kabir, who attempted comprehensive reforms. Amir Kabir sought to reduce expenditures, rationalize administration, combat corruption, strengthen central authority over provinces, and modernize the military. His most enduring achievement was establishing the Dar al-Fonun in 1851, a European-style polytechnic college teaching military science, engineering, medicine, and other technical subjects with European instructors. The Dar al-Fonun represented Persia's most serious educational reform initiative. Students received instruction in mathematics, science, foreign languages, and technical subjects rather than traditional religious education. European instructors, primarily Austrian and French, taught using European textbooks and methods. Graduates entered state service as military officers, administrators, and technical specialists, creating a small Western-educated elite. The institution produced several hundred graduates over subsequent decades, some of whom would play important roles in later reform movements and the constitutional revolution.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 5: Iran Under the Qajars - Weakness and Concessions (1800-1906)
text: Amir Kabir's other reforms faced resistance from vested interests and were cut short by his dismissal and execution in 1851. Court factions opposed his efforts to reduce expenditures that enriched them. Provincial governors resisted centralization that would reduce their autonomy and revenues. The shah's mother, whose influence Amir Kabir tried to limit, worked against him. European powers disliked his attempts to reduce foreign influence and protect Persian industries. Within three years of implementing reforms, Amir Kabir was dismissed, exiled, and murdered on the shah's order. His death ended Persia's most promising reform effort and demonstrated the political obstacles reformers faced—entrenched interests were powerful enough to destroy reform initiatives that threatened their positions.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 5: Iran Under the Qajars - Weakness and Concessions (1800-1906)
text: Baron Julius de Reuter received the most notorious concession in 1872—a seventy-year monopoly over Persia's railways, mines, forests, and various industries, plus the right to establish a national bank. The concession was so comprehensive that Lord Curzon later described it as "the most complete and extraordinary surrender of the entire industrial resources of a kingdom into foreign hands that has probably ever been dreamed of." Russian diplomatic pressure and Persian popular opposition forced cancellation, but the episode revealed the shah's willingness to sell Persian sovereignty for immediate revenue.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 5: Iran Under the Qajars - Weakness and Concessions (1800-1906)
text: The Imperial Bank of Persia, established in 1889 as a British company, received rights to issue currency and conduct banking operations, controlling Persian monetary policy and finance. The telegraph system was built and operated by British companies, giving foreigners control over Persian communications and access to government correspondence. Mining concessions transferred mineral rights to European companies. Railway concessions, though slower to materialize than in the Ottoman Empire or Egypt, eventually gave foreign companies control over transportation infrastructure.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 5: Iran Under the Qajars - Weakness and Concessions (1800-1906)
text: The Baha'i faith, emerging from Babism in the mid-nineteenth century, faced intense persecution as heretical. Baha'is were executed, their properties confiscated, and their communities attacked. The government's treatment of religious minorities reflected both traditional Islamic law's subordination of non-Muslims and popular hostility that authorities sometimes encouraged and sometimes restrained depending on circumstances.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 5: Iran Under the Qajars - Weakness and Concessions (1800-1906)
text: Naser al-Din Shah's assassination in 1896 by a follower of Afghani symbolized growing opposition to autocracy and foreign exploitation. The shah was shot and killed at the shrine of Shah Abdol-Azim while preparing to celebrate his jubilee. The assassin's motives combined religious opposition to the shah's impiety and westernization, political opposition to autocracy, and anger at concessions to foreigners. The assassination demonstrated that opposition had radicalized beyond protests and petitions to violence against the shah himself.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 5: Iran Under the Qajars - Weakness and Concessions (1800-1906)
text: Minor protests and demonstrations in 1905-1906 escalated into sustained opposition. In December 1905, Tehran merchants and sugar dealers were bastinadoed (beaten on the soles of their feet) by the governor's order for refusing to lower prices. This sparked protest—merchants and ulama took bast (sanctuary) in mosques, demanding dismissal of the governor and reforms. The government eventually conceded, dismissing the governor, but the episode demonstrated opposition's capacity to force concessions through collective action.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 6: The Eastern Question - Great Power Competition Over Ottoman Territories (1820s-1878)
text: Greek nationalism, inspired by Enlightenment ideas about liberty and nationalism, encouraged by European philhellenism romanticizing classical Greek civilization, and motivated by grievances against Ottoman taxation and governance, produced revolutionary organizations seeking independence. The Filiki Eteria (Society of Friends), founded in 1814, recruited members across the Ottoman Empire's Greek communities and planned rebellion.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 6: The Eastern Question - Great Power Competition Over Ottoman Territories (1820s-1878)
text: The Treaty of London (July 1827) demanded Ottoman acceptance of Greek autonomy under Ottoman suzerainty. When the Sultan refused, the three powers dispatched naval squadrons to Greek waters. At the Battle of Navarino (October 1827), the combined British-French-Russian fleet destroyed the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet in Navarino Bay. The battle was technically unintended—fleet commanders exceeded instructions—but European governments accepted the accomplished fact. The naval disaster crippled Ottoman capacity to supply forces in Greece and shifted military balance decisively. Russia declared war on the Ottoman Empire in April 1828, ostensibly over Greek issues but motivated by broader territorial ambitions. Russian forces invaded the Balkans and the Caucasus, achieving significant victories. Ottoman forces, weakened by Greek campaigns and military backwardness, could not resist effectively. Russian troops advanced toward Constantinople, threatening the capital. Britain and France, alarmed by Russian gains, pressured Russia to moderate demands. The Treaty of Adrianople (September 1829) ended the war with Russia gaining territories in the Caucasus, mouth of the Danube, and commercial privileges, while Greece gained autonomy.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 6: The Eastern Question - Great Power Competition Over Ottoman Territories (1820s-1878)
text: The Lebanon crisis of 1860 demonstrated sectarian tensions the Tanzimat reforms exacerbated and European intervention patterns. Mount Lebanon's complex sectarian demography—Maronite Christians, Druze, Greek Orthodox, Sunni Muslims, Shia Muslims—had coexisted under Ottoman rule with Druze emirs dominating politically while Maronites formed the largest single community. Tanzimat reforms granting Christians greater rights and autonomy upset traditional power balances. Economic changes benefiting Maronites engaged in silk cultivation and trade while harming Druze cultivators created additional tensions. Violence erupted in 1860 with Druze-Maronite fighting in Mount Lebanon. Druze forces, better organized militarily, massacred thousands of Maronite civilians and destroyed Christian villages. The violence spread to Damascus in July 1860, where Muslim mobs attacked Christian quarters, killing thousands and destroying property. The massacres reflected sectarian hostility, economic competition, and resentment of European protection of Christians and reform policies perceived as favoring minorities.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 7: Financial Collapse and the Debt Regime (1850s-1882)
text: The 1854 loan of £3 million was arranged through British and French banks at terms that would establish patterns for subsequent borrowing. The nominal loan amount was £3 million but the government received only £2.2 million after deduction of commissions, fees, and discounting. The loan carried 6% annual interest plus 1% annual sinking fund payments for amortization. Repayment was secured on Egyptian tribute—the annual payments Egypt made to Istanbul as an Ottoman province—providing creditors with specific revenue streams. These terms—nominal amounts exceeding actual disbursements, high interest rates, fees and commissions enriching intermediaries, and designation of specific revenues for repayment—would characterize Ottoman and Egyptian borrowing for decades.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 7: Financial Collapse and the Debt Regime (1850s-1882)
text: Between 1854 and 1875, the Ottoman Empire contracted fifteen foreign loans totaling nominally over £200 million. The actual amounts received were substantially less—perhaps £140-150 million—with the difference consumed by commissions, discounts, and fees enriching European banks and intermediaries. Interest rates varied but were generally between 5-6% annually, plus sinking fund provisions for amortization. Some loans were issued at substantial discounts—bonds nominally worth £100 sold for £65-75, with the government obligated to repay the full £100 plus interest but receiving only the discounted amount. The cumulative effect was debt growing faster than the government's capacity to service it.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 7: Financial Collapse and the Debt Regime (1850s-1882)
text: The Suez Canal project, completed in 1869, was financed partly through Egyptian borrowing and government purchases of shares in the Suez Canal Company. Ismail invested enormous sums in the canal—some estimates suggest £20-30 million—far exceeding the project's value to Egypt. The canal was strategically valuable to Britain and France as a route to Asia but less obviously beneficial to Egypt, which gained transit revenues but also saw European powers acquire controlling interest in infrastructure crossing Egyptian territory. The canal's completion was celebrated with elaborate ceremonies attended by European royalty and dignitaries, celebrations that cost millions and displayed Ismail's grandiosity while demonstrating Egypt's subordination to European interests.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 7: Financial Collapse and the Debt Regime (1850s-1882)
text: Between 1863 and 1876, Egypt contracted loans totaling nominally over £100 million but received perhaps £50-60 million after deductions for commissions, discounts, and fees. Interest rates on Egyptian loans were even higher than Ottoman rates—often 7-12%—reflecting Egypt's greater credit risk and the more predatory nature of some lending. Several loans were contracted at extreme discounts—bonds issued at 60-70% of nominal value—making effective interest rates even higher than stated rates. European banking houses, particularly those of the Rothschilds and other major firms, profited enormously from arranging these loans. The terms of some Egyptian loans were scandalous even by the standards of the time. The 1864 loan nominally for £5.7 million provided Egypt with only £3.3 million after deductions, with repayment required on the full nominal amount plus 7% interest—an effective interest rate exceeding 12%. The 1866 loan, the Oppenheim loan named after the banker who arranged it, provided Egypt with about half the nominal amount while requiring repayment of the full sum plus interest. These were not commercial transactions on normal market terms but exploitation of a desperate borrower by creditors with superior information, negotiating power, and knowledge that their governments would support them if Egypt defaulted.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 7: Financial Collapse and the Debt Regime (1850s-1882)
text: In October 1875, the Ottoman government announced it could pay only half of debt service due, the remainder would be repaid later. This effective default triggered crisis. European bondholders demanded their governments intervene. Diplomatic pressure intensified. The Ottoman government attempted to negotiate with creditors, proposing consolidation of debts and reduced payments. Negotiations proceeded against the background of renewed Balkan crisis and the impending war with Russia, which would further devastate Ottoman finances. Egypt declared bankruptcy in April 1876, unable to meet debt obligations. Khedive Ismail attempted to manage the crisis by establishing the Caisse de la Dette Publique, an organization with British and French representatives authorized to collect specific Egyptian revenues and allocate them to debt servicing. This represented direct foreign control over Egyptian finances—European officials collected customs revenues, railway income, and other designated sources, deducted amounts needed for debt payments, and transferred the remainder to the Egyptian government. Egyptian sovereignty over its own revenues was effectively surrendered.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 7: Financial Collapse and the Debt Regime (1850s-1882)
text: Comparisons with other peripheral economies experiencing similar debt crises in the late nineteenth century—Latin American states, China, Siam—show common patterns. European lenders extended credit on predatory terms to governments with weak revenue bases and limited administrative capacity. Borrowing was encouraged to finance infrastructure projects that benefited European commercial interests and to purchase European manufactured goods and weapons. Debt accumulated faster than revenue-producing capacity grew. Default or inability to fully service debts triggered intervention—sometimes military, sometimes financial control, sometimes territorial concessions. The debt became a mechanism for establishing informal empire, gaining control over economies and policies without the costs of direct colonial administration.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 8: The British Occupation of Egypt (1882-1914)
text: The Urabi Revolt of 1881-1882 originated in multiple grievances among Egyptian military officers, merchants, and intellectuals against the khedival regime's subordination to European control, financial policies that enriched foreigners while burdening Egyptians, and domination of the military officer corps by Turco-Circassian elites who excluded native Egyptians from advancement. Ahmad Urabi, an Egyptian-born colonel in the army, emerged as leader of the nationalist movement that challenged both foreign domination and khedivial autocracy. The immediate trigger was military grievances. Native Egyptian officers faced discrimination in promotion and pay compared to officers of Turco-Circassian origin who dominated the higher ranks. Khedive Tewfik, who had been installed in 1879 with European support after his father Ismail's deposition, maintained the traditional system where military leadership positions were reserved for the Ottoman-Egyptian elite rather than opened to Egyptians on merit. Budget cuts imposed by European financial controllers reduced military expenditures, threatening officers' salaries and positions. In January 1881, Egyptian officers petitioned the War Minister demanding redress. When the minister dismissed their complaints, discontent intensified.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 8: The British Occupation of Egypt (1882-1914)
text: Mustafa Kamil founded the National Party in 1907, advocating for complete independence, end to British occupation, and constitutional government. Kamil was a fiery orator, effective writer, and charismatic leader who mobilized urban middle-class support through nationalist rhetoric combining appeals to Egyptian identity, Islamic solidarity, and liberal political principles. His newspaper al-Liwa served as a forum for nationalist discourse. Though Kamil died young in 1908, his movement influenced Egyptian politics for decades.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 8: The British Occupation of Egypt (1882-1914)
text: The Dinshaway Incident of 1906 crystallized nationalist resentment and demonstrated British occupation's brutality. British officers hunting pigeons near the village of Dinshaway clashed with villagers who objected to foreigners shooting their domesticated birds. Violence erupted with unclear responsibility—British accounts claimed unprovoked attack, Egyptian accounts described British arrogance and provocation. Several villagers and one British officer died. British authorities responded with exemplary brutality, staging trials that convicted dozens of villagers, executing four by hanging in the village as public spectacle, and sentencing others to flogging and imprisonment.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 8: The British Occupation of Egypt (1882-1914)
text: Educational limitations under British occupation created another nationalist grievance. Cromer's deliberate restriction of education meant literacy rates remained below 10% of the population. Secondary and higher education were severely limited, producing few Egyptian doctors, engineers, lawyers, and other professionals. The educated elite that did emerge faced blocked opportunities—top government positions were reserved for British advisors and foreign experts, professional advancement was constrained by capitulations and foreign privilege, and Egyptians in their own country were systematically subordinated to foreigners. This generated frustration among precisely the educated class most capable of organizing political opposition.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 8: The British Occupation of Egypt (1882-1914)
text: The Suez Canal, in which Britain had acquired controlling shares in 1875, remained outside Egyptian control despite being physically located in Egypt. The Suez Canal Company, nominally international but British-dominated, operated the canal, collected transit revenues, and made policy decisions without Egyptian input. Egypt received a share of revenues but far less than the canal's value justified. The canal's strategic importance to British imperial communications made British control absolute—Egypt could not affect canal operations or use it as leverage in negotiations. The canal was a prime example of how territorial presence did not ensure control when foreign economic power and political domination were comprehensive.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 9: French North Africa - Conquest and Colonial Administration (1830-1914)
text: French forces landed near Algiers in June 1830 with 37,000 troops, overwhelming the dey's defenses. Algiers capitulated within weeks. The French government, which fell to revolution in July 1830, had not planned beyond initial conquest, and subsequent governments debated whether to retain Algeria or withdraw. The decision to remain and expand conquest was driven by military momentum, prestige considerations, and lobbying by officers who saw opportunities for glory and advancement. What began as a limited punitive expedition became permanent conquest and colonization.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 9: French North Africa - Conquest and Colonial Administration (1830-1914)
text: French forces, under governors-general including Clauzel, Damrémont, Valée, and particularly Bugeaud who commanded from 1840 to 1847, pursued total war strategies to break resistance. Bugeaud's tactics—razzia raids that systematically destroyed crops, livestock, and settlements; scorched-earth policies that starved populations; collective punishment of tribes supporting resistance; and mobile columns that pursued fighters relentlessly—were explicitly designed to terrorize populations into submission. French columns burned crops before harvest, slaughtered livestock, destroyed grain stores, and killed civilians indiscriminately. Entire regions were depopulated, their populations fleeing to mountains or dying from starvation and disease.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 9: French North Africa - Conquest and Colonial Administration (1830-1914)
text: Abd al-Qadir's state collapsed in 1847 when he surrendered to French forces after being driven into Morocco and facing Moroccan withdrawal of support under French pressure. He was imprisoned briefly before being sent to exile in Damascus, where he would later save thousands of Christians during the 1860 massacres, demonstrating the irony of a leader French colonialism painted as barbaric acting more humanely than European forces who claimed civilizing mission.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 9: French North Africa - Conquest and Colonial Administration (1830-1914)
text: The land tenure transformation resembled colonization patterns elsewhere—North American indigenous land seizure, South African land appropriation, Australian Aboriginal dispossession—where European settlers used legal mechanisms, violence, and state power to transfer land from indigenous to settler ownership. The distinctive feature in Algeria was the scale—a substantial European settler population dominating politics and economy while the indigenous Muslim majority was systematically subordinated.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 9: French North Africa - Conquest and Colonial Administration (1830-1914)
text: Legal discrimination institutionalized inequality. The Code de l'indigénat (Native Code) enacted in 1881 created separate legal systems for Europeans and Muslims. Muslims were subject to arbitrary administrative punishments for offenses like disrespecting French authority, refusing labor requisitions, or unauthorized assembly, punishable by fines, imprisonment, or sequestration without trial. French authorities could imprison Muslims administratively, confiscate property, impose collective fines, and assign forced labor without judicial process. Europeans were subject to regular French law with judicial protections, presumption of innocence, and due process. Muslims could not vote, hold office above local level, or participate in governance beyond advisory councils with no real power. They faced travel restrictions, needed permits for assemblies, and were subject to surveillance. Muslims who acquired French citizenship (which required renouncing Islamic personal status law) numbered only a few thousand by 1914 despite a Muslim population in millions, demonstrating that assimilation was practically impossible rather than genuinely available.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 9: French North Africa - Conquest and Colonial Administration (1830-1914)
text: Economic exploitation concentrated wealth in European hands. Large estates (latifundia) producing wine, citrus, grain, and other export crops for French markets were owned by European settlers or companies. These estates employed Algerian agricultural workers at subsistence wages with harsh working conditions. Viticulture particularly enriched European settlers—Algeria became a major wine producer despite Islam's prohibition on alcohol, with wines exported to France or consumed by European settlers. The irony of Muslim-majority Algeria being a major wine producer under French rule illustrated colonial priorities.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 9: French North Africa - Conquest and Colonial Administration (1830-1914)
text: Cultural suppression targeted Islamic and Arab identity. Arabic language was marginalized in education and administration, with French imposed as the sole official language. Islamic institutions faced restrictions—mosques required permits, religious education was limited, waqf properties were confiscated, and religious authorities were subordinated to colonial administration. Traditional dress, particularly women's veiling, was condemned as backward while adoption of European clothing was encouraged. These policies aimed at cultural assimilation but were incompatible with legal discrimination—Muslims were told to adopt French culture but denied citizenship even when they did.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 9: French North Africa - Conquest and Colonial Administration (1830-1914)
text: Settler colonialism's distinctive features made North African decolonization particularly difficult and violent. European settlers, numbering in hundreds of thousands by the twentieth century, claimed North Africa as their homeland, resisted granting equality to Muslims, and opposed independence that would subject them to Muslim-majority rule. This created conflicts impossible to resolve peacefully when colonized populations demanded independence—settlers would not accept subordination or departure, while indigenous populations would not accept continued colonial domination. Algeria's independence war (1954-1962) would be catastrophically violent partly because settler colonialism created zero-sum conflicts where compromise was impossible.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 10: The Persian Constitutional Revolution (1905-1911)
text: The revolution began in December 1905 with protests over bread prices and the punishment of merchants. Sugar dealers were bastinadoed on the governor of Tehran's orders for refusing to lower prices—the punishment was common under traditional Persian governance but now triggered broader protest. Merchants and ulama took bast (sanctuary) in the Hazrat Shah Abd al-Azim shrine outside Tehran, a traditional form of protest where religious sanctuaries provided protection from government authority. Protesters numbered thousands and included prominent ulama and influential merchants. Their demands extended beyond the immediate issue to call for dismissal of the governor, establishment of an adalat-khana (house of justice) to ensure rule of law, and reforms limiting arbitrary government actions.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 10: The Persian Constitutional Revolution (1905-1911)
text: The slogan "Mashruteh" (constitution) was presented as compatible with "Mashru'a" (Islamic law), arguing that constitutional government could implement Islamic justice better than autocratic tyranny.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 10: The Persian Constitutional Revolution (1905-1911)
text: Article 2 of the Supplementary Fundamental Laws demonstrated this synthesis attempt and created tensions that would affect constitutional implementation. The article established a committee of senior ulama with authority to ensure Majlis legislation did not violate Islamic law. This gave religious authorities veto power over legislation, potentially subordinating parliamentary sovereignty to religious oversight. Modernists accepted Article 2 as necessary compromise to gain ulama support, while conservative ulama saw it as safeguard ensuring constitutionalism would not deviate from Islam. In practice, Article 2 was never fully implemented during the constitutional period, and debates about its proper interpretation continue in Iranian political discourse to the present.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 10: The Persian Constitutional Revolution (1905-1911)
text: Constitutional fighters (mojahedin) organized armed resistance, holding the city against royalist forces.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 10: The Persian Constitutional Revolution (1905-1911)
text: The Second Majlis sought to address fiscal problems by hiring foreign advisors who would work for Persia rather than creditor interests. Morgan Shuster, an American financial expert, was hired in 1911 as Treasurer-General with broad authority over Persian finances. Shuster attempted to rationalize revenue collection, reduce corruption, and establish fiscal independence from foreign control. But Shuster's efforts threatened Russian and British interests. Russia particularly opposed Shuster's attempts to collect taxes in northern Persia, where Russian interests benefited from Persian fiscal weakness and where Russian creditors had claims on revenues. When Shuster attempted to hire British officers to organize a Treasury Gendarmerie that would collect taxes including in the Russian sphere, Russia delivered an ultimatum demanding Shuster's dismissal and Persian acceptance of Russian oversight over foreign advisors. The Russian ultimatum, backed by military pressure including troop deployments and threats of invasion, forced capitulation. In December 1911, the Persian government dismissed Shuster and accepted Russian demands. This effectively ended the Constitutional Revolution's attempt to establish autonomous government. Foreign control over Persia was confirmed, constitutional government's capacity to implement policies was demonstrated to be contingent on foreign approval, and hopes for genuine independence were crushed.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 11: The Young Turk Revolution and Constitutional Restoration (1908-1914)
text: The Committee of Union and Progress originated in opposition movements to Abdülhamid II's autocracy that had coalesced since the 1889 formation of the Committee of Ottoman Union by military academy students. These opposition groups, operating underground in the empire and openly in European exile, included military officers frustrated by professional stagnation and political impotence, civilian intellectuals advocating constitutional government, members of ethnic and religious minorities seeking reforms, and Ottoman subjects of diverse backgrounds united by opposition to autocracy. The movement was initially pan-Ottoman, including Turks, Arabs, Armenians, Greeks, Albanians, and others who believed constitutional government and equal citizenship could preserve the empire against European intervention and nationalist separatism. The Young Turk label derived from European press references to opposition reformers, analogous to "Young Italy" and similar nationalist movements. The actual organization, the CUP, was secretive, hierarchical, and disciplined, with cells in military units, civilian bureaucracy, and provincial centers. The CUP's ideology combined constitutionalism, Ottomanism (equal citizenship regardless of religion or ethnicity), administrative centralization, and modernization. They criticized Abdülhamid's autocracy not only for moral reasons but because they believed autocratic mismanagement made the empire vulnerable to European intervention and territorial dismemberment.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 11: The Young Turk Revolution and Constitutional Restoration (1908-1914)
text: The Armenian question became an early crisis testing constitutional government. Armenians had supported the revolution, hoping constitutionalism would protect minority rights and prevent the massacres that had occurred in the 1890s. Armenian revolutionaries, particularly the Dashnaktsutiun (Armenian Revolutionary Federation), initially cooperated with the CUP. But tensions emerged over Armenian demands for autonomy or administrative reforms in eastern provinces where Armenians were minorities but constituted significant populations. The CUP, committed to centralization and fearing that autonomy would lead to separatism and European intervention, resisted Armenian demands. The April 1909 Adana massacres demonstrated constitutional government's failure to prevent communal violence. In Adana province in southern Anatolia, violence erupted between Armenians and Muslims, killing thousands—estimates range from 15,000 to 30,000 dead, mostly Armenians. The massacres' causes were complex: economic competition, tensions over constitutional changes that alarmed some Muslims who saw Christians gaining power, provocations by both communities, and possible manipulation by counter-revolutionary forces seeking to destabilize the new regime. The constitutional government's response was inadequate, with military forces arriving too late to prevent massacres and with subsequent investigations failing to assign clear responsibility or deliver justice. The Adana massacres shattered Armenian faith in Ottomanism and constitutional government's capacity to protect minorities. They demonstrated that constitutional restoration had not eliminated the sectarian tensions and violence that plagued the empire. They showed that the CUP government, despite constitutional commitments to equality, could not or would not protect Armenian populations from massacre. The failure influenced Armenian political calculations, shifting some toward seeking European protection or eventual independence rather than trusting Ottoman constitutional government.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 11: The Young Turk Revolution and Constitutional Restoration (1908-1914)
text: By 1913, a triumvirate of Enver Pasha, Talaat Pasha, and Cemal Pasha controlled the government, with parliament becoming subordinate to CUP authority.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 11: The Young Turk Revolution and Constitutional Restoration (1908-1914)
text: The Treaty of London (May 1913) ending the First Balkan War reduced Ottoman Europe to a small region around Constantinople and eastern Thrace. The empire lost Macedonia, Albania, most of Thrace, and the Aegean islands. The territorial losses were massive—approximately 83% of Ottoman Europe and 69% of European population. The empire's remaining European territory was a small bridgehead, making the Ottoman Empire effectively an Asian power.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 12: Abdülhamid II's Reign - Pan-Islamism and Autocracy (1876-1909)
text: Censorship was comprehensive and systematic. Newspapers were strictly controlled, with editors required to submit content for pre-publication approval. Publications that criticized the sultan, discussed constitutionalism, or addressed sensitive topics were closed. Books were censored, with imported works inspected for subversive content. Even words could be prohibited—"constitution," "liberty," "revolution," and similar terms were banned from publication. The censorship extended to absurd extremes: references to the deposition of rulers in historical texts were removed, plays depicting regicide were banned, and even chemical formulas using elements with suggestive names were censored.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 12: Abdülhamid II's Reign - Pan-Islamism and Autocracy (1876-1909)
text: The Hamidian regiments' role in the Armenian massacres of 1894-1896 demonstrated the dark side of this policy. When Armenian revolutionary organizations emerged demanding reforms or autonomy, and when isolated incidents of Armenian violence against officials occurred, Abdülhamid authorized massive retaliation. The Hamidian regiments participated in massacres alongside regular Ottoman forces and Muslim civilians, killing an estimated 100,000-300,000 Armenians across eastern Anatolia in 1894-1896. The violence was systematic, targeting Armenian communities regardless of their actual involvement in revolutionary activities, destroying churches and schools, and forcing conversions to Islam.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 13: Arab Provinces - Autonomy, Nationalism, and Ottoman Control (1800-1914)
text: The Wahhabi-Saudi challenge to Ottoman authority was ideological as well as political. Wahhabism condemned Ottoman religious practices as innovations and idolatry, rejected the caliphate's spiritual authority, and viewed Ottoman rule as illegitimate. This religious opposition was more fundamental than the political autonomy other Arab regions sought—it denied Ottoman religious legitimacy entirely. The Ottoman response combined military campaigns when possible, support for Saudi rivals, and rhetoric denouncing Wahhabism as heresy.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 13: Arab Provinces - Autonomy, Nationalism, and Ottoman Control (1800-1914)
text: The Arab cultural renaissance (Nahda) of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries represented the intellectual and cultural ferment that would contribute to Arab nationalist movements. The Nahda began in Egypt and Syria/Lebanon, driven by interactions between Arab intellectuals and European culture, translation movements making European texts available in Arabic, growth of Arabic-language journalism, establishment of modern schools teaching both traditional Islamic subjects and modern European knowledge, and debates about modernization, identity, and the Arab future.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 13: Arab Provinces - Autonomy, Nationalism, and Ottoman Control (1800-1914)
text: Arab secret societies formed in the early twentieth century, advocating for Arab independence or autonomy. Al-Fatat (The Young Arab Society) founded in Paris in 1911, and al-Ahd (The Covenant) formed by Arab officers in the Ottoman military, represented this shift. These societies remained small, their memberships limited to educated elites, and Arab populations generally remained loyal to the Ottoman Empire. But the societies established organizational frameworks and ideological positions that would become important when World War I created opportunities for Arab revolt.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 13: Arab Provinces - Autonomy, Nationalism, and Ottoman Control (1800-1914)
text: The Arab Revolt of 1916-1918, launched by Sharif Hussein of Mecca with British support, was the culmination of these developments. Hussein, promised British support for Arab independence and concerned about Ottoman policies threatening his position, declared revolt in June 1916. Arab forces, supported by British gold, weapons, and advisors (including T. E. Lawrence), fought against Ottoman forces in Arabia and Syria. The revolt's military significance was limited—it tied down some Ottoman forces and disrupted communications—but its political significance was immense, demonstrating Arab nationalism's maturation from intellectual discourse to armed rebellion.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 14: Petroleum - The Emerging Strategic Resource (1900-1914)
text: The first significant petroleum industry developed in the United States in the 1860s following the 1859 Drake well in Pennsylvania. The industry initially focused on kerosene for lighting, replacing whale oil and providing illumination before electric lighting became widespread. Russian oil fields in Baku on the Caspian Sea developed in the 1870s and 1880s, controlled by Russian and European capital including the Nobel and Rothschild families. By 1900, these were the world's two major oil-producing regions, with smaller production in Romania, Burma, and the Dutch East Indies.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 14: Petroleum - The Emerging Strategic Resource (1900-1914)
text: The Middle East's entry into petroleum production began in Persia. William Knox D'Arcy, a British speculator who had made a fortune in Australian gold mining, negotiated a concession with the Qajar government in 1901 for oil exploration and exploitation rights covering most of Persia. The D'Arcy concession terms were extraordinarily favorable to the concessionaire and unfavorable to Persia—D'Arcy received exclusive rights for sixty years over 480,000 square miles (excluding the five northern provinces where Russia claimed influence), paid only £20,000 upfront plus £20,000 in shares, and committed to paying Persia only 16% of net profits, a percentage that could be manipulated through accounting. The concession granted D'Arcy control over resources he would extract, exempted his operations from taxes, and provided minimal benefit to Persia beyond the modest payments specified.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 14: Petroleum - The Emerging Strategic Resource (1900-1914)
text: D'Arcy's exploration efforts faced difficulties. Initial drilling in southwest Persia found oil shows but not commercial quantities. The venture consumed enormous capital without producing revenues. By 1908, D'Arcy was nearly bankrupt and the British Admiralty, which had become interested in Persian oil as potential fuel for the Royal Navy, arranged for Burmah Oil Company to take over the concession. In May 1908, at Masjid-i-Suleiman in southwestern Persia near the Iraqi border, drilling struck oil in quantities that were clearly commercial—the first major oil discovery in the Middle East.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 14: Petroleum - The Emerging Strategic Resource (1900-1914)
text: The concession agreements' terms systematically favored foreign companies and disadvantaged producing countries. Concessions typically covered vast territories, granted exclusive rights for decades (often sixty to seventy-five years), provided companies with extensive legal and tax immunities, required minimal payments to governments, calculated royalties as percentages of profits rather than production allowing accounting manipulation, and gave companies control over production levels and investment decisions. Governments received some revenue but had no control over resources extracted from their territories and no capacity to develop petroleum industries themselves. The Anglo-Persian Oil Company's operations in Persia exemplified colonial patterns. The company employed British managers and technical staff, who received high salaries and lived in segregated compounds with amenities unavailable to Iranian workers. Iranian workers performed manual labor at low wages in difficult and dangerous conditions. The refinery at Abadan became one of the world's largest, but it was an enclave of British control on Iranian territory with minimal integration into the Iranian economy. Profits flowed to British shareholders and the British government, which received tax revenues and military fuel supplies. Persia received modest royalty payments that were small fractions of the oil's value.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 15: Zionism and Early Jewish Settlement in Palestine (1880-1914)
text: Palestine in 1880 was an Ottoman province, administratively divided between the Damascus vilayet (northern regions including Galilee) and the independent sanjak of Jerusalem (central and southern regions). The population was predominantly Arab—approximately 400,000-500,000 people, mostly Sunni Muslim with significant Christian minorities (perhaps 10-15% of the population) and a small Jewish community of perhaps 25,000, primarily concentrated in Jerusalem, Hebron, Tiberias, and Safed. These traditional Jewish communities (the "Old Yishuv") were religious, non-nationalist, living from charity collected from diaspora Jews, and generally maintaining peaceful relations with Muslim and Christian neighbors.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 15: Zionism and Early Jewish Settlement in Palestine (1880-1914)
text: The First Aliyah (1882-1903) brought approximately 25,000-35,000 Jews to Palestine, primarily from Russia and Romania fleeing pogroms, economic hardship, and discrimination. These immigrants were motivated by Hibbat Zion (Love of Zion) ideology, which advocated Jewish return to Palestine and agricultural settlement as solutions to antisemitism and Jewish vulnerability in Europe. Unlike the Old Yishuv's religious communities, First Aliyah immigrants were largely secular or moderately religious, nationalist, and committed to physical labor and agricultural colonization.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 15: Zionism and Early Jewish Settlement in Palestine (1880-1914)
text: Agricultural colonies were established with support from Baron Edmond de Rothschild, a French Jewish philanthropist who provided substantial financial backing. Colonies like Rishon LeZion, Zikhron Ya'akov, and Rosh Pinna were founded on land purchased from Arab owners, with colonists attempting to farm despite limited agricultural experience and difficult environmental conditions. Initial failures were common—crops failed, colonists fell ill from malaria, financial losses accumulated. Rothschild's continued support, including hiring expert managers and providing ongoing subsidies, kept colonies viable but also created dependency.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 15: Zionism and Early Jewish Settlement in Palestine (1880-1914)
text: Theodor Herzl and political Zionism emerged in the 1890s, transforming Zionism from a small-scale settlement movement into a political program seeking international diplomatic support for Jewish statehood. Herzl, an assimilated Viennese Jewish journalist, was radicalized by the Dreyfus Affair in France, concluding that antisemitism was ineradicable and that Jews required their own state. His 1896 pamphlet "Der Judenstaat" (The Jewish State) articulated political Zionism's core arguments: Jews were a nation requiring national sovereignty, antisemitism made Jewish existence in Europe untenable, and a Jewish state would solve both the "Jewish problem" for Europeans and Jewish insecurity.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 15: Zionism and Early Jewish Settlement in Palestine (1880-1914)
text: The Second Aliyah (1904-1914) brought approximately 35,000-40,000 Jews to Palestine, primarily from the Russian Empire following the failed 1905 revolution and continued pogroms. Second Aliyah immigrants were more ideologically committed than First Aliyah colonists, influenced by socialist, Labor Zionist, and revolutionary ideologies developed in the Russian Jewish intelligentsia. Figures like David Ben-Gurion, who would become Israel's first prime minister, arrived during this wave.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 15: Zionism and Early Jewish Settlement in Palestine (1880-1914)
text: Labor Zionism synthesized Jewish nationalism with socialist ideology, arguing that Jewish national redemption required not just statehood but social transformation through physical labor, particularly agricultural work. The ideology romanticized manual labor as morally superior to commercial and intellectual pursuits historically associated with diaspora Jewish life. Labor Zionists promoted "conquest of labor" (Kibbush Ha'avodah)—insisting that Jews perform labor in settlements rather than hiring Arabs. This policy aimed to create a self-sufficient Jewish working class but also systematically excluded Arabs from employment in Jewish economic sectors.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 15: Zionism and Early Jewish Settlement in Palestine (1880-1914)
text: Land purchases were central to Zionist colonization strategy. The Jewish National Fund (Keren Kayemeth LeYisrael), established in 1901, collected donations from Jews worldwide to purchase land that would be held permanently for Jewish settlement. Land purchased by the JNF became inalienable Jewish property that could never be sold to non-Jews. The principle was creating irreversible Jewish territorial control through permanent alienation from Arab ownership.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 15: Zionism and Early Jewish Settlement in Palestine (1880-1914)
text: Ottoman policies toward Zionism were restrictive in principle but inconsistent in enforcement. Abdülhamid II and subsequent Ottoman governments prohibited large-scale Jewish immigration and restricted land purchases in Palestine, viewing Zionism as a nationalist threat similar to Armenian, Greek, and Arab nationalisms that endangered territorial integrity. Regulations limited Jewish immigrants' length of stay, restricted land purchases to Ottoman subjects, and required permits for residency in Palestine.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 15: Zionism and Early Jewish Settlement in Palestine (1880-1914)
text: The demographics of Palestine by 1914 showed significant Jewish population growth but Arab numerical dominance. Jewish population had grown from approximately 25,000 in 1880 to perhaps 85,000 by 1914—a more than threefold increase. But Arab population had also grown, from approximately 450,000 to approximately 650,000, meaning Jews remained roughly 12% of total population. The Jewish community was concentrated in certain areas—Jerusalem, Jaffa, and agricultural colonies—but had not achieved majority status in any significant region.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 15: Zionism and Early Jewish Settlement in Palestine (1880-1914)
text: Weizmann cultivated relationships with British political figures, particularly those who would form wartime governments. His advocacy emphasized Zionism's compatibility with British imperial interests, arguing that a Jewish Palestine would be pro-British, that Jewish scientific and organizational capabilities would develop Palestine's resources, and that Zionist success would demonstrate British beneficence. These arguments would influence the 1917 Balfour Declaration, though in 1914 that outcome was not predictable.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 15: Zionism and Early Jewish Settlement in Palestine (1880-1914)
text: The relationship between Zionism and existing Middle Eastern Jewish communities was complex and often tense. Mizrahi and Sephardi Jews living in the Ottoman Empire, Persia, and Arab countries had experienced centuries of coexistence with Muslim and Christian neighbors, operating within dhimmi status structures but generally maintaining communal autonomy. These communities generally did not support Zionism, viewing it as European Jewish phenomenon disconnected from their experiences and potentially dangerous to their relationships with Muslim authorities and populations. The European Ashkenazi Zionists who dominated the movement often regarded Middle Eastern Jews with condescension, seeing them as backward and needing Europeanization. This cultural chauvinism reflected broader European orientalism and created tensions that would persist after Israeli statehood when Mizrahi Jews immigrated and faced discrimination from Ashkenazi-dominated Israeli institutions.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 16: Religious Reform and Revival Movements
text: The Salafiyya movement emerged in late nineteenth century as a distinct current of Islamic modernist thought, though its intellectual roots extended back to earlier reformers. The term "Salafi" referred to the pious ancestors (al-salaf al-salih), the first generations of Muslims whose practice adherents sought to emulate. Unlike Wahhabis, Salafis generally operated within urban intellectual contexts, wrote extensively for print publications, and engaged seriously with European thought while maintaining Islamic authenticity. Muhammad Abduh (1849-1905), Grand Mufti of Egypt from 1899, exemplified this approach. Trained at Al-Azhar but influenced by his teacher Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, Abduh argued that Islam properly understood aligned with reason and modern science. He advocated reformed interpretation (ijtihad) rather than blind adherence to medieval jurisprudence (taqlid), called for educational modernization, and insisted Islam could accommodate constitutional government and technological progress. Abduh's legal opinions (fatwas) addressed modern issues—permissibility of interest in postal savings, Muslims eating meat slaughtered by Christians, wearing European hats—with pragmatic flexibility that scandalized conservatives while appealing to emerging educated classes.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 16: Religious Reform and Revival Movements
text: Abduh's student Rashid Rida (1865-1935) pushed Salafi thought in more conservative directions through his influential journal al-Manar (The Lighthouse), published from Cairo beginning in 1898. Rida shared Abduh's rejection of blind tradition but grew increasingly hostile to Western cultural influence and increasingly sympathetic to Wahhabi-style scripturalism. His writings emphasized Islamic solidarity against colonial domination, the caliphate as necessary political institution, and the need to purify Islamic practice of innovations. Al-Manar reached readers throughout the Muslim world, making Cairo a center of Islamic intellectual debate and spreading Salafi ideas to Southeast Asia, India, and North Africa. The journal addressed practical questions—how should Muslims respond to European law codes, what forms of government does Islam permit, how to reform educational curricula—with responses grounded in Quranic exegesis and Prophetic tradition (hadith). Rida's growing conservatism reflected broader patterns as initial enthusiasm for European political models dimmed with the reality of colonial domination. His thought would influence twentieth-century Islamic movements that combined scriptural literalism with political activism.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 16: Religious Reform and Revival Movements
text: The Ahmadiyya movement, founded in India by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad (1835-1908), represented a more radical break with Islamic orthodoxy, one that most Muslims rejected as heretical. Ahmad claimed prophetic status (or at minimum divine inspiration) and apocalyptic significance, presenting himself as the promised Messiah and Mahdi. His followers established active missionary efforts, publishing literature in multiple languages and sending preachers to Europe, Africa, and Southeast Asia. The Ahmadiyya reached Middle Eastern populations primarily through published materials and convert communities rather than local movements. Orthodox Muslim scholars, both traditionalist and modernist, united in condemning Ahmad's prophetic claims as contradicting Islam's fundamental doctrine of Muhammad's finality (khatm al-nubuwwa). The controversy forced Islamic authorities to define boundaries of acceptable belief more explicitly, producing declarations that Ahmadis stood outside Islam. Yet the movement's missionary success—its willingness to engage Western audiences, produce apologetic literature, and organize systematically—influenced Muslim approaches to religious outreach and highlighted tensions between universalist aspirations and doctrinal boundaries.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 16: Religious Reform and Revival Movements
text: The Baha'i faith emerged from Iranian Shi'ism in the mid-nineteenth century, beginning with the Babi movement led by the Bab (Sayyid Ali Muhammad Shirazi, 1819-1850), who claimed to be the gateway (bab) to the Hidden Imam and later implied divine status. The movement spread rapidly among some Iranians during the 1840s, attracting urban artisans, merchants, and discontented clergy with its millenarian message and promise of social reform. Qajar authorities, orthodox clergy, and the Russian government (fearing social upheaval in Caucasian provinces) cooperated in violent suppression. The Bab was executed in 1850, and thousands of his followers died in persecutions. From Babi remnants emerged the Baha'i faith, led by Baha'ullah (Mirza Husayn Ali Nuri, 1817-1892), who proclaimed himself the promised one foretold by the Bab. Exiled by Iranian authorities, Baha'ullah eventually settled in Ottoman Palestine (Acre) under house arrest, where he developed Baha'i theology emphasizing universal peace, religious unity, and progressive revelation.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 16: Religious Reform and Revival Movements
text: Baha'i teachings represented radical departure from Islamic orthodoxy, claiming that divine revelation continued beyond Muhammad, that all religions shared essential truth, and that humanity approached an age of global unity requiring abandonment of particularist identities. Both Sunni and Shi'a authorities condemned Baha'is as apostates, subject to death under Islamic law. Iranian Baha'is faced periodic persecutions, property confiscation, and social ostracism throughout the period and beyond. The movement spread beyond Iran to Ottoman territories, India, and eventually Europe and America through missionary activity and published literature. Its universalist theology appealed to some modernizing intellectuals seeking alternatives to both traditional religion and secular materialism, though adherents remained a small minority facing severe repression. The Baha'i experience highlighted the limits of tolerance for religious innovation in societies where religious identity remained legally and socially fundamental.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 17: Infrastructure, Technology, and Economic Transformation
text: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869 after ten years of construction by the Suez Canal Company led by Ferdinand de Lesseps, fundamentally altered global maritime geography and Egyptian political economy. The 101-mile canal connecting Mediterranean and Red Sea eliminated the need to sail around Africa, reducing London-to-Bombay journey time from three months to three weeks. This transformation made Egypt the pivot of British imperial strategy, as the canal became essential to maintaining communications with India. The canal's construction had cost Egyptian labor and treasure disproportionately—forced labor (corvée) requisitioned from Egyptian peasants dug most of the canal, with tens of thousands dying from disease, exhaustion, and accidents. Ismail's government provided 44% of construction capital while receiving only minority shareholding, and the canal agreement granted the company extensive land concessions and transit fees that enriched European investors while burdening Egypt's budget. Financial crisis forced Ismail to sell Egypt's shares to the British government in 1875 for £4 million, far below their value, eliminating Egyptian ownership of the strategic asset running through its territory.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 17: Infrastructure, Technology, and Economic Transformation
text: Credit relationships transformed alongside agricultural production. Peasants growing cash crops needed credit to purchase seed, tools, and food until harvest, then repay loans from crop sales. Moneylenders—often grain merchants, local notables, or wealthy peasants—provided credit at exorbitant interest rates, sometimes exceeding 50% annually. Debt trapped peasant households in cycles of borrowing, as bad harvests or low prices left them unable to repay, forcing new loans at even worse terms. Creditors often preferred indebted peasants to foreclosed land, since debt peonage provided both labor and land use rights without management obligations. Islamic law's prohibition of interest (riba) was circumvented through various legal fictions—advance purchase of crops at below-market prices, rental arrangements disguising interest, partnership structures where lender shared harvest—that maintained the substance while avoiding the form of interest transactions. European banks entering the region offered lower rates but demanded collateral and documentation peasants could not provide, limiting their clientele to wealthy urban borrowers.

book: The Long 19th Century- Reforms & Imperialism
section: Chapter 18: Intellectual Currents and Political Thought
text: The Arabic cultural renaissance (Nahda) of the nineteenth century began with literary revival—renewed attention to classical Arabic poetry, grammar, and lexicography—driven partly by European Orientalist scholarship and Christian Arab educators. Syrian Christian intellectuals like Butrus al-Bustani (1819-1883) played disproportionate roles, establishing Arabic-language journals, dictionaries, and educational institutions. Bustani founded the Majallat al-Jinan in 1870, promoting modern Arabic prose and scientific knowledge. His vision combined Ottoman loyalty, Arabic cultural pride, and secular nationalism transcending religious divisions. Other Christian Arabs, educated in mission schools, found in Arab identity an alternative to both Islamic solidarity (which excluded them) and Ottoman loyalty (which subordinated Arabic to Turkish). Their promotion of Arabic language and literature provided cultural foundations for later nationalist politics.

text: By 1914 the OPDA was collecting approximately one-third of all Ottoman state revenues. The empire was servicing a debt of approximately £161 million (roughly $800 million at 1914 exchange rates), the accumulated product of European loans taken to finance wars the empire had largely lost: the Crimean War (1853–1856), the Russo-Turkish War (1877–1878), and the Italian-Turkish War (1911–1912). Interest payments consumed a portion of state revenue that left minimal fiscal space for military modernisation, infrastructure investment, or social administration.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The Ottoman navy had two partially modern battleships on order from British shipyards — the Sultan Osman I and the Reşadiye — paid for in part by public subscription in a nationalist fundraising campaign. They were requisitioned by the British Admiralty in August 1914, as Britain entered the war and could not permit modern capital ships to go to a potentially hostile power. The seizure enraged Ottoman public opinion and contributed materially to the alignment decision — a point whose significance must not be underestimated. The British action was legally defensible but strategically myopic; it handed CUP leadership a propaganda tool of considerable value.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The Goeben was a German battlecruiser of the Moltke class, commissioned in 1912 — among the most powerful warships in the Mediterranean. The Breslau was a light cruiser accompanying her. Together they constituted a German naval detachment operating in the Mediterranean under Admiral Wilhelm Souchon, tasked with disrupting French troop transports from North Africa at the outbreak of war. On August 3–4, 1914, as Britain entered the war and the Mediterranean became a war zone, Souchon was in a precarious position. His ships needed coaling; he was surrounded by superior Entente naval forces; and his orders were ambiguous. Souchon received new orders: proceed to Constantinople. The Goeben had a boiler problem that reduced her speed — she trailed coal dust like a flag — but she was still faster than anything the British had in pursuit range. The British pursuit, under Admiral Ernest Troubridge, was a study in misapplied caution that would subsequently result in a court martial. Troubridge had a squadron of armoured cruisers that outgunned the Breslau but were individually inferior to the Goeben. His orders specified avoiding action with a "superior force." Troubridge interpreted the Goeben alone as a "superior force" and broke off pursuit — a decision that the subsequent court martial condemned as an "error in judgment" (he was acquitted, but not exonerated). The Goeben and Breslau passed through the Aegean and anchored at the entrance to the Dardanelles on August 10.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The Ottoman government was now presented with an extraordinary opportunity and an extraordinary dilemma. The two German warships requested permission to enter the Dardanelles. Under international law, a neutral state could admit belligerent warships for a maximum of 24 hours, after which they must be interned or expelled. Enver Pasha, operating in advance of the Cabinet, gave permission for entry. The Entente powers demanded the ships be interned. The Ottoman government announced that it had "purchased" the Goeben and Breslau from Germany — renaming them Yavuz Sultan Selim and Midilli — and that the German crews were Ottoman naval personnel who had simply changed uniform. Admiral Souchon was appointed commander of the Ottoman fleet. This transparent legal fiction satisfied no one, but it accomplished what Enver needed: the warships were inside the Straits, beyond Entente reach, providing the Ottoman navy with a genuine capital ship capability it had not previously possessed, and committing the empire more deeply than any paper treaty to the German cause. If the empire subsequently returned to neutrality, the ships would have to be surrendered — a political impossibility given how publicly their "purchase" had been celebrated.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: Cemal's approach to Arab nationalism was surveillance, co-optation, and exemplary punishment. He had access, through the capture of French consular documents in Damascus in 1915, to the correspondence of Arab secret societies — the al-Fatāt (Young Arab Society) and al-'Ahd (The Covenant, an officers' organisation) — with French diplomatic personnel in Syria. These documents provided the pretext for the mass arrests, military trials, and executions of August 1915 and May 1916 that eliminated much of the educated Arab nationalist leadership in Syria.

text: The Najd — the central plateau of the peninsula — was controlled by Abdul Aziz ibn Saud (Ibn Saud), leader of the Al Saud family and the Wahhabi religious movement that had been its ideological partner since the eighteenth century. Ibn Saud had reconquered Riyadh from the Al Rashid dynasty (Ottoman clients) in 1902, and by 1914 he controlled most of central Arabia through a combination of military force, tribal alliance, and Wahhabi religious authority. The Ikhwan — the militarised brotherhood of Wahhabi converts, settled in agricultural communes (hijar) and trained as shock troops — was his principal military instrument. Britain had recognised Ibn Saud's independent authority in the Treaty of Darin (December 1915) and was paying him an annual subsidy of £5,000 (later increased substantially).

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The Siege of Kut (December 1915 – April 1916) was 147 days of slow strangulation. Three relief attempts — at Sheikh Sa'ad, the Wadi, and Dujaila — failed to break through the Ottoman defensive lines south of Kut, each at heavy cost. Townshend's garrison — 13,000 British and Indian troops — was reduced by hunger, disease, and casualties. When surrender came on April 29, 1916, it was the largest British military surrender since the American Revolutionary War. Of the 13,000 prisoners, approximately 4,000 died in Ottoman captivity from starvation, disease, and deliberate brutality on the march to prisoner of war camps in Anatolia — a death rate that constitutes a serious war crime.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: Hussein bin Ali, Sharif of Mecca and Emir of the Hejaz, was in 1914 simultaneously a client of the Ottoman state and a potential rebel against it. The CUP had appointed him Sharif in 1908 — preferring him to other candidates as manageable — and had subsequently come to regret the appointment as his independence became apparent. Hussein had resisted CUP attempts to extend direct Ottoman administration into the Hejaz and had refused several orders from Constantinople that would have compromised his local authority. His political calculation in 1914 was genuinely complex. He was nearly sixty years old. He had four sons — Faisal, Abdullah, Ali, and Zaid — whose futures depended on what he built. He had spent nearly fifteen years in Constantinople as an effectively captive guest of Abdülhamid's court and understood Ottoman palace politics with the clarity of long observation. He saw the war as an opportunity: the same kind of opportunity that ambitious subordinates of weakened empires had seized throughout Islamic history to establish independent dynasties.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: British financial support was essential and immediate: £200,000 per month, paid in gold sovereigns, channelled through the Arab Bureau in Cairo and distributed to Hussein and his sons. This subsidy was the material foundation of the revolt's continuation. Without it — without the gold to pay tribal warriors who fought for wages as well as ideology — the revolt would have collapsed within weeks. The Arab Revolt of 1916–1918 was, from the British perspective, a subsidised military auxiliary operation. From Hussein's perspective it was the founding act of an Arab kingdom. The gap between these two understandings would prove politically fatal after the war.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: Britain's relationship with Ibn Saud was managed from the Gulf side — the India Office and the Political Resident at Bushire, rather than the Cairo Arab Bureau that managed the Hussein relationship. The two British bureaucracies had different views of which Arab leader was more valuable: Cairo backed Hussein; the India Office backed Ibn Saud. The conflict between these two bureaucratic preferences mirrored the ultimate political conflict between the two Arab leaders.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The operation — the Battle of Sarıkamış (December 1914 – January 1915) — was an Anatolian version of Napoleon's Russian campaign in miniature. The Third Army advanced into the Caucasian mountains in December, in snow and temperatures reaching -30°C, with inadequate clothing, inadequate food, and a logistical system that had not been designed for winter mountain warfare. The Russian defenders — better supplied, better clothed, and defending prepared positions — held their ground and then counterattacked. The Ottoman Tenth Corps was encircled and destroyed at Sarıkamış. The Third Army's casualties were approximately 90,000 men — the majority killed not by Russian bullets but by cold, hunger, and disease. Of the approximately 150,000 men Enver had committed to the offensive, fewer than a quarter survived as effective soldiers. Enver returned to Constantinople. He did not announce the scale of the disaster publicly. He did not resign. He drew conclusions. The conclusions he drew were about the Armenian population of eastern Anatolia.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The deportation and massacre were implemented through overlapping mechanisms. The Regular army and gendarmerie conducted the roundup and initial deportation marches. The Special Organisation (Teşkilât-ı Mahsusa), operating under CUP party orders, organised the killing squads — drawn substantially from criminals released from Ottoman prisons for this purpose — that intercepted the deportation columns. Kurdish tribal irregulars (Hamidiye, now reorganised as tribal militias) attacked the columns in the mountains and participated in the killing of men, and the seizure of women and children. The telegraph network allowed the coordination of operations across thousands of miles; the documented telegrams from Talat Pasha's Interior Ministry to provincial governors specifying that the deportations were to be conducted with finality — that the Armenians were not to survive them — are among the most direct documentary evidence of state-organised genocide available for any historical event.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The pre-war Armenian population of the Ottoman Empire is estimated at 1.5 to 2 million. Post-war estimates of the dead range from 600,000 (Turkish nationalist scholarship, arguing that many deaths resulted from wartime famine and disease rather than organised killing) to 1.5 million (Armenian scholarship and the higher end of Western academic estimates). The scholarly consensus in Western academic historiography places the death toll at approximately 800,000 to 1.2 million — roughly half to two-thirds of the pre-war Armenian population. The survivors who escaped massacre were primarily those who fled to Russian-controlled territory, those hidden by Kurdish and Arab families, and those in communities (like Istanbul and Smyrna) where the European diplomatic presence made wholesale massacre politically risky.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The Armenian genocide had direct consequences for the Arab Middle East. The Syrian desert — Deir ez-Zor, the Euphrates valley, the Syrian hinterland — received hundreds of thousands of Armenian survivors as refugees in 1915–1916. These communities, settling in Aleppo, Damascus, Homs, and smaller Syrian towns, became permanent elements of Syrian society. The Syrian and Lebanese Armenian communities of today are the descendants of genocide survivors.

text: The British internal record does not support the British public position. A 1939 Foreign Office memorandum, written after examination of the original Arabic text and correspondence, concluded that "on a strict reading of the Arabic text" Palestine was not, in fact, excluded by the October 24 letter. The Foreign Office recommended against publishing this conclusion; it was suppressed and became publicly available only through archival research decades later. The 1939 government's public position — that Palestine had been excluded — was not, by its own internal assessment, defensible on the textual evidence.

The Foreign Office recommended against publishing this conclusion; it was suppressed and became publicly available only through archival research decades later. What is clear from the overall correspondence is that McMahon was operating under instructions to commit to as little as possible while committing enough to move Hussein toward the revolt. The deliberate ambiguity was not accidental; it was the product of a diplomatic process conducted in bad faith by a party that had already committed to a different disposition of Palestine in the Sykes-Picot negotiations that were occurring simultaneously. McMahon was promising Hussein something about Palestine while Sykes and Picot were designing Palestine's international administration — and none of the parties knew what the others were doing.
