book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: Hussein, who could not have known about Sykes-Picot (the agreement was kept secret), accepted the McMahon correspondence as a British commitment to an Arab state that included Palestine. The British, who knew about Sykes-Picot, knew they had made a commitment they could not honour. The Arab "betrayal" narrative that has structured Arab-British relations and the Palestinian question ever since has its roots in this specific transaction: a promise made in writing, by a British official with the authority to make it, that the British government subsequently redefined as never having been made.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The status of Palestine under Sykes-Picot was neither British nor French but international — a status that the Balfour Declaration of 1917 would implicitly contest and that the British mandate would effectively override.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: On November 23, 1917 — three weeks after the Bolshevik seizure of power in Petrograd — the new Soviet government published the secret treaties of the Tsarist regime, including the Sykes-Picot Agreement. The Soviet action was a deliberate ideological embarrassment directed at the capitalist Entente powers, and it succeeded beyond expectation. The Arab world learned that Britain had promised Hussein an Arab state while simultaneously negotiating its partition with France. The Ottoman government — which had intercepted various Allied communications and had partial knowledge of the agreement already — immediately communicated its contents to Sharif Hussein, hoping to detach him from the British alliance. Hussein confronted the British, who offered a series of explanations that were not fully satisfactory but were sufficient to keep the revolt intact: the agreement was a wartime contingency, not a final settlement; the ultimate disposition of Arab territories would be determined at the peace conference in consultation with Arab representatives; the Sykes-Picot arrangement did not preclude Arab independence in the areas where Arab governance was envisaged.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: Chaim Weizmann was a Russian-born biochemist at the University of Manchester who had become the principal political organiser of British Zionism. He combined scientific distinction — his development of a fermentation process for producing acetone from maize, essential for manufacturing the smokeless powder used in naval artillery, earned him direct access to Lloyd George and Balfour at the critical junctures of the war — with the political intelligence of a career diplomat and the emotional intensity of a man who had grown up in the Russian Pale of Settlement and understood the insecurity of Jewish existence in Europe with the authority of personal experience. Weizmann's lobbying for a British declaration of support for Zionism began seriously in 1916 and intensified through 1917. He worked on multiple tracks simultaneously: direct access to Lloyd George, Balfour, and other Cabinet members; coordination with American Zionist leaders (particularly Louis Brandeis, Associate Justice of the Supreme Court and a close advisor to President Wilson) to maximise American political pressure; intelligence on German Zionist overtures that could be used to suggest Britain was at risk of losing Jewish opinion to Germany; and the systematic development of the argument that British support for Zionism was compatible with, and indeed required by, British strategic interests.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The most consequential objection came from Edwin Montagu, Secretary of State for India and the only Jewish member of the Cabinet. Montagu opposed the Declaration on the grounds that it was antisemitic in structure: by designating Palestine as the national home of the Jewish people, it implied that Jews in Britain, France, and elsewhere were in some sense aliens in their countries of citizenship whose true homeland was elsewhere. Montagu argued that he was "not a Zionist" and that the Declaration would damage the position of assimilated Jews in Europe by undermining their claim to full citizenship of the countries they lived in. His objection carried significant weight; it was not dismissed but incorporated into the drafting process.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The contradiction at the heart of the Declaration — that it promised to be simultaneously for a Jewish national home and against anything that would prejudice Arab civil rights, in a territory where the practical realisation of the first commitment required the demographic and political transformation of the existing majority — was not an oversight. It was the recognition that the Declaration was making incompatible promises and that the incompatibility would have to be managed in the future by whoever administered the territory. That administrator, as of December 1917, was the British army.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: George Antonius's The Arab Awakening (1938) was the first systematic academic argument that Britain had betrayed the Arabs: that the McMahon correspondence constituted a genuine commitment to an Arab state including Palestine, that Sykes-Picot violated this commitment, and that the Balfour Declaration compounded the violation by introducing a third claimant without Arab consent. Antonius, a Palestinian Arab Christian educated in Britain and employed by the Mandate government, wrote with the controlled anger of a man who had seen the consequences of British policy from the inside.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: Other colonial conflicts produced displacement, resistance, and violence. Palestine produced something structurally different: a conflict in which both sides had genuine legal and historical arguments, both sides had been promised something by the same external power, and neither side's claim could be fully honoured without violating the other's. That

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: Religion in this period was a mobilising framework that amplified material grievances rather than a primary cause of political action. The promise architecture of 1915–1917 was made and unmade by states pursuing material interests; it was resisted and accepted by peoples pursuing material survival. The religious dimensions of the Palestine conflict — the contest over the holy places, the invocation of divine right by both sides — were genuine and had real political consequences. They were not, however, the root causes. Those lay in the demographics, the economics, and the administrative decisions that the mandate system would produce.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The three men most responsible for the Ottoman war — Enver, Talat, and Cemal Pasha — fled Constantinople on a German submarine on November 2, 1918, three days after the armistice. Talat was assassinated in Berlin in 1921 by an Armenian survivor. Enver died fighting the Bolsheviks in Central Asia in 1922, still pursuing his Pan-Turanist fantasy. Cemal was assassinated in Tiflis in 1922 by Armenian avengers of the genocide. The Turkish courts-martial of 1919–1920 tried and convicted the triumvirate in absentia for the crimes of the war, including the Armenian deportations — the only official Ottoman-Turkish acknowledgment of legal responsibility for the genocide, subsequently disavowed by the Kemalist government that succeeded the Ottoman state.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The legal argument Britain subsequently deployed — that the armistice required Ottoman withdrawal to positions held before certain specified operations, and that these operations had moved the armistice line northward — was technically strained. The practical argument was transparent: Mosul was known to sit atop what might be substantial petroleum deposits. The Turkish Petroleum Company's 1914 concession, which gave a British-controlled consortium rights over the Mosul and Baghdad vilayets, would be worth nothing if Mosul became Turkish territory at the peace settlement. Possession, in 1918 as in most of history, was nine-tenths of negotiation.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The most significant event of Faisal's Paris sojourn was not his presentation to the Supreme Council but his meeting with Chaim Weizmann, which produced the Faisal-Weizmann Agreement of January 3, 1919. This document — signed before the conference opened — contained Faisal's apparent acceptance of large-scale Jewish immigration to Palestine and of the Balfour Declaration's goals, in exchange for a commitment to Arab independence in the broader region. Faisal added a handwritten marginal note in Arabic that made the agreement conditional on the full implementation of the Arab independence he had been promised — a condition that the subsequent history made impossible to fulfil.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The King-Crane Commission is significant not for what it achieved — nothing — but for what its suppression reveals about the character of the peace settlement. The principal Allied powers had decided the outcome before the investigation of Arab preferences was complete, and they were not prepared to allow those preferences to alter the outcome. Self-determination, in the Paris Peace Conference's application to the Arab Middle East, was a principle invoked in the rhetoric of the settlement and systematically violated in its substance.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points, announced in January 1918, had included Point Twelve: "The Turkish portions of the present Ottoman Empire should be assured a secure sovereignty, but the other nationalities which are now under Turkish rule should be assured an undoubted security of life and an absolutely unmolested opportunity of autonomous development." This was a reasonable description of the principle that would govern the peace settlement — but its application was constrained by several factors that Wilson did not fully control.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: France had argued at San Remo that since the Mosul vilayet fell within the original Zone A of Sykes-Picot — French sphere of influence — France was entitled to a share of any Mosul oil revenues under British administration. The compromise reached was a French share of 25% of Mosul oil revenues for 25 years — a financial concession that bought French acceptance of British control of Mosul. This arrangement was the direct predecessor of the Turkish Petroleum Company's reorganisation into the Iraq Petroleum Company (IPC) in 1929 and the Red Line Agreement of 1928 that governed Middle Eastern oil production for two decades.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: While the San Remo powers were settling the fate of Syria from the Italian Riviera, the political situation in Damascus was moving in a direction that the San Remo decisions would almost immediately reverse. A Syrian General Congress — convened in March 1920 with delegates from Syria, Palestine, and Lebanon — declared the independence of a United Arab Kingdom of Greater Syria on March 8, 1920, with Faisal as King. A companion declaration proclaimed Abdullah (Faisal's brother) as King of Iraq. These declarations were the Arab population's response to the evidence — now substantial and documented — that the Paris Peace Conference intended to impose mandatory rule without consulting them. The Congress explicitly invoked Wilson's Fourteen Points and the principle of self-determination. It rejected the Sykes-Picot framework, rejected the French mandate for Syria, and rejected the Balfour Declaration's application to Palestine. The declarations had no military force behind them. Faisal's government in Damascus controlled a modest military establishment consisting primarily of veterans of the Arab Revolt, the former Ottoman Arab officers who had defected to the Arab cause, and small units that had been training under British supervision. This force was not capable of resisting the French army that was being positioned in Lebanon for exactly the operation that the Syrian independence declaration was designed to forestall.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: In May 1919 Kemal was sent by the Istanbul government to Samsun on the Black Sea coast as an inspector-general — ostensibly to supervise the disarmament of Ottoman forces in Anatolia as required by the armistice terms. His actual purpose, which he pursued from the moment of his arrival, was to organise resistance. He made contact with surviving Ottoman military commanders throughout Anatolia, established communication networks, and convened the Congresses of Erzurum (July 1919) and Sivas (September 1919) at which the principles of the national resistance were formally articulated: the integrity of Anatolia and eastern Thrace, the rejection of partition, and the demand for a peace settlement based on the armistice lines — not the Sèvres dismemberment. The Ankara government that Kemal established — the Grand National Assembly, convened in April 1920 — was a rival government to the Sultan's administration in Constantinople. The Sultan's government signed the Treaty of Sèvres; the Ankara government repudiated it. The legal question of which government represented the Ottoman state — the sultan who had signed the armistice and the peace treaty, or the nationalist assembly that rejected both — was ultimately resolved by military force.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The Greek occupation of Smyrna was conducted with substantial violence against the Turkish population — an atrocity documented in the Allied High Commission's reports, which attributed the killings primarily to Greek Evzone troops and Greek irregular militia. These killings, reported in the Turkish press and spread by word of mouth through Anatolia, were the emotional catalyst that transformed Kemal's military organisation into a genuine mass movement. The Greek occupation of Smyrna became the symbol of what Sèvres meant in practice for ordinary Anatolian Turks. The military campaign that followed — 1920 to 1922 — went through several phases. The Greek army advanced deep into Anatolia, reaching and briefly holding Eskişehir and Afyonkarahisar. The Ankara government's forces — reorganised, re-equipped with French and Italian military support (both powers having withdrawn from Lloyd George's pro-Greek policy), and commanded by Kemal with the operational skill he had demonstrated throughout the war — counter-attacked in August 1922 with the Great Offensive (Büyük Taarruz). The Greek military collapse was rapid and complete. Within weeks, the Greek army's front had broken, its retreat had become a rout, and Greek and Armenian civilian populations in western Anatolia were fleeing toward the coast. The Greek military and civilian catastrophe — the Asia Minor Disaster (Μικρασιατική Καταστροφή) — ended the Greek presence in Anatolia that had existed for three thousand years.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: On September 9–13, 1922, as Turkish forces entered Smyrna, a fire destroyed most of the city's Christian (Greek and Armenian) quarters. Approximately 100,000 people were killed or drowned attempting to reach Allied ships in the harbour. The Allied naval squadron — British, American, French, Italian — observed the fire and the massacre from their ships and initially declined to rescue the civilian population, citing neutrality. The American consul George Horton and a small number of Allied naval officers eventually organised rescue operations against orders, saving several hundred thousand lives. The question of who started the fire has been contested since 1922. Turkish official history attributed it to Greek and Armenian arsonists; Greek and Armenian accounts attributed it to Turkish soldiers or arsonists. The physical evidence — the fire began in the Armenian quarter, spread rapidly to the Greek quarter, and spared the Turkish and Jewish quarters — and the eyewitness testimony of Allied officers present in the city are more consistent with Turkish military responsibility, though the documentary evidence for a direct military order to burn the city has never been found.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: Article 1 of the separate Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations, concluded simultaneously with Lausanne, provided for the compulsory exchange of Greek Orthodox Christians in Turkey and Muslims in Greece, regardless of their actual language or ethnic identification. Approximately 1.2 million Greek Orthodox Christians from Anatolia and approximately 400,000 Muslims from Greece were exchanged. The exchange was "compulsory" — people who had lived in their communities for generations, who might speak Turkish rather than Greek or Greek rather than Turkish, were classified by religion and relocated regardless of their wishes. It was the largest forced population transfer in history to that point.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The Class A mandate's explicit independence commitment created a genuine legal obligation that the mandatory powers consistently sought to minimise. The mandate charters — drafted by the Permanent Mandates Commission of the League of Nations — specified that the mandatory power must report annually to the Commission on the administration of the territory, must not exploit the territory for commercial advantage beyond the terms of the mandate charter, and must work actively toward the conditions that would permit the recognition of independence.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The Commission's functioning revealed the structural contradiction at the heart of the mandate system. The mandatory powers were simultaneously the administering authorities being overseen and the members of the League Council that appointed the Commission and received its reports. There was no independent enforcement mechanism because the powers that would have enforced compliance against mandatory violations were the mandatory powers themselves. The Commission was, in practice, a forum for public discussion and reputational management rather than a genuine accountability mechanism.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: In Palestine, the mandate's economics were unusual because the Zionist Organisation's financial apparatus — primarily the Jewish National Fund and the Palestine Foundation Fund (Keren Hayesod) — operated as a parallel capital import mechanism independent of the British administration. Jewish immigrants brought capital from Europe; the Keren Hayesod raised funds from Jewish diaspora communities worldwide; the JNF accumulated land through purchase. The result was a Palestinian Jewish economic sector that was capital-rich by the standards of the surrounding economy, technologically advancing, and largely self-financing. This economic dynamism was not produced by British policy — it was produced by the Zionist movement's own institutional investment — but it was enabled by British administration and by the security that British mandate rule provided.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The reorganised Turkish Petroleum Company, renamed the Iraq Petroleum Company (IPC) in 1929, reached the Red Line Agreement in the same year. This agreement — negotiated at Ostend by representatives of the major international oil companies — established that none of the signatories would develop oil independently within a zone defined by a red line on a map, encompassing most of the former Ottoman Empire's Asian territories. The zone included the Arabian Peninsula (except Kuwait), Iraq, Syria, Turkey, and Palestine. The agreement was a cartel arrangement that allocated development rights and prevented competitive bidding for concessions within the red line area.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: In Syria and Lebanon, the mission civilisatrice translated into direct administrative control — French officers governing at the provincial level, French-educated local elites serving as junior partners in administration, French as the language of official communication and higher education — combined with a deliberate strategy of exploiting communal divisions to prevent the emergence of a unified Arab nationalist movement capable of challenging French control. This strategy is accurately described in the French documents of the period as politique des minorités — minority policy — and it worked through the systematic elevation of minority communities to positions of administrative and military privilege.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The creation of Greater Lebanon — the state whose borders the French drew in 1920 to ensure a Christian majority — was done in partnership with Maronite political leadership, which actively lobbied for the incorporation of Muslim-majority coastal and inland areas on the grounds that a smaller Lebanon would not be economically viable.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The political legacy of the politique des minorités in Syria extended well beyond the French mandate period. The over-representation of Alawites in the Syrian military — the product of a French administrative decision taken in the 1920s — was the structural precondition for the Ba'athist coup of 1963 and for the Assad family's subsequent dominance of Syrian politics. Hafez al-Assad, the son of an Alawite family from the Jabal Ansariya, rose through a military disproportionately Alawite in composition because the French had made it so. The French politique des minorités of the 1920s produced the Syrian political structure of the late twentieth century. This is not post-hoc causation; it is the documented consequence of a deliberate administrative strategy.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: In Iraq, the Assyrian massacre of 1933 — in which the Iraqi army and Kurdish tribes killed approximately 3,000 Assyrian Christians after independence — was directly connected to the Assyrians' role as the primary personnel of the British-organised Iraq Levies. In Syria, the identification of Alawites and Druze with French colonial administration produced hostility from the Sunni Arab nationalist movement that shaped inter-communal politics for decades. In Lebanon, the Maronite community's partnership with France produced the National Pact and confessional system of 1943 — an arrangement that reflected the specific demographic and political position created by French mandatory engineering, and that eventually produced the civil war of 1975–1990.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: Herbert Samuel's appointment as the first High Commissioner for Palestine was the most striking illustration of the British government's determination to proceed as if the dual obligation were manageable. Samuel was a Liberal politician who had been a senior Cabinet minister during the war; he was also a committed Zionist who had written a memorandum in early 1915 proposing the establishment of a Jewish state in Palestine as a British protectorate — a document that had contributed directly to the political climate in which the Balfour Declaration was eventually issued. Appointing a Zionist Jew as the first administrator of a territory where Arabs were the 89% majority — in a mandate explicitly charged with balancing Jewish and Arab interests — was either remarkable political obtuseness or a deliberate signal that the "balance" being promised was not to be taken at face value. It was, in any case, a decision that made the task Samuel was given structurally more difficult than it needed to be.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: Samuel's approach was genuinely honest within its constraints. He attempted even-handedness. He appointed Arab as well as Jewish officials to the administration. He regulated Jewish immigration at levels that were lower than the Zionist Organisation wanted. He established the principle — maintained by his successors — that the administration would make land available for Jewish settlement only where it could be demonstrated that the land was not already being cultivated by Arab peasants. He created an Advisory Council with both Arab and Jewish representation. But each of these even-handed measures encountered a structural problem: the Arab majority refused to participate in institutions that gave them no power to prevent the immigration and settlement the mandate charter required, and the Zionist Organisation lobbied consistently against restrictions on immigration that it regarded as violations of the mandate's Jewish national home commitment. Samuel was administering a mandate designed to be impossible and discovering, in real time, that it was impossible. His most consequential decision was the appointment of Haj Amin al-Husseini as Grand Mufti of Jerusalem and president of the Supreme Muslim Council in 1921. The appointment requires explanation because it was genuinely paradoxical: Samuel was appointing the man who had been involved in inciting the 1920 Nebi Musa riots, had fled prosecution, and had been convicted in absentia, to the most powerful Islamic religious position in Palestine, after granting him an amnesty.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The Third Aliyah's institutional legacy was the kibbutz movement's expansion and the consolidation of the Histadrut (General Organisation of Hebrew Workers), founded in 1920. The Histadrut was not merely a trade union; it was a comprehensive socialist institution that operated its own employment exchange, its own health fund (Kupat Holim), its own construction company (Solel Boneh), its own agricultural marketing cooperative, and its own bank. It was the institutional spine of the Jewish labour economy in Palestine — the mechanism through which the labour Zionist ideology of Avodah Ivrit (Hebrew labour) was implemented, and the mechanism through which Arab workers were systematically excluded from the Jewish economic sector. The Avodah Ivrit principle — that Jewish agricultural settlements and urban enterprises should employ only Jewish labour — was an explicitly ideological programme with clear economic consequences. Its justification was nationalist: building a Jewish working class required that Jewish workers not be undercut by cheaper Arab labour; the Jewish national economy could only develop if it was economically self-contained. Its effect was a complete ethnic segmentation of the Palestine labour market: Jewish enterprises employing Jewish workers at wages calibrated to a Jewish standard of living, Arab enterprises employing Arab workers at wages calibrated to the lower Arab rural standard. The two labour markets barely intersected.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The Fourth Aliyah transformed Tel Aviv. The city — founded in 1909 as a garden suburb north of Jaffa on land purchased by the Ahuzat Bayit society — grew from approximately 15,000 in 1922 to approximately 46,000 by 1929. It developed a commercial economy, a newspaper culture, a theatre, a nascent industrial sector, and an urban character that was distinctly Jewish and distinctly modern: European bourgeois culture transplanted to the eastern Mediterranean, self-consciously building a "Hebrew city" in deliberate contrast to the Arab urban environment of Jaffa immediately adjacent. The physical and cultural proximity of Jaffa and Tel Aviv — two cities on the same coastal strip, economically interdependent in some respects, socially segregated in most — was a spatial metaphor for the entire mandate's condition.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: By 1929 the Jewish community of Palestine — the Yishuv — had built an institutional infrastructure of remarkable comprehensiveness. The Jewish Agency, formally established by the 1922 mandate charter as the "appropriate Jewish agency" for advising the mandatory administration on matters concerning the Jewish national home, served as the Yishuv's representative body with semi-governmental status: it negotiated with the British, managed immigration, allocated land, and coordinated development investment. The Jewish National Fund owned approximately 100,000 dunams of land (100 square kilometres) and was steadily acquiring more through systematic purchase. The Haganah — formed in 1920 as a clandestine self-defence organisation after the 1920 riots — was developing from a local watchman network into a structured paramilitary organisation with regional commands and a nascent officer corps. The Hebrew education system — from primary schools through the Hebrew University on Mount Scopus (opened 1925) — was creating a Hebrew-language cultural environment entirely independent of the British administration and the Arab majority.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The British mandatory administration's Land Ordinance of 1921 inherited and modified the Ottoman mawat definition — a modification that substantially increased the amount of land classifiable as mawat and therefore available for registration. The Zionist land-purchasing organisations benefited from this classification change because it made previously uncultivated or lightly cultivated land available for purchase or registration in ways that displaced Arab usage without requiring the purchase of formally titled property.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The critical mechanism of displacement involved miri land

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The critical mechanism of displacement involved miri land and absentee landlords. Large portions of the fertile Palestinian coastal plain — the Sharon, the Jezreel Valley, portions of the Galilee — had been accumulated during the late Ottoman period by large landowning families, many of them resident in Beirut, Damascus, or other Syrian cities rather than in Palestine itself. The Sursock family of Beirut, for example, owned approximately 80,000 dunams (80 square kilometres) of the Jezreel Valley — acquired from an Ottoman government desperate to monetise its landholdings. The families who lived on and cultivated this land were Arab tenant farmers (fellahin) with heritable usage rights but without formal registered title. The Jewish National Fund and related purchasing organisations systematically identified and purchased these absentee landlord holdings. The legal transaction was straightforward: the Sursocks or their equivalents, residing in Beirut or Damascus, had formal title and could sell. The sale price was paid to the absentee owner. The tenant farmers were given notice and, in many cases, a small compensation payment — but they had no legal standing to prevent the sale and no alternative land to farm. The sale of the Sursock holdings in the Jezreel Valley in 1920–1925 displaced approximately 8,000 Arab tenant farmers — the largest single displacement event of the early mandate period — and transformed the valley into the heartland of the kibbutz movement.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: By 1936 — the year the Arab Revolt began — Jewish land ownership in Palestine amounted to approximately 1,200,000 dunams (1,200 square kilometres), or approximately 5.5% of the total land area. This figure understates the economic significance of the Jewish land holdings because the acquired land was disproportionately located in the most fertile zones: the coastal plain, the Jezreel Valley, and the lower Galilee. The Arab population retained ownership of the central highlands, the Hebron hills, and the Galilee mountains — hillier, less productive, more dependent on subsistence agriculture.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: Both positions contain truth. The purchases were legally conducted; no land was seized by force in the pre-1948 period. The displacement of tenant farmers was real and was not prevented by the voluntary character of the absentee owners' sales. The combination of these two facts — legal process producing material dispossession — was the core of the land conflict and the core of why a formula for "safeguarding Arab civil rights" while "facilitating Jewish settlement" could not be found: because the legal settlement mechanism that facilitated Jewish settlement simultaneously produced Arab dispossession that could not be described as anything other than a prejudice to Arab position.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The Ghor Mudawwara land case (1921–1925) established the legal precedent that tenant farmers displaced by sales to the JNF were entitled only to compensation from the seller, not to block the sale. The Land Transfer Ordinance of 1920 and its subsequent modifications attempted to define the protection owed to sitting tenants, but the definitions were narrow enough that large-scale transfers could be conducted with only minimal tenant protections. It was not until the 1940 Land Transfer Regulations — issued in conjunction with the 1939 White Paper — that the British made a serious attempt to restrict Jewish land purchase. The 1940 regulations divided Palestine into three zones: Zone A (approximately 63% of the country, including the hill districts with the heaviest Arab population density) where Jewish land purchase was essentially prohibited; Zone B (approximately 32%) where purchase required government permission; and Zone C (approximately 5%, primarily in the coastal plain) where purchase was unrestricted. These regulations came twenty years too late to alter the basic geographic pattern of Jewish settlement already established, and they were in any case widely evaded through legal mechanisms and nominal Arab intermediaries.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: Palestinian Arab politics in the early mandate period was structured by the same notable family system that had governed Arab political life throughout the Ottoman period. The large landowning and religious families of Jerusalem, Nablus, Jaffa, Haifa, and Hebron — the Husseinis, the Nashashibis, the Khalidis, the Abd al-Hadis, the Jayyusis — were the political actors who negotiated with the British, organised petitions, convened congresses, and claimed to speak for the Palestinian Arab population. This system had two fundamental weaknesses that would prove fatal in the confrontation with a much better-organised Zionist movement. The first weakness was the Husseini-Nashashibi rivalry. The two most politically significant Jerusalem families were in active political competition that often overrode the common interest of opposition to the Jewish national home. The Husseinis, led by Haj Amin, occupied the religious position (Grand Mufti, Supreme Muslim Council) and took the maximalist nationalist position: total rejection of the Balfour Declaration, total opposition to Jewish immigration, total refusal of any institutional cooperation with the mandate that might imply acceptance of its premises. The Nashashibis, led by Raghib al-Nashashibi (Mayor of Jerusalem for most of the 1920s), were more pragmatic: they too opposed Zionism and the mandate's Jewish national home commitment, but they were willing to cooperate with British administrative bodies as a means of maintaining influence, and they were occasionally willing to consider compromise proposals that the Husseinis rejected.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The second weakness was the class structure of Palestinian Arab politics. The notable families who dominated political life had an equivocal relationship to the rural majority they claimed to represent. Some of them — including members of the Husseini family — had sold land to the JNF. The fellahin being displaced from the Jezreel Valley and the coastal plain had interests that were not identical to those of the Beirut-resident landlords who had sold the land, the Jerusalem lawyers who drew up the petitions, or the newspaper editors who wrote the nationalist manifestos. The notable leadership of the Palestinian Arab movement consistently failed to build cross-class political institutions — organisations that would have given the peasant majority a structural role in political decision-making rather than a mobilisable mass to be invoked in manifestos.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: Its fundamental structural problem was that the British mandatory administration refused to grant it official recognition. The British dealt with individual notable families — the Husseinis through the Supreme Muslim Council, the Nashashibis through the Jerusalem mayoralty — but they did not recognise the Arab Executive as a representative body with legitimate political authority, for the same reason that they did not constitute a legislative council: to do so would have created an institution through which the Arab majority could formally challenge the Jewish national home commitment through democratic procedures, and the mandate charter's dual obligation could not survive democratic Arab majority rule. The Arab Executive's refusal,

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The Nebi Musa festival was an annual Muslim pilgrimage from Jerusalem to a site near Jericho traditionally associated with the tomb of Moses. The timing of the festival — during the Christian Holy Week and the Jewish Passover period, when Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims of all three faiths — had historically been managed by the Ottoman authorities as a potential flashpoint. In April 1920, with the Ottoman administration gone, the British military government in place, and tensions running high over the Balfour Declaration and the confirmation at San Remo that the British mandate was imminent, the festival became the occasion for the mandate period's first major communal violence. On April 4, inflamed speeches by Haj Amin al-Husseini and other nationalist leaders at the festival's departure ceremony produced a mob that attacked the Jewish quarter of the Old City. The riots lasted four days; 5 Jews and 4 Arabs were killed, 216 Jews and 23 Arabs were wounded. The British military response was delayed and inadequate; the Jewish community's self-defence organisation (Haganah precursor) that intervened was subsequently arrested by the British military for illegal weapons possession, while the Arab instigators — including Haj Amin — were not prosecuted until after the riots.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: The 1921 riots were triggered by a different cause and had a different character. On May 1, two Jewish political groups — a communist May Day demonstration and a competing Histadrut-organised march — clashed with each other in Jaffa. Arab onlookers, interpreting the fighting as a Jewish attack on Arabs, began attacking Jewish pedestrians and then Jewish properties. The violence spread from Jaffa to the surrounding Jewish agricultural settlements and lasted five days. The death toll was substantially higher than 1920: 47 Jews and 48 Arabs were killed. The Arab casualties included men killed by British forces attempting to restore order — a demographic detail that has been selectively cited by both sides in subsequent historical debates. The riots spread to Petah Tikva, Hadera, and other Jewish settlements; the attacks on the settlements had the character of organised raids rather than spontaneous communal violence, involving Arab villagers from surrounding areas who attacked with agricultural tools and firearms. The Haycraft Commission, appointed to investigate the riots, found that the immediate cause was the May Day procession clash but that the underlying cause was Arab political anxiety about Zionist immigration and the Balfour Declaration. The commission's report was the first official British document to state explicitly that Arab violence against Jews in Palestine was primarily politically motivated — a response to the perceived threat of demographic and political displacement — rather than the product of religious hostility or criminal opportunism.

book: World War I to 1948 Mandates & Partition
text: On the national home: the White Paper insisted that the Balfour Declaration did not imply "the imposition of a Jewish nationality upon the inhabitants of Palestine as a whole, or the disappearance or the subordination of the Arabic population, language or customs." The national home was to be developed "in Palestine, not the whole of Palestine." This formulation left the core ambiguity intact — what did "a national home" mean if not a state, and how would Jewish and Arab political interests be balanced when their fundamental conflict was not about language or customs but about sovereignty and land? On Transjordan: Churchill's White Paper confirmed that Transjordan — the territory east of the Jordan River — was excluded from the terms of the Jewish national home commitment. This exclusion, formalized in a British memorandum of September 1922 and approved by the League of Nations, significantly reduced the geographic scope of the Balfour Declaration: the "Palestine" within which a Jewish national home would be established was defined as west of the Jordan only.
